text:
Healthcare professionals worry that many emerging machine‑learning tools are being built more for revenue generation than for patient benefit. In the United States this tension is especially pronounced, reflecting a long‑standing ethical conflict between the goal of advancing care and the drive to increase profits. One concrete worry is that the proprietary algorithms behind these systems could be programmed—or unintentionally tuned—to recommend extra diagnostic tests or medications that are unnecessary, allowing the owners of the technology to profit from the resulting prescriptions or procedures.  

Despite these concerns, the same technology holds promise as an additional instrument for clinicians, potentially helping them to identify illnesses, select appropriate treatments, and design recovery plans. Realizing that promise, however, hinges on successfully identifying and reducing the profit‑driven biases that may be embedded in the algorithms. Only by addressing these conflicts can machine learning become a truly valuable aid in health‑care decision‑making.

Machine learning has been used as a strategy to update the evidence related to a systematic review and increased reviewer burden related to the growth of biomedical literature. While it has improved with training sets, it has not yet developed sufficiently to reduce the workload burden without limiting the necessary sensitivity for the findings research itself.

A program can make biased decisions even if the data does not explicitly mention a problematic feature (such as "race" or "gender"). The feature will correlate with other features (like "address", "shopping history" or "first name"), and the program will make the same decisions based on these features as it would on "race" or "gender". Moritz Hardt said "the most robust fact in this research area is that fairness through blindness doesn't work."

Atomic, molecular, and optical physics (AMO) is the study of matter—matter and light—matter interactions on the scale of single atoms and molecules. The three areas are grouped together because of their interrelationships, the similarity of methods used, and the commonality of their relevant energy scales. All three areas include both classical, semi-classical and quantum treatments; they can treat their subject from a microscopic view (in contrast to a macroscopic view).

The opinions amongst experts and industry insiders are mixed, with sizeable fractions both concerned and unconcerned by risk from eventual superintelligent AI. Personalities such as Stephen Hawking, Bill Gates, and Elon Musk, as well as AI pioneers such as Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, Demis Hassabis, and Sam Altman, have expressed concerns about existential risk from AI.

Sub‑symbolic methods, such as those based on large statistical models, are prone to the same kinds of opaque errors that human intuition can produce—algorithmic bias being a prime example. Because these systems often cannot reveal the reasoning behind a particular output, they drift away from the goal of explainable artificial intelligence. Scholars like Noam Chomsky contend that, in order to reach truly general intelligence, research on symbolic AI must continue; symbolic approaches keep the decision process transparent and therefore remain essential. To reconcile the strengths and weaknesses of both traditions, a new discipline called neuro‑symbolic artificial intelligence is emerging, seeking to merge statistical learning with the clarity of symbolic reasoning.

Supervised learning works by constructing a mathematical representation of a data set that includes both the predictor variables and the corresponding target values.  The collection of such paired examples is called the training set.  Every entry in this set supplies one or more input measurements together with the correct answer, often referred to as the supervisory signal.  In the model, each entry is encoded as a numeric array—sometimes termed a feature vector—while the entire training set can be viewed as a matrix whose rows are these vectors.

The algorithm repeatedly adjusts the model’s parameters so as to minimize a chosen objective (or loss) function.  Through this iterative optimisation it discovers a mapping from inputs to outputs that can be applied to data it has never seen before.  When the resulting function yields correct predictions for new inputs, the model is considered optimal for the task.  An algorithm that steadily refines its predictions and raises its accuracy over successive iterations is said to have learned to perform the designated task.

Researchers in the 1960s and the 1970s were convinced that their methods would eventually succeed in creating a machine with general intelligence and considered this the goal of their field. In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted, "machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do".In 1967 Marvin Minsky agreed, writing that "within a generation ... the problem of creating 'artificial intelligence' will substantially be solved". They had, however, underestimated the difficulty of the problem. In 1974, both the U.S. and British governments cut off exploratory research in response to the criticism of Sir James Lighthill and ongoing pressure from the U.S. Congress to fund more productive projects. Minsky and Papert's book Perceptrons was understood as proving that artificial neural networks would never be useful for solving real-world tasks, thus discrediting the approach altogether. The "AI winter", a period when obtaining funding for AI projects was difficult, followed.

Experimental physics grows hand‑in‑hand with engineering and technology, each field driving the other forward. Physicists who focus on fundamental questions typically devise and run investigations using sophisticated apparatus such as particle accelerators and high‑power lasers. In contrast, those who apply experimental methods often find employment in industrial settings, where they create practical devices—examples include magnetic resonance imaging systems and semiconductor transistors. As Richard Feynman observed, experimental researchers frequently turn their attention to domains that remain relatively untouched by theoretical work, probing uncharted territory in the laboratory.

Scientific computing—also called computational science—is the discipline that builds mathematical models and quantitative analysis methods, then employs computers to investigate and resolve scientific questions. Its most widespread application is the simulation of diverse phenomena. Researchers use it to mimic fluid flows, model physical and electrical systems, design electronic circuits, recreate social dynamics such as war‑gaming scenarios, and study the environments in which these processes occur. It also enables the exploration of interactions at the cellular level in biology.  

Because contemporary computers possess great processing power, they make it possible to refine complex designs, exemplified by the complete optimisation of aircraft. In the realm of electronics, the field relies heavily on tools such as SPICE and other software that translate theoretical circuit concepts into tangible hardware. These programs are indispensable for developing new integrated‑circuit designs or modifying existing ones.

Computer science explores how we compute, handle data, and automate tasks, along with the phenomena that arise from these activities. Positioned within the broader scientific landscape, the discipline bridges purely theoretical work—such as the study of algorithms, the foundations of computation, and the principles of information theory—with practical engineering that creates and builds both hardware and software systems. Those who specialize in this field are referred to as computer scientists.

The regulation of artificial intelligence is the development of public sector policies and laws for promoting and regulating AI; it is therefore related to the broader regulation of algorithms. The regulatory and policy landscape for AI is an emerging issue in jurisdictions globally. According to AI Index at Stanford, the annual number of AI-related laws passed in the 127 survey countries jumped from one passed in 2016 to 37 passed in 2022 alone. Between 2016 and 2020, more than 30 countries adopted dedicated strategies for AI. Most EU member states had released national AI strategies, as had Canada, China, India, Japan, Mauritius, the Russian Federation, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, U.S., and Vietnam. Others were in the process of elaborating their own AI strategy, including Bangladesh, Malaysia and Tunisia. The Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence was launched in June 2020, stating a need for AI to be developed in accordance with human rights and democratic values, to ensure public confidence and trust in the technology. Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, and Daniel Huttenlocher published a joint statement in November 2021 calling for a government commission to regulate AI. In 2023, OpenAI leaders published recommendations for the governance of superintelligence, which they believe may happen in less than 10 years. In 2023, the United Nations also launched an advisory body to provide recommendations on AI governance; the body comprises technology company executives, government officials and academics. On 1 August 2024, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act entered into force, establishing the first comprehensive EU-wide AI regulation. In 2024, the Council of Europe created the first international legally binding treaty on AI, called the "Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law". It was adopted by the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other signatories.

During the 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, researchers presented a study in which a robot that relied on CLIP (Contrastive Language‑Image Pre‑training) exhibited gender‑ and race‑related biases while performing a simulated object‑handling task. The findings highlighted that the system’s behavior reinforced harmful stereotypes. In response, the authors urged that any robot‑learning approaches capable of manifesting such inequities should be halted, revised, or even discontinued until clear evidence demonstrates that they operate safely, effectively, and equitably.

AI agents are computer programs that sense their surroundings, choose what to do, and act on their own in order to reach particular objectives. They may communicate with people, respond to changes in the physical or virtual world, or coordinate with other agents. Because of this autonomy, they appear in many domains such as personal digital helpers, conversational bots, self‑driving cars, video‑game competitors, and factory‑floor robots.

Each agent works inside the boundaries set by its code, the processing power it can access, and the hardware it runs on. Consequently, an agent can only carry out tasks that fall within its predefined role, and its memory and computational speed are limited. In practical settings, agents must also make decisions and perform actions within tight time windows.

A large portion of modern agents includes learning mechanisms. By employing machine‑learning techniques, they can refine their actions based on past experience or training data, allowing them to adjust to novel conditions and fine‑tune their behavior for the tasks they were built to perform.

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational structure made up of many interconnected units called artificial neurons, inspired loosely by the cells of a biological brain. The links that join these neurons—often referred to as edges—carry numerical signals from one unit to another, much like synapses transmit impulses between real neurons.  

When a neuron receives a signal, it combines all incoming values, adds them together, and then passes the total through a nonlinear function to produce its own output. This output, which is also a real number, can then be sent onward along the edges to subsequent neurons.  

Both the neurons and the edges typically possess a weight that is modified during the learning phase. Adjusting a weight changes how strongly a signal is amplified or diminished as it moves across the connection. Some neurons also include a threshold condition, meaning they will emit a signal only when the accumulated input exceeds a specified level.  

Neurons are usually organized into successive groups called layers. Each layer may perform a distinct type of transformation on the data it receives. Information enters the network at the first group—the input layer—and proceeds forward through the intermediate layers until it reaches the final group, the output layer. In certain designs the data may circulate through the layers more than once before producing a result.

A genetic algorithm (GA) is a search algorithm and heuristic technique that mimics the process of natural selection, using methods such as mutation and crossover to generate new genotypes in the hope of finding good solutions to a given problem. In machine learning, genetic algorithms were used in the 1980s and 1990s. Conversely, machine learning techniques have been used to improve the performance of genetic and evolutionary algorithms.

Dimensionality reduction is a process of reducing the number of random variables under consideration by obtaining a set of principal variables. In other words, it is a process of reducing the dimension of the feature set, also called the "number of features". Most of the dimensionality reduction techniques can be considered as either feature elimination or extraction. One of the popular methods of dimensionality reduction is principal component analysis (PCA). PCA involves changing higher-dimensional data (e.g., 3D) to a smaller space (e.g., 2D).

Early work, based on Noam Chomsky's generative grammar and semantic networks, had difficulty with word-sense disambiguation unless restricted to small domains called "micro-worlds" (due to the common sense knowledge problem). British linguist and philosopher Margaret Masterman believed it was meaning and not grammar that was the key to understanding languages, and that dictionaries and especially thesauri should be the basis of computational language structure.

In November 2023, the first global AI Safety Summit was held in Bletchley Park in the UK to discuss the near and far term risks of AI and the possibility of mandatory and voluntary regulatory frameworks. 28 countries including the United States, China, and the European Union issued a declaration at the start of the summit, calling for international co-operation to manage the challenges and risks of artificial intelligence. In May 2024 at the AI Seoul Summit, 16 global AI tech companies agreed to safety commitments on the development of AI.

Concurrency describes a situation in which a system runs several computational tasks at the same time, and those tasks may communicate or affect one another. To reason about this kind of behavior, researchers have created a variety of abstract frameworks, such as Petri nets, the different families of process calculi, and the parallel random‑access machine model.  

When concurrency is applied across a network of separate computers, the overall arrangement is referred to as a distributed system. In such a system each machine maintains its own local memory, while the nodes exchange messages or data so that they can cooperate toward shared objectives.

Machine learning originated as a branch of the broader scientific pursuit of artificial intelligence. In the formative years when AI first became an academic field, a subset of researchers began to explore how computers could acquire knowledge directly from data. Their early experiments combined two main strategies.  

One line of work relied on symbolic techniques, attempting to encode reasoning through explicit, rule‑based representations. At the same time, investigators experimented with what were then called “neural networks,” most famously the perceptron and similar structures. Later analysis revealed that these early network models were essentially re‑discoveries of the statistical framework known as generalized linear models.  

A complementary approach employed probabilistic reasoning, which proved especially useful in domains such as automated medical diagnosis, where uncertainty and statistical inference play a central role. Together, these symbolic, neural‑network, and probabilistic methods laid the groundwork for the modern field of machine learning.

In 2006, the media-services provider Netflix held the first "Netflix Prize" competition to find a program to better predict user preferences and improve the accuracy of its existing Cinematch movie recommendation algorithm by at least 10%. A joint team made up of researchers from AT&T Labs-Research in collaboration with the teams Big Chaos and Pragmatic Theory built an ensemble model to win the Grand Prize in 2009 for $1 million. Shortly after the prize was awarded, Netflix realised that viewers' ratings were not the best indicators of their viewing patterns ("everything is a recommendation") and they changed their recommendation engine accordingly. In 2010, an article in The Wall Street Journal noted the use of machine learning by Rebellion Research to predict the 2008 financial crisis. In 2012, co-founder of Sun Microsystems, Vinod Khosla, predicted that 80% of medical doctors jobs would be lost in the next two decades to automated machine learning medical diagnostic software. In 2014, it was reported that a machine learning algorithm had been applied in the field of art history to study fine art paintings and that it may have revealed previously unrecognised influences among artists. In 2019 Springer Nature published the first research book created using machine learning. In 2020, machine learning technology was used to help make diagnoses and aid researchers in developing a cure for COVID-19. Machine learning was recently applied to predict the pro-environmental behaviour of travellers. Recently, machine learning technology was also applied to optimise smartphone's performance and thermal behaviour based on the user's interaction with the phone. When applied correctly, machine learning algorithms (MLAs) can utilise a wide range of company characteristics to predict stock returns without overfitting. By employing effective feature engineering and combining forecasts, MLAs can generate results that far surpass those obtained from basic linear techniques like OLS.

An "agent" is any entity (artificial or not) that perceives and takes actions in the world. A rational agent has goals or preferences and takes actions to make them happen. In automated planning, the agent has a specific goal. In automated decision-making, the agent has preferences—there are some situations it would prefer to be in, and some situations it is trying to avoid. The decision-making agent assigns a number to each situation (called its "utility") that measures how much the agent prefers it. For each possible action, it can calculate the "expected utility": the utility of all possible outcomes of the action, weighted by the probability that the outcome will occur. It can then choose the action with the maximum expected utility.

Philosophers of mind remain divided over whether a machine could possess a mind, consciousness, or subjective experience comparable to that of humans. The debate centers on the machine’s inner phenomenology rather than on observable actions or performance. In contrast, the majority of artificial‑intelligence researchers regard the issue as beside the point, because their primary aim is to create systems that solve problems with intelligence, not to replicate human‑like consciousness. As Russell and Norvig observe, the task of endowing a machine with consciousness exactly as humans experience it lies beyond the scope of their discipline. Nonetheless, the question has taken on great importance within philosophical discussions about the mind and often serves as the pivotal theme in works of AI‑focused fiction.

Object‑oriented programming is a style of writing software that revolves around “objects.” Each object bundles together two kinds of elements: data, which appear as fields or attributes, and behavior, expressed as procedures or methods. The methods belonging to an object are allowed to read and usually change the object’s own data fields. Consequently, a program built with this paradigm consists of a collection of such objects that communicate and work together to achieve the desired functionality.

The "black box theory" poses another yet significant challenge. Black box refers to a situation where the algorithm producing an output is entirely opaque, meaning that even the designers of an application cannot audit the pattern that the machine extracted from the data. The House of Lords Select Committee, which claimed that such an "intelligence system" that could have a "substantial impact on an individual's life" would not be considered acceptable unless it provided "a full and satisfactory explanation for the decisions" it makes.

Modern genetics traces its intellectual roots to Gregor Mendel’s 1865 experiments, which first described how traits are passed from one generation to the next. Although Mendel’s principles lay dormant for decades, they gained prominence in the early 1900s when the modern synthesis united Darwinian natural selection with classical genetics, giving a coherent framework for evolution.

Mid‑20th‑century work shifted the focus from abstract inheritance patterns to the molecular carriers of those patterns. In the 1940s and early 1950s, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase demonstrated that DNA, rather than protein, constitutes the portion of chromosomes that houses genes. Around the same time, researchers began exploiting simple model organisms—such as bacteria and viruses—to probe genetic mechanisms. The breakthrough came in 1953, when James Watson and Francis Crick revealed DNA’s double‑helical architecture, heralding the birth of molecular genetics. From that point forward, biology increasingly operated at the molecular level.

Subsequent advances decoded the language of DNA. Har Gobind Khorana, Robert W. Holley, and Marshall Warren Nirenberg identified the genetic code, showing that sequences of three nucleotides—codons—specify amino acids. Building on this molecular understanding, the scientific community launched the Human Genome Project in 1990, an ambitious effort to map every gene in the human genome. Together, these milestones trace a continuous progression from Mendel’s pea‑plant ratios to the comprehensive, DNA‑based view of heredity that underpins contemporary biology.

Belief functions—also known as evidence theory or Dempster‑Shafer theory—offer a broad mathematical setting for dealing with uncertain information.  The approach is linked to other uncertainty formalisms such as classical probability, possibility theory, and the broader family of imprecise‑probability models.  In much the same way that a Bayesian model combines probability mass functions, belief‑function methods provide a rule (the Dempster rule of combination) for merging pieces of evidence, giving them a learner‑like character.

When contrasted with Bayesian techniques, belief‑function models bring distinct challenges.  They must address how to represent complete ignorance and how to quantify uncertainty, issues that are handled differently in the Bayesian framework.  

In practical machine‑learning applications, practitioners often embed belief‑function ideas within ensemble‑fusion schemes.  By merging the outputs of several base learners, these systems aim to sharpen decision boundaries, cope with very small training sets, and resolve classes that are otherwise ambiguous—situations where conventional algorithms tend to falter.  

A notable drawback of the belief‑function‑based pipelines is their computational demand.  The amount of work grows with the number of propositions (i.e., the possible classes), so the time required can be considerably larger than that of many standard machine‑learning approaches.

In 2015, AlphaGo, developed by DeepMind, beat the world champion Go player. The program taught only the game's rules and developed a strategy by itself. GPT-3 is a large language model that was released in 2020 by OpenAI and is capable of generating high-quality human-like text. ChatGPT, launched on 30 November 2022, became the fastest-growing consumer software application in history, gaining over 100 million users in two months. It marked what is widely regarded as AI's breakout year, bringing it into the public consciousness. These programs, and others, inspired an aggressive AI boom, where large companies began investing billions of dollars in AI research. According to AI Impacts, about US$50 billion annually was invested in "AI" around 2022 in the U.S. alone and about 20% of the new U.S. computer science PhD graduates have specialised in "AI". About 800,000 "AI"-related U.S. job openings existed in 2022. According to PitchBook research, 22% of newly funded startups in 2024 claimed to be AI companies.

Supervised‑learning methods can be grouped into three main families: active learning, classification, and regression.  

When a model must assign each observation to one of a predefined categories, a classification algorithm is employed. Its predictions are limited to a fixed list of possible labels. A practical illustration is an email‑sorting system: the program receives an incoming message as input and decides which mailbox—such as “Inbox,” “Spam,” or “Promotions”—the message belongs to.  

Conversely, regression algorithms handle situations where the result is a continuous number that can vary across a spectrum. These models are suitable for estimating quantities like a person’s height from variables such as age and genetic background, or for projecting future temperature values based on past climate records.  

Active learning, another branch of supervised learning, complements the other two by strategically selecting which data points should be labeled next, though the source does not elaborate further on its mechanics.

Sparse dictionary learning is a feature learning method where a training example is represented as a linear combination of basis functions and assumed to be a sparse matrix. The method is strongly NP-hard and difficult to solve approximately. A popular heuristic method for sparse dictionary learning is the k-SVD algorithm. Sparse dictionary learning has been applied in several contexts. In classification, the problem is to determine the class to which a previously unseen training example belongs. For a dictionary where each class has already been built, a new training example is associated with the class that is best sparsely represented by the corresponding dictionary. Sparse dictionary learning has also been applied in image denoising. The key idea is that a clean image patch can be sparsely represented by an image dictionary, but the noise cannot.

Governments are finding it progressively simpler to monitor and steer their populations thanks to a suite of artificial‑intelligence technologies. Systems that recognize faces and voices give authorities the capacity to watch large numbers of people constantly, turning surveillance from a selective practice into a pervasive one. When the collected data are fed into machine‑learning models, those models can sort individuals into categories, flagging those deemed hostile to the state and making it harder for them to remain hidden.

The same AI mechanisms also shape the information that citizens receive. Recommendation algorithms can be programmed to deliver tailored propaganda and false narratives, maximizing their persuasive impact. In parallel, generative tools such as deep‑fake generators enable the rapid creation of fabricated audio‑visual material, further fueling misinformation campaigns.

Beyond influencing public opinion, advanced AI bolsters the operational efficiency of authoritarian regimes. Centralised decision‑making structures that rely on AI can compete with, and at times outpace, the more dispersed, market‑driven approaches typical of liberal societies. The technology also reduces the expense and technical barriers associated with digital warfare and sophisticated spyware, giving repressive governments more reach with fewer resources.

A concrete illustration of these trends is the extensive deployment of facial‑recognition platforms for mass monitoring in China, demonstrating how AI can be harnessed to sustain a digital authoritarian apparatus.

Evolutionary developmental biology compares the developmental processes of different organisms to infer how developmental processes evolved. The field grew from 19th-century beginnings, where embryology faced a mystery: zoologists did not know how embryonic development was controlled at the molecular level. Charles Darwin noted that having similar embryos implied common ancestry, but little progress was made until the 1970s. Then, recombinant DNA technology at last brought embryology together with molecular genetics. A key early discovery was that of homeotic genes that regulate development in a wide range of eukaryotes. The field explores deep homology, the finding that dissimilar organs such as the eyes of insects, vertebrates and cephalopod molluscs, long thought to have evolved separately, are controlled by similar genes from the evo-devo gene toolkit.

Friendly AI are machines that have been designed from the beginning to minimise risks and to make choices that benefit humans. Eliezer Yudkowsky, who coined the term, argues that developing friendly AI should be a higher research priority: it may require a large investment and it must be completed before AI becomes an existential risk.

The word “biology” comes from the Greek βίος (*bíos*), meaning “life,” and λογία (*logia*), meaning “the study of.” Its earliest known occurrence is in the title of a 1766 publication by Michael Christoph Hanow—*Philosophiae naturalis sive physicae dogmaticae: Geologia, biologia, phytologia generalis et dendrologia*.  

The sense we now attach to the term—referring to the scientific discipline that investigates living organisms—appears to have been coined around the turn of the nineteenth century by several scholars working independently. Thomas Beddoes used it in 1799; a year later, Karl Friedrich Burdach adopted the name; in 1802, Gottfried Reinhold Treviranus presented his work *Biologie oder Philosophie der lebenden Natur*; and in the same year Jean‑Baptiste Lamarck employed the term in *Hydrogéologie*. Each of these contributions marks an early, parallel step in establishing “biology” as the modern field of study of life.

Explainable AI—also called Interpretable AI or Explainable Machine Learning (XML)—refers to artificial‑intelligence systems whose decisions and predictions can be understood by people. This stands in opposition to the “black‑box” situation common in many machine‑learning models, where even the developers are unable to articulate why a particular outcome was produced. By improving users’ mental models of how AI works and correcting any misunderstandings they may have, XAI is intended to boost the effectiveness with which people employ AI‑driven tools. Moreover, offering such transparency can be viewed as an enactment of a societal right to receive explanations.

Game playing programs have been used since the 1950s to demonstrate and test AI's most advanced techniques. Deep Blue became the first computer chess-playing system to beat a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, on 11 May 1997. In 2011, in a Jeopardy! quiz show exhibition match, IBM's question answering system, Watson, defeated the two greatest Jeopardy! champions, Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings, by a significant margin. In March 2016, AlphaGo won 4 out of 5 games of Go in a match with Go champion Lee Sedol, becoming the first computer Go-playing system to beat a professional Go player without handicaps. Then, in 2017, it defeated Ke Jie, who was the best Go player in the world. Other programs handle imperfect-information games, such as the poker-playing program Pluribus. DeepMind developed increasingly generalistic reinforcement learning models, such as with MuZero, which could be trained to play chess, Go, or Atari games. In 2019, DeepMind's AlphaStar achieved grandmaster level in StarCraft II, a particularly challenging real-time strategy game that involves incomplete knowledge of what happens on the map. In 2021, an AI agent competed in a PlayStation Gran Turismo competition, winning against four of the world's best Gran Turismo drivers using deep reinforcement learning. In 2024, Google DeepMind introduced SIMA, a type of AI capable of autonomously playing nine previously unseen open-world video games by observing screen output, as well as executing short, specific tasks in response to natural language instructions.

Computer architecture, or digital computer organization, is the conceptual design and fundamental operational structure of a computer system. It focuses largely on the way by which the central processing unit performs internally and accesses addresses in memory. Computer engineers study computational logic and design of computer hardware, from individual processor components, microcontrollers, personal computers to supercomputers and embedded systems. The term "architecture" in computer literature can be traced to the work of Lyle R. Johnson and Frederick P. Brooks Jr., members of the Machine Organization department in IBM's main research center in 1959.

In 1931, Karl Jansky uncovered that the heavens themselves produce radio emissions, a discovery that gave birth to the field of radio astronomy. Since then, humanity’s reach beyond the planet has pushed astronomical research into new territory. Because the Earth's atmosphere distorts and blocks certain wavelengths, researchers must place telescopes in space to study the universe in infrared, ultraviolet, X‑ray, and gamma‑ray light. These space‑borne instruments allow astronomers to capture signals that would otherwise be lost or corrupted by atmospheric interference, broadening our view of the cosmos.

AI gradually restored its reputation in the late 1990s and early 21st century by exploiting formal mathematical methods and by finding specific solutions to specific problems. This "narrow" and "formal" focus allowed researchers to produce verifiable results and collaborate with other fields (such as statistics, economics and mathematics). By 2000, solutions developed by AI researchers were being widely used, although in the 1990s they were rarely described as "artificial intelligence" (a tendency known as the AI effect).

Bioenergetics is a discipline that sits at the intersection of biochemistry and cell biology, focusing on how energy moves within living organisms. It represents a dynamic branch of biological research, devoted to uncovering the ways in which organisms convert and manage energy. Scientists in this field examine a vast array of cellular activities—ranging from the well‑known process of cellular respiration to countless other metabolic and enzymatic reactions—that together allow cells to capture, transform, and utilize energy for their needs.

According to Peter Denning, the fundamental question underlying computer science is, "What can be automated?" Theory of computation is focused on answering fundamental questions about what can be computed and what amount of resources are required to perform those computations. In an effort to answer the first question, computability theory examines which computational problems are solvable on various theoretical models of computation. The second question is addressed by computational complexity theory, which studies the time and space costs associated with different approaches to solving a multitude of computational problems.

Condensed‑matter physics stands as the most expansive branch of modern physics. Its origins lie in what was once called solid‑state physics; over time this earlier discipline became one of the core areas within the broader field. The name “condensed matter physics” entered the scientific lexicon in 1967 when Philip Anderson retitled his research team, which had previously been known as solid‑state theory. The evolution of the terminology was later reflected in the professional societies: in 1978 the American Physical Society’s Division of Solid State Physics adopted the new title Division of Condensed Matter Physics. Because the subject deals with the collective behavior of large assemblies of atoms and molecules, it naturally intersects with several other realms of science and technology, including chemistry, materials science, nanotechnology, and various engineering disciplines. This extensive reach and its foundational role in understanding everyday materials make condensed‑matter physics a central pillar of contemporary research.

Regression analysis encompasses a large variety of statistical methods to estimate the relationship between input variables and their associated features. Its most common form is linear regression, where a single line is drawn to best fit the given data according to a mathematical criterion such as ordinary least squares. The latter is often extended by regularisation methods to mitigate overfitting and bias, as in ridge regression. When dealing with non-linear problems, go-to models include polynomial regression (for example, used for trendline fitting in Microsoft Excel), logistic regression (often used in statistical classification) or even kernel regression, which introduces non-linearity by taking advantage of the kernel trick to implicitly map input variables to higher-dimensional space.

Artificial intelligence was founded as an academic discipline in 1956. The field went through multiple cycles of optimism throughout its history, followed by periods of disappointment and loss of funding, known as AI winters. Funding and interest increased substantially after 2012, when graphics processing units (GPUs) started being used to accelerate neural networks, and deep learning outperformed previous AI techniques. This growth accelerated further after 2017 with the transformer architecture. In the 2020s, an AI boom coincided with advances in generative AI, which became widespread and allowed for the creation and modification of media. In addition to AI safety and unintended consequences and harms from the use of AI, ethical concerns, AI's long-term effects, environmental effects, and potential existential risks have prompted discussions of AI regulation.

When an agent must act in environments that include other agents or people, it often does not know exactly what its own preferences should be. In such cases the agent can try to infer those preferences—for example, by applying inverse reinforcement‑learning techniques that deduce what is valuable from observed behavior. Alternatively, the agent may actively gather data that clarifies its goals, treating the act of seeking information as a purposeful step.

To decide whether exploring or running experiments is worthwhile, the agent can rely on information‑value theory, which provides a way to compare the expected benefit of acquiring new knowledge against the cost of the action. Because the set of all possible future actions and the situations they might produce is usually far too large to enumerate, the agent must make decisions while accepting considerable uncertainty about the results it will obtain. In short, agents facing ambiguous preferences must balance learning, exploration, and the inherent unpredictability of complex future states.

Many scholars view computer science as being unusually close to mathematics, with some even describing computing as a branch of mathematical science. The discipline’s origins were shaped by several prominent mathematicians—among them Kurt Gödel, Alan Turing, John von Neumann, Rózsa Péter, Stephen Kleene, and Alonzo Church. Their contributions laid the groundwork for a lasting dialogue between the two fields. Today, concepts from mathematics continue to inform computer science, especially in areas such as mathematical logic, category theory, domain theory, and algebra, where ideas flow back and forth with ongoing mutual benefit.

Reinforcement learning describes a situation where a software agent operates inside a changing environment while trying to accomplish a specific objective—examples include steering a car or competing in a game. As the agent moves through the range of possible actions, the environment supplies it with reward signals that serve as feedback. The agent’s purpose is to increase these rewards over time, so it continuously adapts its behavior based on the outcomes it experiences. In this way, learning emerges from the accumulation of trial‑and‑error experiences guided by the reward information.

Rule-based machine learning is a general term for any machine learning method that identifies, learns, or evolves "rules" to store, manipulate or apply knowledge. The defining characteristic of a rule-based machine learning algorithm is the identification and utilisation of a set of relational rules that collectively represent the knowledge captured by the system. This is in contrast to other machine learning algorithms that commonly identify a singular model that can be universally applied to any instance in order to make a prediction. Rule-based machine learning approaches include learning classifier systems, association rule learning, and artificial immune systems.

Molecular biology is the branch of biology that seeks to understand the molecular basis of biological activity in and between cells. It is centered largely on the study of nucleic acids (such as DNA and RNA) and proteins. It examines the structure, function, and interactions of these macromolecules as they orchestrate processes such as replication, transcription, translation, protein synthesis, and complex biomolecular interactions.

Russell and Norvig share Turing’s view that intelligence should be judged by how a system behaves outwardly, not by what its internal mechanisms look like. Yet they take issue with the classic Turing test because it insists that a machine must masquerade as a human in order to be considered intelligent. To illustrate why this requirement is unnecessary, they point to aeronautical engineering: the discipline does not set its objective as creating aircraft that fly so exactly like pigeons that they could deceive other pigeons. In the same vein, AI pioneer John McCarthy has emphasized that the field of artificial intelligence is not defined by trying to mimic human cognition. Both perspectives argue for evaluating intelligence on functional performance rather than on human‑like imitation.

Researchers have demonstrated how backdoors can be placed undetectably into classifying (e.g., for categories "spam" and "not spam" of posts) machine learning models that are often developed or trained by third parties. Parties can change the classification of any input, including in cases for which a type of data/software transparency is provided, possibly including white-box access.

Feature learning can be either supervised or unsupervised. In supervised feature learning, features are learned using labelled input data. Examples include artificial neural networks, multilayer perceptrons, and supervised dictionary learning. In unsupervised feature learning, features are learned with unlabelled input data.  Examples include dictionary learning, independent component analysis, autoencoders, matrix factorisation and various forms of clustering.

Hallucinations in generative AI are errors that arise without any intent or awareness on the part of the model. Unlike deliberate deception, a hallucinating model does not “know” that a statement is false; it simply outputs text that, while statistically likely, is not grounded in the prompt, its training material, or any external evidence. This mismatch occurs when the system creates a continuation that sounds plausible but lacks factual support.

To reduce the likelihood of such spurious output, practitioners employ several strategies. Adding a retrieval‑augmented step lets the model consult external documents before responding. Checking citations can expose unfounded claims, while imposing strict output formats can constrain the model’s freedom to fabricate. Finally, involving human reviewers provides an additional layer of verification. Although these techniques lower the risk of hallucination, none can assure complete factual correctness in every instance.

Public sentiment about artificial intelligence in the United States is varied and has shifted over recent years, as reflected in a series of polls.

A 2022 Ipsos questionnaire highlighted an international gap: while nearly four‑fifths (78 %) of people in China said that AI‑driven products and services bring more advantages than disadvantages, just over a third (35 %) of Americans shared that view.

The following year, a Reuters‑Ipsos survey asked Americans whether they believed AI could endanger humanity. A clear majority—61 %—answered affirmatively, whereas 22 % expressed disagreement.

Attitudes toward government oversight were captured in a 2023 Fox News poll. More than three‑quarters of respondents considered regulation important: 35 % said it was “very important” and another 41 % rated it “somewhat important.” Only a small share—13 % and 8 % respectively—felt it was “not very important” or “not at all important.”

By 2026, an NBC News Decision Desk poll (conducted via SurveyMonkey) revealed how Americans actually interact with AI. Over half of adult participants (52 %) reported using AI tools either frequently or occasionally. Despite this usage, trust remains limited; merely 18 % said they could rely on AI‑generated information most of the time. Moreover, a sizeable majority (70 %) said they feel more apprehensive than enthusiastic about AI’s impact.

Across these surveys, the dominant worries expressed by U.S. respondents center on four themes: the prospect of job displacement, the risk of impersonation, the spread of misinformation, and threats to personal data privacy. Together, these findings paint a picture of a public that is both engaged with AI technology and cautious about its broader implications.

For example, the ancient Chinese observed that certain rocks (lodestone and magnetite) were attracted to one another by an invisible force. This effect was later called magnetism, which was first rigorously studied in the 17th century. But even before the Chinese discovered magnetism, the ancient Greeks knew of other objects such as amber, that when rubbed with fur would cause a similar invisible attraction between the two. This was also first studied rigorously in the 17th century and came to be called electricity. Thus, physics had come to understand two observations of nature in terms of some root cause (electricity and magnetism). However, further work in the 19th century revealed that these two forces were just two different aspects of one force—electromagnetism. This process of "unifying" forces continues today, and electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force are now considered to be two aspects of the electroweak interaction. Physics hopes to find an ultimate reason (theory of everything) for why nature is as it is (see section Current research below for more information).

Computer science is the study of computation, information, and automation, together with their associated phenomena. Included broadly in the sciences, computer science spans theoretical disciplines (such as algorithms, theory of computation, and information theory) to applied disciplines (including the design and implementation of hardware and software). An expert in the field is known as a computer scientist.

Several groups are driving the open‑source wave in artificial intelligence. Among the most active are Hugging Face, Google, EleutherAI and Meta. They have helped make a number of high‑profile models—such as Llama 2, Mistral and Stable Diffusion—available as “open‑weight” resources, meaning that both the network design and the learned parameters are posted publicly.

Because the full weight files are accessible, anyone can further train these models on their own datasets. This freedom lets businesses adapt the systems to specific tasks or domains, and it also fuels academic research and experimental development.  

However, the same openness introduces significant hazards. When a model’s weights can be altered, safety features that were originally baked into the model—like refusing unsafe or harmful prompts—can be overwritten or weakened, potentially rendering them ineffective. Some scholars warn that future, more capable models might be repurposed for malicious ends, including activities that could dramatically accelerate bioterrorism. Once such a model is distributed on the internet, it cannot be completely retracted.

To balance the promise of rapid innovation with these threats, experts advise conducting thorough audits before releasing a model and weighing the expected benefits against the possible risks. This pre‑release scrutiny aims to catch dangerous capabilities early and to inform decisions about whether—and how—to share the model openly.

Such information can be used as the basis for decisions about marketing activities such as promotional pricing or product placements. In addition to market basket analysis, association rules are employed today in application areas including Web usage mining, intrusion detection, continuous production, and bioinformatics. In contrast with sequence mining, association rule learning typically does not consider the order of items either within a transaction or across transactions.

The story of machine‑learning’s expansion beyond niche research began in the mid‑2000s with a public challenge launched by a major streaming service. In 2006 the company offered a million‑dollar prize for any algorithm that could improve its existing film‑suggestion system, Cinematch, by at least ten percent. A collaborative effort that combined the expertise of AT&T Labs‑Research with the groups Big Chaos and Pragmatic Theory eventually produced an ensemble model that clinched the grand award in 2009, earning the prize money.

The aftermath of the contest revealed a surprising insight: the simple rating scores supplied by viewers were not the most reliable cues for forecasting what they would watch next. Recognizing that every user interaction could be interpreted as a recommendation, the service redesigned its recommendation engine to incorporate a broader set of signals.

Around the same period, machine‑learning techniques began to surface in other domains. In 2010 a Wall Street Journal piece highlighted how a firm called Rebellion Research employed these methods to anticipate the 2008 financial crisis. Two years later, Sun Microsystems co‑founder Vinod Khosla warned that automated diagnostic software powered by machine learning might displace up to 80 % of physicians’ roles within twenty years. By 2014, art historians were using algorithms to examine fine‑art paintings, uncovering possible artistic influences that had previously gone unnoticed.

The momentum continued into the next decade. In 2019 Springer Nature released the first research monograph entirely generated by machine‑learning tools. The following year, the same technology assisted clinicians in diagnosing COVID‑19 and supported scientists working toward a cure. More recent applications include predicting travellers’ environmentally friendly choices, tailoring smartphone performance and thermal management to individual usage patterns, and forecasting stock returns by exploiting a wide array of corporate variables without succumbing to overfitting. When practitioners apply careful feature engineering and combine multiple forecasts, machine‑learning algorithms can deliver accuracy far beyond that of traditional linear models such as ordinary least squares.

Generative‑AI systems are frequently built by feeding them huge collections of material that the creators do not own the rights to—ranging from pictures to software code. The companies that develop these models often defend the practice by invoking “fair use,” but legal scholars are divided on whether that argument would survive a court challenge. Courts might look at whether the use adds something new or merely copies the original, and at how the AI’s output could affect the original work’s market.

Web‑site operators can try to discourage automatic copying by publishing a robots.txt file that tells crawlers not to harvest their pages. In practice, the file has no binding power, and some firms continue to scrape content despite the notice.

The controversy moved into the courtroom in 2023 when a group of prominent writers—including John Grisham and Jonathan Franzen—filed lawsuits against AI firms for employing their books as training data without permission. One alternative that has been suggested is to create a new, specific form of protection for works produced by AI. Such a regime would aim to guarantee that human creators receive proper credit and compensation when their creations are incorporated into AI‑generated results.

Theorists seek to develop mathematical models that both agree with existing experiments and successfully predict future experimental results, while experimentalists devise and perform experiments to test theoretical predictions and explore new phenomena. Although theory and experiment are developed separately, they strongly affect and depend upon each other. Progress in physics frequently comes about when experimental results defy explanation by existing theories, prompting intense focus on applicable modeling, and when new theories generate experimentally testable predictions, which inspire the development of new experiments (and often related equipment).

In the first few years of the 2020s, generative‑artificial‑intelligence systems reached a point where the pictures, sounds, and written passages they produced could no longer be reliably told apart from genuine photographs, recordings, or human‑authored text. By the middle of the decade, the technology had progressed enough to make realistically looking video clips possible as well.  

These capabilities open the door for malicious actors to generate huge volumes of false information and to run large‑scale computational propaganda campaigns, for example through the use of deepfake media. The risk is not merely theoretical. A study has demonstrated that AI‑driven content can actually sway voter opinions, confirming that the technology can be weaponised to influence electorates. Intriguingly, the same research also found that the models tend to produce a higher rate of inaccurate statements when they are used to champion candidates on the political right.  

Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneering figure in artificial intelligence who has also been awarded the Nobel Prize in computer science, has warned that such tools could empower authoritarian leaders to manipulate large numbers of voters. He lists this manipulation alongside other serious threats posed by the rapid advancement of AI.

Up to this point, most of AI's funding had gone to projects that used high-level symbols to represent mental objects like plans, goals, beliefs, and known facts. In the 1980s, some researchers began to doubt that this approach would be able to imitate all the processes of human cognition, especially perception, robotics, learning and pattern recognition, and began to look into "sub-symbolic" approaches. Rodney Brooks rejected "representation" in general and focussed directly on engineering machines that move and survive. Judea Pearl, Lotfi Zadeh, and others developed methods that handled incomplete and uncertain information by making reasonable guesses rather than precise logic. But the most important development was the revival of "connectionism", including neural network research, by Geoffrey Hinton and others. In 1990, Yann LeCun successfully showed that convolutional neural networks can recognise handwritten digits, the first of many successful applications of neural networks.

Molecular physics focuses on multi-atomic structures and their internal and external interactions with matter and light. Optical physics is distinct from optics in that it tends to focus not on the control of classical light fields by macroscopic objects but on the fundamental properties of optical fields and their interactions with matter in the microscopic realm.

Biology investigates life and the organisms that possess it, positioning itself as a comprehensive natural science. It seeks to uncover the principles that link the myriad sub‑disciplines, providing explanations for how living things are built, how they operate, how they develop, where they originated, how they have changed over time, and how they are spread across the planet.  

The discipline rests on five core concepts. First, every living entity is composed of cells, which serve as the fundamental building blocks of life. Second, the transmission of traits from one generation to the next is governed by genes, making heredity the foundation of inheritance. Third, the vast variety of forms observed in nature stems from evolutionary processes that continually generate and reshape diversity. Fourth, organisms must convert energy from their surroundings to power the biochemical activities essential for survival. Finally, maintaining a stable internal environment—homeostasis—is crucial for sustaining life’s functions. Together, these themes provide a unifying framework for understanding the complexity of the biological world.

Recent research shows that hidden “backdoors” can be slipped into machine‑learning classifiers—such as those that decide whether a message is “spam” or “not spam”—without any obvious signs. These vulnerabilities often arise in models that are built or trained by external parties. After a backdoor is embedded, an attacker can force the model to produce whichever label they choose for any chosen input. This manipulation remains possible even when the system advertises full transparency of its data and code, and it can work even if the adversary has white‑box (complete) access to the model. In short, the backdoor is invisible, yet it lets a malicious party override the model’s decisions at will.

Machine learning (ML), reorganised and recognised as its own field, started to flourish in the 1990s. The field changed its goal from achieving artificial intelligence to tackling solvable problems of a practical nature. It shifted focus away from the symbolic approaches it had inherited from AI, and toward methods and models borrowed from statistics, fuzzy logic, and probability theory.

Some other researchers were more optimistic. AI pioneer Jürgen Schmidhuber did not sign the joint statement, emphasising that in 95% of all cases, AI research is about making "human lives longer and healthier and easier." While the tools that are now being used to improve lives can also be used by bad actors, "they can also be used against the bad actors." Andrew Ng also argued that "it's a mistake to fall for the doomsday hype on AI—and that regulators who do will only benefit vested interests." Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner, disagreed with the idea that AI will subordinate humans "simply because they are smarter, let alone destroy [us]", "scoff[ing] at his peers' dystopian scenarios of supercharged misinformation and even, eventually, human extinction." In contrast, he claimed that "intelligent machines will usher in a new renaissance for humanity, a new era of enlightenment." In the early 2010s, experts argued that the risks are too distant in the future to warrant research or that humans will be valuable from the perspective of a superintelligent machine. However, after 2016, the study of current and future risks and possible solutions became a serious area of research. Some have argued that concerns about existential risks of AI could draw attention away from other AI risks.

Algorithms and data structures are central to computer science. The theory of computation concerns abstract models of computation and general classes of problems that can be solved using them. The fields of cryptography and computer security involve studying the means for secure communication and preventing security vulnerabilities. Computer graphics and computational geometry address the generation of images. Programming language theory considers different ways to describe computational processes, and database theory concerns the management of repositories of data. Human–computer interaction investigates the interfaces through which humans and computers interact, and software engineering focuses on the design and principles behind developing software. Areas such as operating systems, networks and embedded systems investigate the principles and design behind complex systems. Computer architecture describes the construction of computer components and computer-operated equipment. Artificial intelligence and machine learning aim to synthesize goal-orientated processes such as problem-solving, decision-making, environmental adaptation, planning and learning found in humans and animals. Within artificial intelligence, computer vision aims to understand and process image and video data, while natural language processing aims to understand and process textual and linguistic data.

The roots of theoretical physics stretch back to philosophical thought, a tradition that helped bring together the separate phenomena of electricity and magnetism into a single framework. Today, the discipline extends its reach beyond the observable cosmos, turning its attention to speculative constructs such as parallel universes, a broader multiverse, and dimensions beyond the familiar three of space and one of time. Physicists adopt these concepts mainly as tools for addressing gaps or inconsistencies in current theories. Once an idea is introduced, they examine the logical outcomes it entails and work to derive consequences that could, in principle, be tested by experiment. This cycle—proposing bold hypotheses, exploring their implications, and seeking empirical verification—drives the ongoing evolution of theoretical physics.

The study of mechanical or "formal" reasoning began with philosophers and mathematicians in antiquity. The study of logic led directly to Alan Turing's theory of computation, which suggested that a machine, by shuffling symbols as simple as "0" and "1", could simulate any conceivable form of mathematical reasoning. This, along with concurrent discoveries in cybernetics, information theory and neurobiology, led researchers to consider the possibility of building an "electronic brain". They developed several areas of research that would become part of AI, such as McCulloch and Pitts design for "artificial neurons" in 1943, and Turing's influential 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', which introduced the Turing test and showed that "machine intelligence" was plausible.

A Markov decision process has a transition model that describes the probability that a particular action will change the state in a particular way and a reward function that supplies the utility of each state and the cost of each action. A policy associates a decision with each possible state. The policy could be calculated (e.g., by policy iteration), determined by a heuristic, or learned.

Several works use AI to force us to confront the fundamental question of what makes us human, showing us artificial beings that have the ability to feel, and thus to suffer. This appears in Karel Čapek's R.U.R., the films A.I. Artificial Intelligence and Ex Machina, as well as the novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, by Philip K. Dick. Dick considers the idea that our understanding of human subjectivity is altered by technology created with artificial intelligence.

Many physicists have written about the philosophical implications of their work, for instance Laplace, who championed causal determinism, and Erwin Schrödinger, who wrote on quantum mechanics. The mathematical physicist Roger Penrose has been called a Platonist by Stephen Hawking, a view Penrose discusses in his book, The Road to Reality. Hawking referred to himself as an "unashamed reductionist" and took issue with Penrose's views.

Systems that are trained on datasets collected with biases may exhibit these biases upon use (algorithmic bias), thus digitising cultural prejudices. For example, in 1988, the UK's Commission for Racial Equality found that St. George's Medical School had been using a computer program trained from data of previous admissions staff and this program had denied nearly 60 candidates who were found to either be women or have non-European-sounding names. Using job hiring data from a firm with racist hiring policies may lead to a machine learning system duplicating the bias by scoring job applicants by similarity to previous successful applicants. Another example includes predictive policing company Geolitica's predictive algorithm that resulted in "disproportionately high levels of over-policing in low-income and minority communities" after being trained with historical crime data.

Computationalism is the position in the philosophy of mind that the human mind is an information processing system and that thinking is a form of computing. Computationalism argues that the relationship between mind and body is similar or identical to the relationship between software and hardware and thus may be a solution to the mind–body problem. This philosophical position was inspired by the work of AI researchers and cognitive scientists in the 1960s and was originally proposed by philosophers Jerry Fodor and Hilary Putnam.

The basis for modern genetics began with the work of Gregor Mendel in 1865. This outlined the principles of biological inheritance. However, the significance of his work was not realized until the early 20th century when evolution became a unified theory as the modern synthesis reconciled Darwinian evolution with classical genetics. In the 1940s and early 1950s, a series of experiments by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase pointed to DNA as the component of chromosomes that held the trait-carrying units that had become known as genes. A focus on new kinds of model organisms such as viruses and bacteria, along with the discovery of the double-helical structure of DNA by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, marked the transition to the era of molecular genetics. From the 1950s onwards, biology has been vastly extended in the molecular domain. The genetic code was cracked by Har Gobind Khorana, Robert W. Holley and Marshall Warren Nirenberg after DNA was understood to contain codons. The Human Genome Project was launched in 1990 to map the human genome.

McCarthy defines intelligence as "the computational part of the ability to achieve goals in the world". Another AI founder, Marvin Minsky, similarly describes it as "the ability to solve hard problems". Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach defines it as the study of agents that perceive their environment and take actions that maximise their chances of achieving defined goals.

In the early 1980s, AI research was revived by the commercial success of expert systems, a form of AI program that simulated the knowledge and analytical skills of human experts. By 1985, the market for AI had reached over a billion dollars. At the same time, Japan's fifth generation computer project inspired the U.S. and British governments to restore funding for academic research. However, beginning with the collapse of the Lisp Machine market in 1987, AI once again fell into disrepute, and a second, longer-lasting winter began.

In recent years the field of artificial intelligence has moved from research labs into everyday life, a shift that can be traced through a series of landmark achievements.  

The first spark came in 2015 when DeepMind’s AlphaGo, a program that was only given the basic rules of the ancient board game Go, learned to devise its own tactics and ultimately defeated the reigning world champion. This feat demonstrated that a system could acquire sophisticated strategies without human‑crafted guidance.  

A few years later, in 2020, OpenAI released GPT‑3, a massive language model capable of producing text that closely mimics human writing. The model’s ability to generate coherent, high‑quality prose captured public imagination and set the stage for even broader adoption.  

The momentum accelerated dramatically with the launch of ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Within just two months the service attracted more than 100 million users, making it the fastest‑growing consumer software ever. That same year is widely seen as the breakout moment for AI, when the technology entered mainstream awareness.  

These breakthroughs triggered an aggressive surge of investment. By 2022, U.S. companies were pouring roughly US $50 billion per year into AI‑related research and development, according to AI Impacts. The academic pipeline reflected the trend as well: about one‑fifth of new computer‑science PhD graduates in the United States chose to specialize in AI, and the labor market responded with roughly 800 000 AI‑related job openings that year.  

The startup ecosystem followed suit. PitchBook’s 2024 data show that 22 % of all newly funded companies described themselves as AI firms, underscoring how the sector has become a major driver of new ventures.  

Together, these milestones—AlphaGo’s self‑taught mastery, GPT‑3’s language generation, ChatGPT’s rapid consumer uptake, and the massive flow of capital, talent, and new companies—illustrate why the early 2020s have been characterized as an AI boom, reshaping both technology and the broader economy.

Artificial intelligence refers to the ability of computers and other digital devices to carry out functions that are usually linked to human intellect. These functions include acquiring knowledge, drawing conclusions, solving problems, interpreting sensory data, and making choices. The discipline draws on engineering, mathematics, and computer‑science research to create algorithms and software that allow machines to sense their surroundings. By applying learned information and intelligent reasoning, such systems can choose actions that best increase the likelihood of reaching specific objectives.

Physics is regarded as the most basic of the sciences because it investigates everything from the tiniest constituents of matter—quarks, neutrinos, electrons—to the grandest structures in the cosmos, such as the superclusters that bind galaxies together. By studying these fundamental building blocks, physics seeks to explain the myriad events we observe in nature in terms of simpler, underlying processes. The discipline therefore strives to trace what we can measure back to its deepest origins and to show how those origins interrelate. In doing so, it builds a chain of understanding that links observable phenomena to their root causes, and then links those causes to one another, offering a unified picture of the physical world.

In a 2022 Ipsos survey, attitudes towards AI varied greatly by country; 78% of Chinese citizens, but only 35% of Americans, agreed that "products and services using AI have more benefits than drawbacks". A 2023 Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 61% of Americans agree, and 22% disagree, that AI poses risks to humanity. In a 2023 Fox News poll, 35% of Americans thought it "very important", and an additional 41% thought it "somewhat important", for the federal government to regulate AI, versus 13% responding "not very important" and 8% responding "not at all important". A 2026 NBC News Decision Desk poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that 52% of American adults used AI tools very often or sometimes, but only 18% said they could trust AI-generated information most or almost all of the time, and 70% were more worried than excited about AI. Polls in the United States found the main public concerns were job losses, impersonation, misinformation and information privacy.

In the early 1960s Raytheon Company built an experimental “learning machine” called Cybertron.  The device stored information on punched‑tape cards and was programmed to process sonar echoes, electro‑cardiogram traces, and spoken sounds.  Its learning method was a primitive form of reinforcement: a human instructor repeatedly presented examples, and an extra “goof” button let the operator force the machine to reassess any mistaken choices.

During the same decade the field of machine learning was summarized in Nils Nilsson’s textbook *Learning Machines*, which mainly dealt with how computers could be trained to classify patterns.  The enthusiasm for pattern‑recognition research did not stop there; by 1973 the topic was still a major focus, as documented in the work of Duda and Hart.

The progression continued into the early 1980s.  A 1981 report described a set of teaching strategies that enabled an artificial neural network to acquire the ability to identify forty different characters— the full alphabet of twenty‑six letters, the ten decimal digits, and four additional symbols—directly from input supplied through a computer terminal.

Significant advances have been achieved in fields such as high‑energy physics, quantum mechanics, and astronomy. Yet many ordinary occurrences that involve intricate, chaotic, or turbulent behavior continue to elude complete scientific explanation. Certain problems that intuitively seem amenable to a clever use of dynamics and mechanical principles remain open. Among these are the way sand piles develop, the appearance of nodal patterns when water flows in a thin stream, the precise geometry adopted by droplets of water, the sudden failures that can occur in surface‑tension‑driven systems, and the spontaneous segregation that happens when mixed, varied objects are shaken. Each of these everyday phenomena illustrates the challenge of translating basic physical laws into a thorough understanding of complex, real‑world behavior.

Biology began to develop quickly with Anton van Leeuwenhoek's dramatic improvement of the microscope. It was then that scholars discovered spermatozoa, bacteria, infusoria and the diversity of microscopic life. Investigations by Jan Swammerdam led to new interest in entomology and helped to develop techniques of microscopic dissection and staining. Advances in microscopy had a profound impact on biological thinking. In the early 19th century, biologists pointed to the central importance of the cell. In 1838, Schleiden and Schwann began promoting the now universal ideas that (1) the basic unit of organisms is the cell and (2) that individual cells have all the characteristics of life, although they opposed the idea that (3) all cells come from the division of other cells, continuing to support spontaneous generation. However, Robert Remak and Rudolf Virchow were able to reify the third tenet, and by the 1860s most biologists accepted all three tenets which consolidated into cell theory.

Aristotle believed that each of the four classical elements (air, fire, water, earth) had its own natural place. Because of their differing densities, each element will revert to its own specific place in the atmosphere. So, because of their weights, fire would be at the top, air underneath fire, then water, then lastly earth. He also stated that when a small amount of one element enters the natural place of another, the less abundant element will automatically go towards its own natural place. For example, if there is a fire on the ground, the flames go up into the air in an attempt to go back into its natural place where it belongs. His laws of motion included: that heavier objects will fall faster, the speed being proportional to the weight and the speed of the object that is falling depends inversely on the density object it is falling through (e.g. density of air). He also stated that, when it comes to violent motion (motion of an object when a force is applied to it by a second object), the speed that object moves will only be as fast or strong as the measure of force applied to it. The problem of motion and its causes was studied carefully, leading to the philosophical notion of a "prime mover" as the ultimate source of all motion in the world (Book 8 of his treatise Physics).

AI developers contend that gathering data is essential for building useful applications, and they have responded by inventing methods that try to keep personal information private while still allowing analysis. These methods include combining data from many users, removing identifying details, and applying differential‑privacy algorithms. Beginning around 2016, some scholars of privacy—among them Cynthia Dwork—started to interpret privacy concerns through the lens of fairness. Writer Brian Christian observes that the conversation has shifted: instead of focusing on the sheer amount of information that companies possess, the emphasis now lies on how that information is employed.

During the 1940s, with the development of new and more powerful computing machines such as the Atanasoff–Berry computer and ENIAC, the term computer came to refer to the machines rather than their human predecessors. As it became clear that computers could be used for more than just mathematical calculations, the field of computer science broadened to study computation in general. In 1945, IBM founded the Watson Scientific Computing Laboratory at Columbia University in New York City. The renovated fraternity house on Manhattan's West Side was IBM's first laboratory devoted to pure science. The lab is the forerunner of IBM's Research Division, which today operates research facilities around the world. Ultimately, the close relationship between IBM and Columbia University was instrumental in the emergence of a new scientific discipline, with Columbia offering one of the first academic-credit courses in computer science in 1946. Computer science began to be established as a distinct academic discipline in the 1950s and early 1960s. The world's first computer science degree program, the Cambridge Diploma in Computer Science, began at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory in 1953. The first computer science department in the United States was formed at Purdue University in 1962. Since practical computers became available, many applications of computing have become distinct areas of study in their own rights.

The UK AI Safety Institute released in 2024 a testing toolset called 'Inspect' for AI safety evaluations available under an MIT open-source licence which is freely available on GitHub and can be improved with third-party packages. It can be used to evaluate AI models in a range of areas including core knowledge, ability to reason, and autonomous capabilities.

Physics uses mathematics to organize and formulate experimental results. From those results, precise or estimated solutions are obtained, or quantitative results, from which new predictions can be made and experimentally confirmed or negated. The results from physics experiments are numerical data, with their units of measure and estimates of the errors in the measurements.
