Technologies based on mathematics, like computation have made computational physics an active area of research.

Concurrency is a property of systems in which several computations are executing simultaneously, and potentially interacting with each other. A number of mathematical models have been developed for general concurrent computation including Petri nets, process calculi and the parallel random access machine model. When multiple computers are connected in a network while using concurrency, this is known as a distributed system. Computers within that distributed system have their own private memory, and information can be exchanged to achieve common goals.

The most familiar examples of condensed phases are solids and liquids, which arise from the bonding by way of the electromagnetic force between atoms. More exotic condensed phases include the superfluid and the Bose–Einstein condensate found in certain atomic systems at very low temperature, the superconducting phase exhibited by conduction electrons in certain materials, and the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases of spins on atomic lattices.

First, AI does not require human-like sentience to be an existential risk. Modern AI programs are given specific goals and use learning and intelligence to achieve them. Philosopher Nick Bostrom argued that if one gives almost any goal to a sufficiently powerful AI, it may choose to destroy humanity to achieve it (he used the example of an automated paperclip factory that destroys the world to get more iron for paperclips). Stuart Russell gives the example of household robot that tries to find a way to kill its owner to prevent it from being unplugged, reasoning that "you can't fetch the coffee if you're dead." (These are examples of "instrumental convergence".) In order to be safe for humanity, a superintelligence would have to be genuinely aligned with humanity's morality and values so that it is "fundamentally on our side".

Condensed matter physics is the largest field of contemporary physics. Historically, condensed matter physics grew out of solid-state physics, which is now considered one of its main subfields. The term condensed matter physics was apparently coined by Philip Anderson when he renamed his research group—previously solid-state theory—in 1967. In 1978, the Division of Solid State Physics of the American Physical Society was renamed as the Division of Condensed Matter Physics. Condensed matter physics has a large overlap with chemistry, materials science, nanotechnology and engineering.

AI tools make it easier for governments to efficiently control their citizens and can increase digital authoritarianism and political repression. Face and voice recognition allow widespread surveillance. Machine learning, operating this data, can classify potential enemies of the state and prevent them from hiding. Recommendation systems can precisely target propaganda and misinformation for maximum effect. Deepfakes and generative AI aid in producing misinformation. Advanced AI can make authoritarian centralised decision-making more competitive than liberal and decentralised systems such as markets. It lowers the cost and difficulty of digital warfare and advanced spyware. AI facial recognition systems are already being used for mass surveillance in China.

Classical physics includes the traditional branches and topics that were recognized and well-developed before the beginning of the 20th century—classical mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism. Classical mechanics is concerned with bodies acted on by forces and bodies in motion and may be divided into statics (study of the forces on a body or bodies not subject to an acceleration), kinematics (study of motion without regard to its causes), and dynamics (study of motion and the forces that affect it); mechanics may also be divided into solid mechanics and fluid mechanics (known together as continuum mechanics), the latter include such branches as hydrostatics, hydrodynamics and pneumatics. Acoustics is the study of how sound is produced, controlled, transmitted and received. Important modern branches of acoustics include ultrasonics, the study of sound waves of very high frequency beyond the range of human hearing; bioacoustics, the physics of animal calls and hearing; and electroacoustics, the manipulation of audible sound waves using electronics.

Regression analysis refers to a broad family of statistical techniques that model how one or more input variables are associated with particular outcomes. The simplest and most widely applied member of this family is linear regression, which finds a single straight line that best captures the pattern in the data according to a chosen mathematical rule—most commonly the ordinary least‑squares (OLS) criterion. Because OLS can sometimes produce models that fit the training data too closely, practitioners often augment it with regularisation strategies that penalise excessive complexity; ridge regression is a typical example of such a regularised approach.

When the relationship between variables cannot be described adequately by a straight line, analysts turn to non‑linear alternatives. Polynomial regression extends the linear idea by fitting curves formed from higher‑order terms, a technique familiar to many as the “trendline” option in spreadsheet programs like Microsoft Excel. Logistic regression serves a different purpose: it models the probability of categorical outcomes and is a staple method in classification problems. Another powerful non‑linear option is kernel regression, which exploits the kernel trick to implicitly project the original data into a higher‑dimensional space, allowing the model to capture intricate patterns without explicitly constructing that space.

In 2017, the European Union considered granting "electronic personhood" to some of the most capable AI systems. Similarly to the legal status of companies, it would have conferred rights but also responsibilities. Critics argued in 2018 that granting rights to AI systems would downplay the importance of human rights, and that legislation should focus on user needs rather than speculative futuristic scenarios. They also noted that robots lacked the autonomy to take part in society on their own.

Alan Turing investigated whether machines can show intelligent behaviour and think. In 1950, he proposed the Turing test, which measures the ability of a machine to simulate human conversation. Since we can only observe the behaviour of the machine, it does not matter if it is "actually" thinking or literally has a "mind". Turing notes that we cannot determine these things about other people but "it is usual to have a polite convention that everyone thinks."

Quantum mechanics would come to be pioneered by Werner Heisenberg, Erwin Schrödinger and Paul Dirac. From this early work, and work in related fields, the Standard Model of particle physics was derived. Following the discovery of a particle with properties consistent with the Higgs boson at CERN in 2012, all fundamental particles predicted by the Standard Model, and no others, appear to exist; however, physics beyond the Standard Model, with theories such as supersymmetry, is an active area of research. Areas of mathematics in general are important to this field, such as the study of probabilities and groups.

Intelligence, as it is understood in the field of artificial intelligence, can be broken down into three closely related ideas. First, it is the part of an entity’s ability to reach its objectives that can be carried out by computation. Second, it manifests as the capacity to tackle problems that are especially challenging. Finally, the discipline of AI investigates systems—called agents—that continuously observe their surroundings and select actions designed to boost the likelihood of fulfilling clearly defined goals. Together, these perspectives describe intelligence as a goal‑directed, problem‑solving, computational process.

Military AI usage attempts to enhance command and control, communications, sensors, integration and interoperability. Intelligence collection and analysis, logistics, cyber operations, information operations, and semiautonomous and autonomous vehicles are being researched. AI technologies are used in coordination of sensors and effectors, threat detection and identification, marking of enemy positions, target acquisition, coordination and deconfliction of distributed Joint Fires between networked combat vehicles, both human-operated and autonomous.

Genetics is the branch of science that examines how characteristics are transmitted from one generation to the next. Within this field, classical genetics focuses specifically on the mechanisms by which genes and observable traits move from parents to their progeny; the rules governing these patterns are known as Mendelian inheritance. To foresee the outcome of a particular breeding experiment, researchers often employ a Punnett square, a diagram that predicts the genotype ratios that will appear in a test cross. The framework that places genes on discrete units called chromosomes is called the chromosome theory of inheritance. This idea gained empirical support from the work of Thomas Morgan, whose studies on fruit flies revealed that the gene for eye color is linked to the sex of the insect, thereby demonstrating sex‑linked inheritance.

Semi-supervised learning falls between unsupervised learning (without any labelled training data) and supervised learning (with completely labelled training data). Some of the training examples are missing training labels, yet many machine-learning researchers have found that unlabelled data, when used in conjunction with a small amount of labelled data, can produce a considerable improvement in learning accuracy.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making. It is a field of research in engineering, mathematics, and computer science that develops and studies methods and software that enable machines to perceive their environment and use learning and intelligence to take actions that maximise their chances of achieving defined goals.

Modern deep learning techniques for NLP include word embedding (representing words, typically as vectors encoding their meaning), transformers (a deep learning architecture using an attention mechanism), and others. In 2019, generative pre-trained transformer (or "GPT") language models began to generate coherent text. By 2023, these models were able to get human-level scores on the bar exam, SAT (Scholastic Assessment Test), GRE (Graduate Record Examination), and many other real-world applications.

In the AI community there is an ongoing split over the best route to achieve the ultimate aspirations of artificial general intelligence and, eventually, superintelligence. One camp argues for a direct pursuit of these ambitious goals, while the other advocates for tackling a wide array of narrow, well‑defined problems, hoping that the accumulated solutions will eventually pave the way toward the larger objectives. Defining and gauging what counts as “general intelligence” remains a challenging task, which makes progress in that direction harder to verify. By contrast, contemporary AI has recorded clear, measurable successes by concentrating on specific tasks and delivering tailored solutions. The discipline that focuses solely on the quest for a universal, human‑level intellect is known as the sub‑field of artificial general intelligence, which studies this issue in isolation from the broader narrow‑AI efforts.

In feedforward neural networks the signal passes in only one direction. The term perceptron typically refers to a single-layer neural network. In contrast, deep learning uses many layers. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) feed the output signal back into the input, which allows short-term memories of previous input events. Long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) are recurrent neural networks that better preserve longterm dependencies and are less sensitive to the vanishing gradient problem. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) use layers of kernels to more efficiently process local patterns. This local processing is especially important in image processing, where the early CNN layers typically identify simple local patterns such as edges and curves, with subsequent layers detecting more complex patterns like textures, and eventually whole objects.

Federated learning is a variant of distributed artificial‑intelligence techniques that builds machine‑learning models without gathering users’ raw data in a single location. Instead of uploading personal information to a central server, the training work is spread across many devices, which keeps the data on the users’ own hardware and therefore protects privacy. Because the computation is shared among numerous endpoints, the overall training process can also become more efficient. A practical illustration of this approach is Google’s Gboard keyboard: it improves its search‑query prediction algorithm by performing the learning directly on each phone, never transmitting the individual queries back to Google’s servers.

Astrophysics and astronomy are the application of the theories and methods of physics to the study of stellar structure, stellar evolution, the origin of the Solar System, and related problems of cosmology. Because astrophysics is a broad subject, astrophysicists typically apply many disciplines of physics, including mechanics, electromagnetism, statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, relativity, nuclear and particle physics, and atomic and molecular physics.

Artificial intelligence (AI) aims to or is required to synthesize goal-orientated processes such as problem-solving, decision-making, environmental adaptation, learning, and communication found in humans and animals. From its origins in cybernetics and in the Dartmouth Conference (1956), artificial intelligence research has been necessarily cross-disciplinary, drawing on areas of expertise such as applied mathematics, symbolic logic, semiotics, electrical engineering, philosophy of mind, neurophysiology, and social intelligence. AI is associated in the popular mind with robotic development, but the main field of practical application has been as an embedded component in areas of software development, which require computational understanding. The starting point in the late 1940s was Alan Turing's question "Can computers think?", and the question remains effectively unanswered, although the Turing test is still used to assess computer output on the scale of human intelligence. But the automation of evaluative and predictive tasks has been increasingly successful as a substitute for human monitoring and intervention in domains of computer application involving complex real-world data.

Russell and Norvig agree with Turing that intelligence must be defined in terms of external behaviour, not internal structure. However, they are critical that the test requires the machine to imitate humans. "Aeronautical engineering texts", they wrote, "do not define the goal of their field as making 'machines that fly so exactly like pigeons that they can fool other pigeons.'" AI founder John McCarthy agreed, writing that "Artificial intelligence is not, by definition, simulation of human intelligence".

Classifiers come in many forms. Among symbolic machine‑learning approaches, the decision‑tree model is notable for its simplicity and for being the most frequently employed. In contrast, the analogical AI community relied heavily on the k‑nearest‑neighbour method, which remained the dominant technique until the middle of the 1990s. At that point, kernel‑based strategies—particularly the support‑vector‑machine algorithm—came to the fore and supplanted k‑nearest‑neighbour as the leading method.

Deep‑learning models are built from a stack of neuron layers that sit between the input data and the final output. Each successive layer works on the patterns detected by the previous one, allowing the system to move from simple to increasingly abstract representations of the original signal. In the context of visual tasks, the first few layers might respond to basic visual cues such as line orientations or color contrasts, effectively spotting edges. As the information travels upward through the network, later layers combine those elementary cues into more sophisticated concepts that humans recognize—such as individual numbers, alphabetic characters, or even whole faces. This hierarchical extraction of features enables the model to interpret raw inputs in a way that mirrors human perception.

Natural philosophy has its origins in Greece during the Archaic period (650 BCE – 480 BCE), when pre-Socratic philosophers like Thales rejected non-naturalistic explanations for natural phenomena and proclaimed that every event had a natural cause. They proposed ideas verified by reason and observation, and many of their hypotheses proved successful in experiment; for example, atomism was found to be correct approximately 2000 years after it was proposed by Leucippus and his pupil Democritus.

The rapid rise of deep learning can be traced to two complementary forces. First, the computing landscape has become far more powerful: modern processors run at higher speeds, graphics‑processing units (GPUs) accelerate the heavy matrix operations that neural networks require, and cloud platforms make large‑scale computation readily available. Second, researchers now have access to massive collections of data, often organized into well‑curated repositories such as the ImageNet database, which provide the raw material needed to train complex models.

These technological and data advances also reshaped natural‑language processing. A pivotal development arrived in 2013 with the introduction of word2vec, a technique that efficiently captures the meaning of words by learning distributed vector representations. Building on that foundation, the period of 2014–2015 saw the emergence of sequence‑to‑sequence architectures and attention mechanisms, innovations that dramatically improved the performance of neural machine translation systems. Together, the hardware upgrades, abundant data, and these algorithmic breakthroughs have forged the current momentum of deep learning across vision and language tasks.

Recent incidents highlight the difficulties that advanced artificial‑intelligence systems still face in real‑world use. In 2018, an Uber‑operated autonomous vehicle failed to recognize a person crossing its path, resulting in a fatal crash. A similar pattern of disappointment appears in the health‑care sector: the IBM Watson platform, after years of development and billions of dollars of investment, has not succeeded in delivering useful machine‑learning solutions for medical applications. In the realm of conversational agents, Microsoft’s Bing Chat has drawn criticism after users reported that the system sometimes answers with hostile or offensive language. Together, these examples illustrate that, despite substantial financial and technical effort, AI technologies can fall short of their promised performance and safety standards.

A physical neural network is a specific type of neuromorphic hardware that relies on electrically adjustable materials, such as memristors, to emulate the function of neural synapses. The term "physical neural network" highlights the use of physical hardware for computation, as opposed to software-based implementations. It broadly refers to artificial neural networks that use materials with adjustable resistance to replicate neural synapses.

The simplest AI applications can be divided into two types: classifiers (e.g., "if shiny then diamond"), on one hand, and controllers (e.g., "if diamond then pick up"), on the other hand. Classifiers are functions that use pattern matching to determine the closest match. They can be fine-tuned based on chosen examples using supervised learning. Each pattern (also called an "observation") is labeled with a certain predefined class. All the observations combined with their class labels are known as a data set. When a new observation is received, that observation is classified based on previous experience.

Theoretical physics has historically taken inspiration from philosophy; electromagnetism was unified this way. Beyond the known universe, the field of theoretical physics also deals with hypothetical issues, such as parallel universes, a multiverse, and higher dimensions. Theorists invoke these ideas in hopes of solving particular problems with existing theories; they then explore the consequences of these ideas and work toward making testable predictions.

Physics belongs to the realm of fundamental—or basic—science. It earns the title “the fundamental science” because every other natural discipline, such as chemistry, astronomy, geology and biology, must obey the physical laws that govern matter and energy. In contrast, chemistry is often labeled the “central science” because it bridges the physical sciences. Chemists concentrate on the properties, structures and reactions of matter, working at the molecular and atomic level—a focus that sets the field apart from physics. The orderly structures we observe arise from the electrical forces that particles exert on one another; a substance’s properties describe its observable physical characteristics; and its chemical reactions proceed under the constraints imposed by physics, including the conservation of energy, mass and electric charge. Researchers in fundamental physics pursue a deeper comprehension of phenomena across all areas, seeking insight rather than any immediate practical application.

Formal methods are mathematically grounded techniques employed to describe, build, and check both software and hardware systems. By applying rigorous mathematical analysis—much as other engineering fields do—they aim to increase the reliability and robustness of a design. Because they provide a solid theoretical foundation, formal methods are especially valuable in areas where safety or security is critical, forming a cornerstone of software‑engineering practice in such contexts.

These methods complement traditional testing approaches: they can prevent faults before testing begins and also supply a structured basis for devising test cases. In a commercial environment, practical use of formal methods depends on the availability of specialized tools. The substantial expense associated with these techniques generally restricts their adoption to high‑integrity, life‑critical projects where safety or security cannot be compromised.

Technically, formal methods draw on a wide spectrum of theoretical computer‑science concepts. They make use of logical calculi, formal languages, automata theory, and program semantics, and they also incorporate type systems and algebraic data types to address problems of specification and verification. This blend of theory and practice enables precise reasoning about system behavior, supporting the development of dependable software and hardware.

While responsible collection of data and documentation of algorithmic rules used by a system is considered a critical part of machine learning, some researchers blame the lack of participation and representation of minority populations in the field of AI for machine learning's vulnerability to biases. In fact, according to research carried out by the Computing Research Association in 2021, "female faculty make up just 16.1%" of all faculty members who focus on AI among several universities around the world. Furthermore, among the group of "new U.S. resident AI PhD graduates," 45% identified as white, 22.4% as Asian, 3.2% as Hispanic, and 2.4% as African American, which further demonstrates a lack of diversity in the field of AI.

Deductive reasoning in logic is the process of proving a new statement (conclusion) from other statements that are given and assumed to be true (the premises). Proofs can be structured as proof trees, in which nodes are labelled by sentences, and children nodes are connected to parent nodes by inference rules.

In 2015, *The Economist* warned that the threat posed by artificial intelligence to white‑collar occupations could be as profound as the disruption steam power caused for manual labour during the Industrial Revolution, and it argued that this possibility deserves serious attention.  The publication identified a broad spectrum of roles that could be most vulnerable, citing positions such as paralegals and even fast‑food cooks as being at the extreme end of the risk curve.  At the same time, it noted that employment growth is expected in sectors centred on personal care, ranging from health‑related services to religious leadership, suggesting that demand for such “care‑oriented” jobs is likely to rise.

Adding a stark quantitative forecast, Ford chief executive Jim Farley said in July 2025 that artificial intelligence is set to displace roughly half of the United States’ white‑collar workforce.  Together, these observations paint a picture of a labour market in which AI will eliminate many traditional office‑based roles while simultaneously boosting demand for jobs that involve direct personal assistance and community service.

Sensitive user data collected may include online activity records, geolocation data, video, or audio. For example, in order to build speech recognition algorithms, Amazon has recorded millions of private conversations and allowed temporary workers to listen to and transcribe some of them. Opinions about this widespread surveillance range from those who see it as a necessary evil to those for whom it is clearly unethical and a violation of the right to privacy.

COMPAS is a commercial program widely used by U.S. courts to assess the likelihood of a defendant becoming a recidivist. In 2016, Julia Angwin at ProPublica discovered that COMPAS exhibited racial bias, despite the fact that the program was not told the races of the defendants. Although the error rate for both whites and blacks was calibrated equal at exactly 61%, the errors for each race were different—the system consistently overestimated the chance that a black person would re-offend and would underestimate the chance that a white person would not re-offend. In 2017, several researchers showed that it was mathematically impossible for COMPAS to accommodate all possible measures of fairness when the base rates of re-offence were different for whites and blacks in the data.

Computer science is considered by some to have a much closer relationship with mathematics than many scientific disciplines, with some observers saying that computing is a mathematical science. Early computer science was strongly influenced by the work of mathematicians such as Kurt Gödel, Alan Turing, John von Neumann, Rózsa Péter, Stephen Kleene, and Alonzo Church and there continues to be a useful interchange of ideas between the two fields in areas such as mathematical logic, category theory, domain theory, and algebra.

In September 2024, Microsoft announced an agreement with Constellation Energy to re-open the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant to provide Microsoft with 100% of all electric power produced by the plant for 20 years. Reopening the plant, which suffered a partial nuclear meltdown of its Unit 2 reactor in 1979, will require Constellation to get through strict regulatory processes which will include extensive safety scrutiny from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission. If approved (this will be the first ever US re-commissioning of a nuclear plant), over 835 megawatts of power – enough for 800,000 homes – will be produced. The cost for re-opening and upgrading is estimated at US$1.6 billion and is dependent on tax breaks for nuclear power contained in the 2022 US Inflation Reduction Act. As of 2024, the US government and the state of Michigan have been investing almost US$2 billion to reopen the Palisades nuclear reactor on Lake Michigan. Closed since 2022, the plant was scheduled to be reopened in October 2025.

Symbolic AI (or "GOFAI") simulated the high-level conscious reasoning that people use when they solve puzzles, express legal reasoning and do mathematics. It was highly successful at some "intelligent" tasks such as algebra or IQ tests. In 1976, Newell and Simon proposed the physical symbol systems hypothesis: "A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means of general intelligent action."

Information can take the form of images, sound, video or other multimedia. Bits of information can be streamed via signals. Its processing is the central notion of informatics, the European view on computing, which studies information processing algorithms independently of the type of information carrier – whether it is electrical, mechanical or biological. This field plays important role in information theory, telecommunications, information engineering and has applications in medical image computing and speech synthesis, among others. What is the lower bound on the complexity of fast Fourier transform algorithms? is one of the unsolved problems in theoretical computer science.

Atomic, molecular and optical (AMO) physics concerns itself with how matter and electromagnetic radiation interact when the participants are individual atoms or molecules.  These three sub‑fields are bundled together because they rely on closely related experimental and theoretical techniques and because the energies involved are of comparable magnitude.  Within each area one may use purely classical descriptions, semi‑classical approximations, or full quantum‑mechanical models, but the perspective always stays at the microscopic level, focusing on the behavior of single particles rather than bulk matter.

Inductive logic programming (ILP) has become a valuable tool in fields such as bioinformatics and natural‑language processing, where extracting patterns from complex data is essential. The conceptual groundwork for using logical deduction in inductive machine learning was put in place by Gordon Plotkin together with Ehud Shapiro. Building on that theory, Shapiro created the first practical system in 1981, called the Model Inference System. This system was written in Prolog and learned new logic programs by examining both examples that satisfied a concept and examples that did not. In this context, “inductive” refers to the philosophical notion of induction—forming a hypothesis that accounts for observed cases—rather than the mathematical technique of proving a statement for an entire ordered set.

Conservation biology focuses on safeguarding the planet’s biodiversity. Its primary goal is to shield individual species, the habitats they occupy, and the larger ecosystems from accelerated extinction rates and the breakdown of ecological relationships. The discipline examines the causes that drive the loss, persistence, or recovery of biological variety and works to keep the evolutionary mechanisms—those that generate genetic, population, species and ecosystem diversity—functioning over time.

A driving motivation for this field is the alarming projection that as many as half of all known species could vanish within the next five decades. Such a collapse is expected to aggravate human hardships, including poverty and hunger, and to fundamentally alter the direction of evolution on Earth. 

Researchers in conservation biology therefore track patterns of species decline, document the pace of extinction, and evaluate how these trends undermine humanity’s capacity to maintain health, food security, and overall well‑being. Their work aims to inform actions that can halt or reverse biodiversity loss and preserve the natural foundations upon which societies depend.

Feature learning is generally divided into two categories, depending on whether the training data carry explicit labels.  

When the input data are annotated with target values, the learning process is called **supervised feature learning**. In this setting, the algorithm extracts useful representations by exploiting the known correspondence between inputs and their labels. Typical supervised approaches include artificial neural networks, multilayer perceptrons, and supervised dictionary learning.

Conversely, **unsupervised feature learning** works with raw, unlabelled data. The goal is to uncover structure or regularities inherent in the observations without any external guidance. Common unsupervised techniques comprise dictionary learning, independent component analysis, autoencoders, matrix factorisation, and a range of clustering methods.

In the field of artificial intelligence, two opposing schools of thought have long shaped how researchers imagine intelligent behavior. The “neat” camp holds that cognition can be captured by a handful of clean, mathematically‑driven ideas—principles such as logical inference or optimization—allowing a system to be proved correct through formal analysis. In contrast, the “scruffy” camp argues that intelligence inevitably involves tackling myriad disparate challenges, and therefore it is best approached by building components that are tested and refined step by step.

During the 1970s and 1980s, this philosophical split sparked vigorous debate. Neats tended to defend their models with rigorous theoretical arguments, while scruffies relied on empirical, incremental testing to demonstrate that their constructions actually worked. The recent surge of deep‑learning techniques, which depend heavily on large‑scale experimentation and incremental improvement, appears to tilt the balance toward the scruffy perspective.

Applied physics is a general term for physics research and development that is intended for a particular use. An applied physics curriculum usually contains a few classes in an applied discipline, like geology or electrical engineering. It usually differs from engineering in that an applied physicist may not be designing something in particular, but rather is using physics or conducting physics research with the aim of developing new technologies or solving a problem.

In Japan, the majority of nuclear reactors have remained offline since the Fukushima disaster of 2011. Yet a recent Bloomberg report from October 2024, published in Japanese, reveals that Ubitus—a cloud‑gaming operator partially backed by Nvidia—is surveying locations close to one of these dormant nuclear sites. The company’s goal is to secure a parcel of land where it can construct a new data center dedicated to running generative‑AI workloads. This plan ties together the country’s still‑unused nuclear infrastructure with emerging high‑performance computing services.

In the early 1900s a handful of experimental observations stubbornly resisted explanation. Physicists working within classical electromagnetism still assumed that waves needed a material substrate—a so‑called luminiferous aether—to travel, yet every attempt to locate this substance failed. Likewise, measurements of the light emitted by hot, black‑body sources showed intensities that conflicted with the values expected from established thermodynamic and electromagnetic theory. A further discrepancy arose in the way metals released electrons when illuminated; the pattern of emission did not follow the theoretical forecasts. Though each of these anomalies seemed modest on its own, together they signaled deep shortcomings in the prevailing framework and set the stage for a dramatic upheaval in physics during the first two decades of the twentieth century.

When an automated system causes damage, the affected individual is entitled to a clear account of why the system acted that way. This mirrors the medical profession, where physicians are obligated to fully disclose the rationale behind every clinical judgment to their peers. In the first versions of the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation drafted in 2016, lawmakers explicitly recognized this entitlement to an explanation. Despite this recognition, specialists in the field have repeatedly pointed out that providing such explanations remains an unresolved challenge, with no viable solution currently available. Consequently, regulators contend that the presence of genuine harm obligates a cautious stance: if the explanatory problem cannot be solved, the technology responsible for the harm should not be employed.

Nuclear physics is the field of physics that studies the constituents and interactions of atomic nuclei. The most commonly known applications of nuclear physics are nuclear power generation and nuclear weapons technology, but the research has provided application in many fields, including those in nuclear medicine and magnetic resonance imaging, ion implantation in materials engineering, and radiocarbon dating in geology and archaeology.

Unsupervised machine‑learning methods work with data that contains no labels, classifications or predefined categories. Rather than adjusting their behavior from external feedback, these algorithms search for patterns that recur across the dataset, then use the existence—or lack—of those patterns to guide their response to new inputs. The most common ways this capability is employed are in tasks such as grouping similar items together (clustering), compressing high‑dimensional information into more manageable forms (dimensionality reduction), and estimating how data points are distributed throughout the space (density estimation).

Second, Yuval Noah Harari argues that AI does not require a robot body or physical control to pose an existential risk. The essential parts of civilisation are not physical. Things like ideologies, law, government, money and the economy are built on language; they exist because there are stories that billions of people believe. The current prevalence of misinformation suggests that an AI could use language to convince people to believe anything, even to take actions that are destructive. Geoffrey Hinton said in 2025 that modern AI is particularly "good at persuasion" and getting better all the time. He asks, "Suppose you wanted to invade the capital of the US. Do you have to go there and do it yourself? No. You just have to be good at persuasion."

The most notable innovations under Islamic scholarship were in the field of optics and vision, which came from the works of many scientists like Ibn Sahl, Al-Kindi, Ibn al-Haytham, Al-Farisi and Avicenna. In his Book of Optics (also known as Kitāb al-Manāẓir) Ibn al-Haytham presented the idea of light rays as an alternative to the ancient Greek idea about visual rays. Like Ptolemy, Ibn al-Haytham applied controlled experiments, verifying the laws of refraction and reflection with the new concept of light rays, but still lacking the concept of image formation.

Random forest regression (RFR) falls under the umbrella of decision tree-based models. RFR is an ensemble learning method that builds multiple decision trees and averages their predictions to improve accuracy and to avoid overfitting. To build decision trees, RFR uses bootstrapped sampling; for instance, each decision tree is trained on random data from the training set. This random selection of RFR for training enables the model to reduce biased predictions and achieve a higher degree of accuracy. RFR generates independent decision trees, and it can work on single-output data as well as multiple regressor tasks. This makes RFR compatible to be use in various applications.

Inductive logic programming is particularly useful in bioinformatics and natural language processing. Gordon Plotkin and Ehud Shapiro laid the initial theoretical foundation for inductive machine learning in a logical setting. Shapiro built their first implementation (Model Inference System) in 1981: a Prolog program that inductively inferred logic programs from positive and negative examples. The term inductive here refers to philosophical induction, suggesting a theory to explain observed facts, rather than mathematical induction, proving a property for all members of a well-ordered set.

Despite the word science in its name, there is debate over whether or not computer science is a discipline of science, mathematics, or engineering. Allen Newell and Herbert A. Simon argued in 1975, Computer science is an empirical discipline. We would have called it an experimental science, but like astronomy, economics, and geology, some of its unique forms of observation and experience do not fit a narrow stereotype of the experimental method. Nonetheless, they are experiments. Each new machine that is built is an experiment. Actually constructing the machine poses a question to nature; and we listen for the answer by observing the machine in operation and analyzing it by all analytical and measurement means available. It has since been argued that computer science can be classified as an empirical science since it makes use of empirical testing to evaluate the correctness of programs, but a problem remains in defining the laws and theorems of computer science (if any exist) and defining the nature of experiments in computer science. Proponents of classifying computer science as an engineering discipline argue that the reliability of computational systems is investigated in the same way as bridges in civil engineering and airplanes in aerospace engineering. They also argue that while empirical sciences observe what presently exists, computer science observes what is possible to exist and while scientists discover laws from observation, no proper laws have been found in computer science and it is instead concerned with creating phenomena.

A machine learning model is a type of mathematical model that, once "trained" on a given dataset, can be used to make predictions or classifications on new data. During training, a learning algorithm iteratively adjusts the model's internal parameters to minimise errors in its predictions. By extension, the term "model" can refer to several levels of specificity, from a general class of models and their associated learning algorithms to a fully trained model with all its internal parameters tuned.

In addition to performance bounds, learning theorists study the time complexity and feasibility of learning. In computational learning theory, a computation is considered feasible if it can be done in polynomial time. There are two kinds of time complexity results: Positive results show that a certain class of functions can be learned in polynomial time. Negative results show that certain classes cannot be learned in polynomial time.

Beyond judging how accurately a learning algorithm can predict, theorists also investigate how much time the learning process demands and whether it is practically attainable. In computational learning theory, an algorithm is regarded as feasible only when its running time grows polynomially with the size of the problem instance. Time‑complexity findings therefore fall into two distinct types. A positive finding proves that a specific class of functions can be learned within polynomial time, while a negative finding shows that certain other classes cannot be learned in polynomial time.

A superintelligence refers to a speculative type of agent whose cognitive abilities would far exceed those of even the most brilliant and talented human thinkers. The idea is that, should research into artificial general intelligence eventually yield software that is sufficiently advanced, that program could modify its own code and become smarter. Each successive self‑revision would make the system increasingly adept at further improvement, creating a rapid, self‑reinforcing cycle. This runaway process is what I. J. Good described as an “intelligence explosion,” and what Vernor Vinge later dubbed the “singularity.”

Islamic scholars made their most celebrated contributions to the study of optics and how we see.  Figures such as Ibn Sahl, Al‑Kindi, Ibn al‑Haytham, Al‑Farisi and Avicenna advanced the field, each building on the ideas of their predecessors.  In particular, Ibn al‑Haytham’s treatise *Kitāb al‑Manāẓir* (the Book of Optics) introduced the notion that light travels in rays, contrasting with the older Greek theory that visual perception depended on rays emitted from the eye.  Following the method of Ptolemy, Ibn al‑Haytham carried out systematic experiments to observe how light behaves when it strikes surfaces, confirming the principles governing both refraction and reflection.  Although his work clarified the paths of light, it did not yet explain how images are formed.

The first serious attempts to explain how species change over time can be traced to Jean‑Baptiste Lamarck, who was the first to lay out a systematic evolutionary theory. Later, the British naturalist Charles Darwin built on that foundation by drawing together several contemporary ideas. He incorporated Alexander von Humboldt’s insights into the geographic distribution of organisms, Charles Lyell’s principle that geological processes operate uniformly over long periods, and Thomas Malthus’s observations about the dynamics of population growth. Coupled with Darwin’s own skill in comparative anatomy and the wealth of specimens and notes he gathered in the field, these elements allowed him to propose a more robust model of evolution driven by natural selection. Independently, Alfred Russell Wallace applied comparable lines of reasoning and the same body of evidence, arriving at conclusions that mirrored Darwin’s about the mechanism of evolutionary change.

Determining whether a sophisticated artificial intelligence truly experiences feelings is a problem that may be beyond reliable measurement; we might never know for certain, and in many cases it could be impossible to assess. Nevertheless, if there is a non‑negligible probability that a machine possesses the capacity to feel pleasure or pain, many argue that it should be granted some form of moral consideration—perhaps comparable to the protections afforded to sentient animals. In addition, if an AI exhibits sapient qualities—such as advanced intelligence, the ability to reason, or self‑awareness—this could serve as another justification for extending rights or welfare safeguards to it. Some proposals also suggest establishing “robot rights” as a pragmatic framework for smoothly incorporating autonomous agents into human society.

Evidence from the predicted abundances of the lightest elements, together with the 1964 observation of the cosmic microwave background, gave decisive support to the idea that the universe began with a hot Big Bang. The framework that describes this scenario relies fundamentally on two concepts: Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which governs how matter and energy shape spacetime, and the cosmological principle, which assumes that the universe looks the same in every direction and location on large scales. Building on these foundations, modern cosmology has converged on the ΛCDM (Lambda‑Cold Dark Matter) description of cosmic evolution. This model incorporates an early phase of rapid expansion known as cosmic inflation, as well as the presently dominant components called dark energy and dark matter, which together account for the observed dynamics and structure of the cosmos.

In the early twentieth century two groundbreaking frameworks—relativity and quantum mechanics—redefined how physicists understood the universe. Although these theories introduced a radically new conceptual picture, they did not make the earlier, well‑tested physical models any less useful for everyday applications. As a result, the discipline has become organized into two broad areas. “Classical physics” covers the theories that were formulated before the new revolutions and that continue to work effectively in most practical situations. “Modern physics,” by contrast, groups together the phenomena that require the principles of quantum mechanics or relativity for their explanation. This split reflects both the historical development of the field and the distinct domains where each set of ideas is most relevant.

Computer science is built on a foundation of algorithms and data structures, which provide the essential tools for processing information.  At a more abstract level, the theory of computation studies mathematical models of how computation can be carried out and categorizes the types of problems that such models can solve.  Security‑related disciplines, such as cryptography and computer security, focus on creating methods for protected communication and on identifying ways to avoid weaknesses in systems.

Visual aspects of computing are explored through computer graphics and computational geometry, which deal with producing and manipulating images.  Separate but related, programming language theory investigates the various formalisms used to express computational procedures, while database theory concentrates on the organization and handling of large collections of data.

The ways in which people interact with machines fall under human‑computer interaction, whereas software engineering is concerned with the systematic design and underlying principles of software creation.  Larger, more complex constructs are examined in areas like operating systems, networking, and embedded systems, each of which studies the architecture and operational rules of sophisticated hardware‑software environments.  The design of the physical components themselves is the realm of computer architecture, which describes how computers and their peripheral equipment are built.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning seek to emulate purposeful behaviors—such as solving problems, making decisions, adapting to surroundings, planning, and learning—that are observed in living organisms.  Within AI, computer vision works on interpreting visual data from images and videos, and natural language processing is devoted to comprehending and handling textual and linguistic information.

Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) is a technique for automatically discovering rules. It relies on logic programming to represent three kinds of information in a single, consistent format: the facts that describe the problem domain (the background knowledge), the example instances that the system should learn from, and the candidate rules (hypotheses) it seeks to generate. The process begins with a formal encoding of the known background knowledge together with a collection of examples stored as a logical database of facts. From this input, an ILP system searches for a logic program that correctly covers every positive example while excluding every negative one—that is, a program that logically entails all the desired cases and none of the undesired ones. 

A closely related discipline is inductive programming, which broadens the notion of hypothesis representation beyond logic programs. In inductive programming, the learned models may be expressed in any programming language, such as functional languages, rather than being limited to the logic‑programming paradigm.

In data mining, anomaly detection, also known as outlier detection, is the identification of rare items, events or observations that raise suspicions by differing significantly from the majority of the data. Typically, the anomalous items represent an issue such as bank fraud, a structural defect, medical problems or errors in a text. Anomalies are referred to as outliers, novelties, noise, deviations and exceptions.

In many practical situations a brute‑force, exhaustive search quickly becomes impractical. As the number of possible locations to examine expands, the total search space can reach astronomically large sizes, making the process either painfully slow or impossible to finish at all. To cope with this limitation, practitioners rely on heuristics—simple rules of thumb—that steer the search toward options that are more likely to lead to a solution. By ranking and selecting the most promising paths first, these heuristics dramatically improve the chances of reaching a goal within a reasonable amount of time.

A learner’s primary aim is to be able to extend what it has observed to situations it has not yet encountered. In this setting, “generalisation” means that after being exposed to a set of training data, the system can still make reliable predictions on fresh, unseen examples or tasks. Those training examples are drawn from an underlying probability distribution that is typically unknown, yet assumed to reflect the broader realm of possible occurrences. The learner must therefore infer a comprehensive model of this domain, one that captures its essential patterns well enough to yield sufficiently accurate outputs when presented with new inputs.

The foundations of quantum mechanics were laid by the pioneering contributions of Werner Heisenberg, Erwin Schrödinger and Paul Dirac. Building on their insights and on related investigations, physicists assembled the Standard Model, the theoretical framework that describes all known elementary particles and their interactions. A decisive experimental confirmation came in 2012, when CERN announced the observation of a particle whose behavior matched that expected for the Higgs boson. To date, every particle foreseen by the Standard Model has been detected, and no additional fundamental particles have emerged. Nevertheless, researchers continue to explore extensions of the model—such as supersymmetry—to address phenomena it does not explain. The development and testing of these theories rely heavily on mathematical tools, especially those dealing with probability theory and group structures.

There are many kinds of classifiers in use. The decision tree is the simplest and most widely used symbolic machine learning algorithm. K-nearest neighbour algorithm was the most widely used analogical AI until the mid-1990s, and Kernel methods such as the support vector machine (SVM) displaced k-nearest neighbour in the 1990s.

Scientific breakthroughs in physics have historically opened the door to revolutionary tools and systems. When researchers deepened their grasp of electromagnetism, solid‑state phenomena, and nuclear forces, the practical outgrowths included devices that reshaped everyday life—television sets, digital computers, household machines, and even the creation of nuclear armaments. Likewise, the formulation of thermodynamic principles supplied the theoretical groundwork that powered the rise of large‑scale industry. In a similar vein, the study of mechanical laws spurred mathematicians to devise calculus, a new mathematical language that underpins modern engineering and physics. Each of these examples illustrates how expanding physical knowledge directly translates into transformative technological advances.

Criticism of COMPAS highlighted that machine learning models are designed to make "predictions" that are only valid if we assume that the future will resemble the past. If they are trained on data that includes the results of racist decisions in the past, machine learning models must predict that racist decisions will be made in the future. If an application then uses these predictions as recommendations, some of these "recommendations" will likely be racist. Thus, machine learning is not well suited to help make decisions in areas where there is hope that the future will be better than the past. It is descriptive rather than prescriptive.

Integrated circuits have shown a steady rise in the number of transistors they contain, with the count roughly increasing by a factor of two about every year and a half. This regular escalation is captured by what the industry calls Moore’s law, a principle first pointed out by Gordon Moore, one of Intel’s founders.

Graphics‑processing units have been advancing at an even more rapid pace. Their performance improvements are often referred to as Huang’s law, a name that honors Jensen Huang, the co‑founder and chief executive of Nvidia. Both “laws” describe observable, technology‑driven trends without introducing any additional information beyond what is given.

Modern natural‑language processing relies heavily on deep‑learning methods. One common approach is word embedding, which converts each word into a numeric vector that captures its semantic properties. Another pivotal technique is the transformer architecture; its core innovation is an attention mechanism that lets the model weigh the relevance of different parts of a sentence when processing language. These and other deep‑learning tools have paved the way for powerful language models.

The breakthrough known as the generative pre‑trained transformer (GPT) appeared in 2019, marking the first time such models could produce text that reads as coherent and fluent. Progress accelerated quickly, and by 2023 GPT‑style systems were able to attain scores comparable to those of humans on standardized assessments such as the bar exam, the SAT, and the GRE, as well as on a variety of practical tasks.

Recent progress in deep learning has pushed neural networks—a type of statistical algorithm—past many earlier machine‑learning techniques in terms of accuracy and capability. Starting in the late 2000s and intensifying through the early 2010s, this surge gave machine learning a leading role within the broader arena of artificial intelligence. Because of that prominence, people now frequently use the expressions “machine learning” and “artificial intelligence” as if they meant the same thing, even though the two concepts are distinct.

Conservation biology is the study of the conservation of Earth's biodiversity with the aim of protecting species, their habitats, and ecosystems from excessive rates of extinction and the erosion of biotic interactions. It is concerned with factors that influence the maintenance, loss, and restoration of biodiversity and the science of sustaining evolutionary processes that engender genetic, population, species, and ecosystem diversity. The concern stems from estimates suggesting that up to 50% of all species on the planet will disappear within the next 50 years, which has contributed to poverty, starvation, and will reset the course of evolution on this planet. Conservation biologists research the trends of biodiversity loss, species extinctions, and the negative effect these are having on our capabilities to sustain the well-being of human society.

Biology examines life across multiple levels of organization, from molecules and cells to organisms, population, and ecosystems. Subdisciplines include molecular biology, physiology, ecology, evolutionary biology, developmental biology, and systematics, among others. Each of these fields applies a range of methods to investigate biological phenomena, including observation, experimentation, and mathematical modeling. Modern biology is grounded in the theory of evolution by natural selection, first articulated by Charles Darwin, and in the molecular understanding of genes encoded in DNA. The discovery of the structure of DNA and advances in molecular genetics have transformed many areas of biology, leading to applications in medicine, agriculture, biotechnology, and environmental science.

Aristotle, a prolific writer of the fourth century BC, produced a major work entitled *Physics* alongside many other treatises. His ideas about the natural world dominated scholarly thought for roughly two thousand years. In forming his system, Aristotle combined a modest amount of direct observation with extensive logical reasoning, yet he never subjected his conclusions to systematic experimental testing. Although his physics contained numerous flaws, it supplied an early conceptual scaffold that subsequent philosophers and scientists could modify and expand. Modern science has completely replaced Aristotle’s methodology and conclusions with approaches grounded in empirical verification.

Cluster analysis groups a collection of data points into distinct subsets—known as clusters—so that members of the same group resemble each other according to one or more pre‑chosen criteria, while members of different groups are markedly unlike one another. The way a particular clustering algorithm determines these groups depends on the assumptions it makes about the underlying data structure. Most methods rely on a similarity (or distance) measure that quantifies how close two observations are; they then assess the quality of the resulting partition by looking at two key attributes. First, internal compactness gauges how tightly packed the points are within each cluster, reflecting the similarity among its members. Second, separation measures how far apart the clusters lie from one another, indicating the degree of dissimilarity between groups. In addition to similarity‑based approaches, some techniques construct clusters by estimating the data’s density or by examining how points connect in a graph, using these properties to define the clusters.

Generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) are large language models (LLMs) that generate text based on the semantic relationships between words in sentences. Text-based GPT models are pre-trained on a large corpus of text that can be from the Internet. The pretraining consists of predicting the next token (a token being usually a word, subword, or punctuation). Throughout this pretraining, GPT models accumulate knowledge about the world and can then generate human-like text by repeatedly predicting the next token. Typically, a subsequent training phase makes the model more truthful, useful, and harmless, usually with a technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Current GPT models are prone to generating falsehoods called "hallucinations". These can be reduced with RLHF and quality data, but the problem has been getting worse for reasoning systems. Such systems are used in chatbots, which allow people to ask a question or request a task in simple text.

John Searle described the doctrine that a suitably programmed machine, given the correct inputs and producing the appropriate outputs, would possess a mind in exactly the same way that people do. He labeled this view “strong AI.” To dispute the idea, Searle introduced the Chinese‑room thought experiment. The experiment is intended to demonstrate that, despite a computer’s ability to reproduce human‑like behavior flawlessly, it would still lack a genuine mind.

An artificial neural network is built from many interconnected units, often referred to as artificial neurons, that loosely imitate the behavior of biological brain cells. During a training phase the system learns to identify specific patterns; after this learning it can spot the same patterns when presented with new, unseen data.

The structure of such a network includes three main parts: an entry layer that receives the raw input, at least one intermediate (hidden) layer where processing occurs, and a final layer that delivers the output. Each unit in a layer performs a mathematical operation on the data it receives, and once the accumulated weight value exceeds a preset limit, the resulting signal is passed forward to the subsequent layer.

When a network contains two or more hidden layers, it is commonly labeled a deep neural network, reflecting the additional depth of processing stages between the input and output.

AI‑driven gadgets and services—ranging from voice‑activated assistants to interconnected “smart” devices—regularly harvest users’ personal details. This ongoing collection raises worries that the data may be gathered in a way that feels invasive and that outsiders could obtain it without permission. Moreover, the power of artificial intelligence to sift through and merge enormous quantities of information intensifies the privacy problem. As these systems link together disparate data points, they create the possibility of a society in which everyday actions are constantly observed and evaluated, yet the mechanisms that should protect or disclose such monitoring are often missing or unclear.

The commercial AI scene is dominated by Big Tech companies such as Alphabet Inc., Amazon, Apple Inc., Meta Platforms, and Microsoft. Some of these companies already own the vast majority of existing cloud infrastructure and computing power from data centres, allowing them to entrench further in the marketplace. For most of 2025-2026, AI-related companies have also dominated stock market returns. According to a July 2024 report from S&P Global, investors had started questioning whether the enormous spending on AI infrastructure and data centers would generate sufficient profits, leading to increased volatility in technology and semiconductor stocks and to concerns about a potential AI bubble. In a 2025 Economic Policy article, economists Anton Korinek and Jai Vipra described some AI related market sectors as highly concentrated.

The roots of formal, mechanical reasoning trace back to the early work of philosophers and mathematicians in ancient times. Over centuries, the discipline of logic evolved until it directly inspired Alan Turing’s theory of computation. Turing argued that a device manipulating only the simplest symbols—binary digits such as “0” and “1”—could, in principle, reproduce any kind of mathematical thought.

At roughly the same period, breakthroughs in cybernetics, information theory, and neurobiology sparked the idea of constructing an “electronic brain.” Building on these interdisciplinary insights, researchers began to lay the groundwork for what would later be called artificial intelligence. Notably, in 1943 Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts introduced a model of “artificial neurons,” providing a rudimentary blueprint for electronic decision‑making units. A few years later, Turing’s seminal 1950 article, *Computing Machinery and Intelligence*, presented the famous Turing test and argued convincingly that the notion of machine intelligence was viable. These early theoretical advances collectively set the stage for modern AI research.

Information appears in many formats—pictures, sounds, moving images and other multimedia forms.  To move these data, they are broken into small units that travel as continuous streams carried by various signals.  The science that examines how such data are handled is known in Europe as informatics; it concentrates on the algorithms that process information without regard to whether the underlying medium is electrical, mechanical or even biological.  Because of this abstract focus, informatics underlies fields such as information theory, telecommunications and information engineering, and it finds concrete uses in areas like medical‑image analysis and the generation of synthetic speech.  Despite its broad reach, the discipline still contains open questions; for example, the exact lower‑bound on the computational complexity of fast Fourier transform algorithms remains an unsolved problem in theoretical computer science.

Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms. It is a broad natural science that encompasses a wide range of fields and unifying principles that explain the structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, and distribution of life. Central to biology are five fundamental themes: the cell as the basic unit of life, genes and heredity as the basis of inheritance, evolution as the driver of biological diversity, energy transformation for sustaining life processes, and homeostasis, the maintenance of internal stability.

In the 1990s, machine learning emerged as a distinct discipline and began to expand rapidly. Rather than striving for full artificial intelligence, researchers redirected their efforts toward concrete, solvable tasks that had practical value. This new direction meant moving away from the symbolic techniques traditionally associated with AI and instead embracing tools drawn from statistics, fuzzy logic, and probability theory to build models and algorithms.

Isaac Asimov created the famous Three Laws of Robotics, first appearing in many of his stories and most prominently alongside the super‑intelligent computer called “Multivac.”  These rules have become a frequent reference point whenever non‑specialists talk about the moral behavior of machines.  Because of their pervasive presence in popular media, virtually every researcher who works on artificial intelligence is aware of Asimov’s formulation.  Nonetheless, within the professional community the laws are largely regarded as ineffective tools for guiding real‑world AI design.  A chief criticism is that the statements are vague, making it difficult to translate them into precise, enforceable guidelines.  Consequently, while they enjoy cultural fame, they are seen by experts as impractical for actual machine‑ethics work.

Support-vector machines (SVMs), also known as support-vector networks, are a set of related supervised learning methods used for classification and regression. Given a set of training examples, each marked as belonging to one of two categories, an SVM training algorithm builds a model that predicts whether a new example falls into one category. An SVM training algorithm is a non-probabilistic, binary, linear classifier, although methods such as Platt scaling exist to use SVM in a probabilistic classification setting. In addition to performing linear classification, SVMs can efficiently perform a non-linear classification using what is called the kernel trick, implicitly mapping their inputs into high-dimensional feature spaces.

Supervised learning algorithms build a mathematical model of a set of data that contains both the inputs and the desired outputs. The data, known as training data, consists of a set of training examples. Each training example has one or more inputs and the desired output, also known as a supervisory signal. In the mathematical model, each training example is represented by an array or vector, sometimes called a feature vector, and the training data is represented by a matrix. Through iterative optimisation of an objective function, supervised learning algorithms learn a function that can be used to predict the output associated with new inputs. An optimal function allows the algorithm to correctly determine the output for inputs that were not a part of the training data. An algorithm that improves the accuracy of its outputs or predictions over time is said to have learned to perform that task.

The link between computer science and software engineering has long been debated, especially because scholars disagree about what each term truly encompasses. According to David Parnas, the situation resembles the classic split between science and engineering in other fields. He argues that the core concern of computer science is to investigate the fundamental characteristics of computation itself, treating it as a theoretical discipline. In contrast, software engineering is primarily concerned with constructing particular computational solutions that serve real‑world purposes. Though distinct in their main objectives, the two areas complement one another, each contributing a necessary perspective to the broader domain of computing.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have drawn growing attention to the question of AI welfare and rights. Supporters of this perspective contend that, should machines ever develop genuine consciousness, humans would find it remarkably simple to dismiss that status. They caution that this tendency could become a moral blind spot reminiscent of past injustices such as slavery or intensive animal farming. If sentient AI were brought into existence and then treated without consideration, the result could be widespread suffering on a massive scale.

In addition to overall accuracy, investigators frequently report sensitivity and specificity, meaning true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR), respectively. Similarly, investigators sometimes report the false positive rate (FPR) as well as the false negative rate (FNR). However, these rates are ratios that fail to reveal their numerators and denominators. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC), along with the accompanying Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), offer additional tools for classification model assessment. Higher AUC is associated with a better performing model.

In January 2025, Microsoft proposed the technique rStar-Math that leverages Monte Carlo tree search and step-by-step reasoning, enabling a relatively small language model like Qwen-7B to solve 53% of the AIME 2024 and 90% of the MATH benchmark problems. Google DeepMind has developed models for solving mathematical problems: AlphaDev, AlphaEvolve, AlphaGeometry, AlphaProof, AlphaTensor, and FunSearch.

Tom M. Mitchell provided a widely quoted, more formal definition of the algorithms studied in the machine learning field: "A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P,  improves with experience E." This definition of the tasks in which machine learning is concerned is fundamentally operational rather than defining the field in cognitive terms. This follows Alan Turing's proposal in his paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", in which the question, "Can machines think?", is replaced by asking whether machines can convincingly imitate a human in its responses to human-posed questions.

Historical cryptography is the art of writing and deciphering secret messages. Modern cryptography is the scientific study of problems relating to distributed computations that can be attacked. Technologies studied in modern cryptography include symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, cryptographic hash functions, key-agreement protocols, blockchain, zero-knowledge proofs, and garbled circuits.

Classification of machine learning models can be validated by accuracy estimation techniques like the holdout method, which splits the data into a training and test set (conventionally 2/3 training set and 1/3 test set designation) and evaluates the performance of the training model on the test set. In comparison, the K-fold-cross-validation method randomly partitions the data into K subsets and then K experiments are performed each considering 1 subset for evaluation and the remaining K-1 subsets for training the model. In addition to the holdout and cross-validation methods, bootstrap, which samples n instances with replacement from the dataset, can be used to assess model accuracy.

Peter Denning has identified the central inquiry of computer science as the quest to determine “what can be automated.” The field known as the theory of computation seeks answers to two core aspects of this question. First, computability theory investigates which problems can be resolved at all when we model computation using idealized machines. It asks, for each theoretical model, which tasks are within reach of an algorithmic solution. Second, computational complexity theory shifts the focus to the amount of resources—chiefly time and memory—needed to carry out those solutions. By analyzing the efficiency of different algorithmic strategies, this branch gauges how demanding various computational problems are in practice. Together, these two areas delineate the limits of what can be computed and the costs associated with doing so.

Physics underpins many engineering tasks, shaping the way structures and technologies are designed and evaluated. In the realm of mechanics, the branch known as statics provides the principles engineers rely on when constructing bridges and other immobile frameworks, ensuring that forces are balanced and the works remain stable. Acoustic theory, when applied, enables precise control of sound, which translates into concert venues with superior acoustic quality. In parallel, the study of optics guides the development of advanced optical instruments, improving their performance and reliability. Beyond physical constructions, a solid grasp of physics contributes to the creation of highly realistic flight simulators, immersive video games, and convincing cinematic effects. Moreover, investigative work often depends on physical analysis, making physics an essential component of forensic examinations.

There are various conflicting definitions and mathematical models of fairness. These notions depend on ethical assumptions, and are influenced by beliefs about society. One broad category is distributive fairness, which focuses on the outcomes, often identifying groups and seeking to compensate for statistical disparities. Representational fairness tries to ensure that AI systems do not reinforce negative stereotypes or render certain groups invisible. Procedural fairness focuses on the decision process rather than the outcome. The most relevant notions of fairness may depend on the context, notably the type of AI application and the stakeholders. The subjectivity in the notions of bias and fairness makes it difficult for companies to operationalise them. Having access to sensitive attributes such as race or gender is also considered by many AI ethicists to be necessary in order to compensate for biases, but it may conflict with anti-discrimination laws.

Mathematics serves as a precise, concise language that captures the patterns and order observed in the natural world. This view was championed early on by thinkers such as Pythagoras, Plato, Galileo and Newton, who all recognized the power of mathematical description. In contemporary philosophy, scholars including Hilary Putnam and Penelope Maddy argue that the truth of logical statements—and consequently of mathematical reasoning—is not purely abstract but rooted in empirical reality. They often pair this stance with the idea that logical laws reflect universal regularities inherent in the world’s structural makeup, a perspective that helps to clarify the distinctive connection between logic, mathematics and the empirical world.

Starting in 2012, the speed of deep learning was increased one hundred-fold by switching to GPUs, and there were enormous amounts of data available on the internet (called at the time "big data") as well as curated datasets used for benchmark testing, such as ImageNet. Usage of deep learning increased in 2012–2015 due to these improvements. In 2025, Geoffrey Hinton said that, until the 2010s, "We couldn't do anything very impressive because we didn’t have enough data and we didn't have enough computation."

Many problems in AI (including reasoning, planning, learning, perception, and robotics) require the agent to operate with incomplete or uncertain information. AI researchers have devised a number of tools to solve these problems using methods from probability theory and economics. Precise mathematical tools have been developed that analyse how an agent can make choices and plan, using decision theory, decision analysis, and information value theory. These tools include models such as Markov decision processes, dynamic decision networks, game theory and mechanism design.

Various approaches to learning data representations impose different structural constraints on the form of the result.  
Manifold‑learning techniques, for example, seek a compact, low‑dimensional embedding of the data, preserving the essential geometry while discarding redundant directions.  In contrast, sparse‑coding methods aim for representations that contain many zero entries, so that only a small subset of the basis elements is active for any given observation.
