Given an encoding of the known background knowledge and a set of examples represented as a logical database of facts, an ILP system will derive a hypothesized logic program that entails all positive and no negative examples. Inductive programming is a related field that considers any kind of programming language for representing hypotheses (and not only logic programming), such as functional programs.

The early 1980s marked a renaissance for artificial‑intelligence research, driven mainly by the emergence of expert‑system programs that could mimic the reasoning of human specialists. These commercial products proved profitable enough that, by 1985, the global AI market was valued at more than one billion dollars. Meanwhile, Japan’s ambitious “fifth‑generation” computer initiative captured the attention of policymakers, prompting both the United States and the United Kingdom to renew financial support for university‑based AI projects. This optimism was short‑lived; the collapse of the Lisp‑machine industry in 1987 stripped away a key source of funding and confidence, ushering in a second, more prolonged period of disappointment for the field that came to be known as an AI winter.

Fairness in artificial intelligence is a contested idea, reflected in a range of mathematical models that hinge on differing ethical viewpoints and societal expectations.  One major strand, often called **distributive fairness**, concentrates on the results that an algorithm produces.  It typically involves identifying particular groups and attempting to correct measurable outcome gaps between them.  A second strand, **representational fairness**, aims to prevent AI from perpetuating harmful stereotypes or from marginalising certain populations by making them invisible in the system’s outputs.  A third perspective, **procedural fairness**, shifts the focus from what is decided to how the decision is reached, emphasizing the fairness of the underlying process itself.

Which of these notions is most appropriate depends heavily on the specific AI application and on who the stakeholders are.  Because concepts of bias and fairness are inherently subjective, firms often find it hard to translate them into concrete practices.  Many AI ethicists argue that having access to protected attributes—such as race or gender—is essential for detecting and correcting unfair patterns.  However, using such sensitive data can clash with anti‑discrimination legislation, creating a tension between the goal of bias mitigation and legal constraints.

For the best performance in the context of generalisation, the complexity of the hypothesis should match the complexity of the function underlying the data. If the hypothesis is less complex than the function, then the model has underfitted the data. If the complexity of the model is increased in response, then the training error decreases. But if the hypothesis is too complex, then the model is subject to overfitting and generalisation will be poorer.

Multivariate linear regression broadens the ordinary linear‑regression framework so that several response variables can be modeled at once. In this technique a single set of predictors is linked to multiple outcomes by means of a linear equation that operates in a higher‑dimensional space. The method works best when the different outputs are related to each other or follow common structures—for example, when one wishes to forecast a group of economic measures together, or when reconstructing an image that naturally contains many pixel values. By fitting such a multidimensional model, the approach captures the shared patterns that drive all the dependent variables simultaneously.

"Neats" hope that intelligent behaviour is described using simple, elegant principles (such as logic or optimisation). "Scruffies" expect that it necessarily requires solving a large number of unrelated problems. Neats defend their programs with theoretical rigour, scruffies rely mainly on incremental testing to see if they work. This issue was actively discussed in the 1970s and 1980s. The rise of deep learning may represent a shift toward the scruffies.

Three broad categories of anomaly detection techniques exist. Unsupervised anomaly detection techniques detect anomalies in an unlabelled test data set under the assumption that the majority of the instances in the data set are normal, by looking for instances that seem to fit the least to the remainder of the data set. Supervised anomaly detection techniques require a data set that has been labelled as "normal" and "abnormal" and involves training a classifier (the key difference from many other statistical classification problems is the inherently unbalanced nature of outlier detection). Semi-supervised anomaly detection techniques construct a model representing normal behaviour from a given normal training data set and then test the likelihood of a test instance being generated by the model.

In particle physics, the first pieces of experimental evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model have begun to appear. Foremost among these are indications that neutrinos have non-zero mass. These experimental results appear to have solved the long-standing solar neutrino problem, and the physics of massive neutrinos remains an area of active theoretical and experimental research. The Large Hadron Collider has already found the Higgs boson, but future research aims to prove or disprove the supersymmetry, which extends the Standard Model of particle physics. Research on the nature of the major mysteries of dark matter and dark energy is also currently ongoing.

In the 2020s, major technology firms have laid down extensive electricity networks and artificial‑intelligence platforms to support the rapid expansion of AI applications. According to a 2025 analysis by the consulting firm McKinsey & Company, investment in U.S. AI infrastructure and data‑center capacity is projected to reach roughly $2.7 trillion by 2030. That level of spending would outpace the monthly outlay of the World War II Manhattan Project, highlighting the scale of financial commitment devoted to building the backbone of the coming AI era.

Finding a provably correct or optimal solution is intractable for many important problems. Soft computing is a set of techniques, including genetic algorithms, fuzzy logic and neural networks, that are tolerant of imprecision, uncertainty, partial truth and approximation. Soft computing was introduced in the late 1980s and most successful AI programs in the 21st century are examples of soft computing with neural networks.

Long before the age of electronic digital machines, the ideas that would later define computer science were already taking shape. Ancient peoples built devices such as the abacus to carry out preset arithmetic operations, allowing them to perform tasks like multiplication and division more efficiently. At the same time, they devised step‑by‑step procedures—early algorithms—to guide these calculations. Thus, both the mechanical tools for fixed numerical work and the conceptual methods for processing numbers have their origins in antiquity, predating any sophisticated computing hardware.

Deductive reasoning in logic involves taking statements that are accepted as true—called premises—and using them to demonstrate the truth of another statement, the conclusion. One common way to display such a demonstration is through a proof tree. In this diagram each point, or node, carries a sentence, and the logical steps that move from earlier sentences to later ones are shown as connections from child nodes up to their parent node, guided by specific inference rules. This structure makes the logical flow from premises to conclusion visible and organized.

Mathematical physics sits at the intersection of two disciplines: it uses the tools of mathematics to address questions that belong to physics. In this field the techniques employed are strictly mathematical, while the phenomena being examined are physical. A typical problem begins by translating a real‑world situation into a mathematical model that represents the system under study. At the same time, a physical law—also expressed in mathematical form—is introduced to act on that model. Throughout the calculation, each intermediate equation or statement carries a physical interpretation, but uncovering that meaning can be difficult. By contrast, the ultimate result of the computation is usually easy to connect with the original physical question, because it directly provides the answer the researcher set out to obtain.

The computational analysis of machine learning algorithms and their performance is a branch of theoretical computer science known as computational learning theory. One major framework is the probably approximately correct learning model. Because training sets are finite and the future is uncertain, learning theory usually does not yield guarantees of the performance of algorithms. Instead, probabilistic bounds on the performance are quite common. The bias–variance decomposition is one way to quantify generalisation error.

Embedded machine learning is a sub-field of machine learning where models are deployed on embedded systems with limited computing resources, such as wearable computers, edge devices and microcontrollers. Running models directly on these devices eliminates the need to transfer and store data on cloud servers for further processing, thereby reducing the risk of data breaches, privacy leaks and theft of intellectual property, personal data and business secrets. Embedded machine learning can be achieved through various techniques, such as hardware acceleration, approximate computing, and model optimization. Common optimization techniques include pruning, quantisation, knowledge distillation, low-rank factorisation, network architecture search, and parameter sharing.

Formal methods are a particular kind of mathematically based technique for the specification, development and verification of software and hardware systems. The use of formal methods for software and hardware design is motivated by the expectation that, as in other engineering disciplines, performing appropriate mathematical analysis can contribute to the reliability and robustness of a design. They form an important theoretical underpinning for software engineering, especially where safety or security is involved. Formal methods are a useful adjunct to software testing since they help avoid errors and can also give a framework for testing. For industrial use, tool support is required. However, the high cost of using formal methods means that they are usually only used in the development of high-integrity and life-critical systems, where safety or security is of utmost importance. Formal methods are best described as the application of a fairly broad variety of theoretical computer science fundamentals, in particular logic calculi, formal languages, automata theory, and program semantics, but also type systems and algebraic data types to problems in software and hardware specification and verification.

Atomic physics studies the electron shells of atoms. Current research focuses on activities in quantum control, cooling and trapping of atoms and ions, low-temperature collision dynamics and the effects of electron correlation on structure and dynamics. Atomic physics is influenced by the nucleus (see hyperfine splitting), but intra-nuclear phenomena such as fission and fusion are considered part of nuclear physics.

Rule‑based machine learning refers to any learning technique that discovers, refines, or evolves explicit “rules” for handling knowledge. The hallmark of such algorithms is that they construct a collection of relational rules, and the ensemble of those rules embodies the information the system has captured. Unlike many other learning methods, which typically produce a single, all‑purpose model that is applied uniformly to every new case, rule‑based approaches rely on the interplay of multiple conditional statements to reach conclusions. Prominent families of rule‑based methods include learning classifier systems, association‑rule learning, and artificial immune systems.

Within the AI community and among technology leaders, attitudes diverge sharply regarding the long‑term hazards of a superintelligent system. A notable segment of experts and industry figures feel uneasy about the possibility that such an intelligence could pose an existential threat, whereas a comparable group does not share that level of alarm. Among those who have publicly highlighted the danger are well‑known scientists and innovators such as Stephen Hawking, Bill Gates, and Elon Musk, together with pioneering AI researchers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, Demis Hassabis, and Sam Altman. Their statements underscore a growing concern that advanced artificial intelligence could eventually endanger humanity.

Learning algorithms often strive to uncover more effective ways to represent the data they are given. Traditional methods such as principal component analysis and clustering serve as early examples of this goal. Modern approaches, frequently referred to as feature‑learning or representation‑learning algorithms, go a step further: they attempt to retain the essential information contained in the raw inputs while reshaping it into a form that is more advantageous for downstream tasks like classification or prediction. In practice, these methods act as a preprocessing stage, converting the original observations into a new set of features that can be fed directly into a task‑specific model.

An important property of such representation learning techniques is their ability to reconstruct the original inputs, even when those inputs are drawn from an unknown data‑generating process. While the reconstructed outputs aim to reflect realistic patterns, the algorithms are not required to reproduce configurations that would be highly unlikely under the underlying distribution. By automating the creation of useful features, these methods replace the traditional, labor‑intensive process of manual feature engineering, allowing the system itself to discover and employ the most relevant characteristics of the data for the problem at hand.

Artificial intelligence seeks to recreate, in machines, the purposeful activities that living beings display—things such as solving problems, making choices, adjusting to surroundings, acquiring knowledge, and exchanging information.  The discipline emerged from early work in cybernetics and was formally launched at the Dartmouth Conference of 1956.  From its inception, AI has required input from many fields, including applied mathematics, formal logic, the study of signs, electrical engineering, the philosophy of mind, brain science, and the analysis of social behavior.

Although the public often equates AI with the creation of robots, the majority of real‑world uses involve embedding intelligent modules within software systems that must interpret and manipulate data.  The seed of the whole endeavor can be traced to Alan Turing’s late‑1940s inquiry “Can computers think?”, a question that still lacks a definitive answer.  Nevertheless, the Turing test continues to serve as a benchmark for judging whether a machine’s output approximates human intelligence.

In practice, AI has become increasingly adept at carrying out evaluative and predictive functions that would otherwise demand human oversight.  These automated capabilities are now regularly employed in complex applications that process large, real‑world data sets, thereby reducing the need for direct human monitoring and intervention.

From the early seventeenth century the ambition to automate arithmetic took shape in a series of ingenious devices. In 1623 Wilhelm Schickard built the first functional mechanical calculator, introducing the concept of a machine that could perform calculations without human intervention. A half‑century later, Gottfried Leibniz unveiled his “Stepped Reckoner,” a digital mechanism that not only added and subtracted but also embodied the binary numeral system—a notion he recorded even though Thomas Harriot had described it earlier.

The practical use of such machines entered the commercial arena when Thomas de Colmar, in 1820, created a simplified arithmometer. This instrument proved robust enough for everyday office work, marking the birth of the mechanical‑calculator industry. Inspired by this progress, Charles Babbage began work on the Difference Engine in 1822, a massive automatic calculator intended to compute tables of numbers. The challenges he encountered led him, in 1834, to sketch the Analytical Engine, a far more ambitious design that incorporated many features of today’s computers. A pivotal element was the adoption of punched cards—borrowed from the Jacquard loom—to store and feed instructions, giving the machine theoretically unlimited programmability.

The theoretical possibilities of programmable computation were illustrated by Ada Lovelace in 1843. While translating a French article on Babbage’s engine, she appended a detailed method for generating Bernoulli numbers, which is now regarded as the earliest published algorithm intended for execution on a machine. Decades later, Herman Hollerith’s 1885 tabulator employed punched cards to tabulate statistical data; his enterprise eventually merged into what became IBM.

Even after Babbage’s era, the quest for analytical engines continued. In 1909 Percy Ludgate produced the second known design for a mechanical analytical engine, working independently of Babbage’s earlier sketches. Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo entered the scene in 1914 with a series of essays that described an electromechanical calculator controlled by a read‑only program and introduced the concept of floating‑point arithmetic. To commemorate the centenary of the arithmometer, he demonstrated a prototype electromechanical arithmometer in Paris in 1920, showing that typed commands could drive automatic printing of results.

The lineage reached a milestone in 1937 when Howard Aiken persuaded IBM to construct the ASCC, also called the Harvard Mark I. Built on the principles of Babbage’s Analytical Engine—punched‑card input and a central processing unit—the massive programmable calculator was hailed as the fulfillment of Babbage’s long‑standing vision. Together, these milestones trace a continuous thread from early hand‑crafted calculators to the programmable machines that laid the groundwork for modern computing.

The COMPAS system is a privately‑developed risk‑assessment tool that many U.S. courts rely on to predict whether a defendant is likely to reoffend. In 2016, journalist Julia Angwin of ProPublica uncovered evidence that the algorithm produced racially disparate outcomes even though it never received the defendants’ race as an input. While the overall error rate was the same for Black and White individuals—61 % for each group—the nature of those errors was not balanced. The model tended to assign higher recidivism probabilities to Black defendants than were warranted, and it tended to give lower probabilities to White defendants than were warranted, effectively over‑predicting crime for the former and under‑predicting it for the latter.

A year later, a team of scholars demonstrated that this inconsistency was not simply a programming flaw but a mathematical inevitability. Because the observed base rates of reoffending differ between Black and White groups in the data, no single algorithm can simultaneously satisfy every common definition of fairness. In other words, when the underlying rates of recidivism are unequal, a tool like COMPAS cannot be calibrated to meet all fairness criteria at once. This finding explains why the system can be both seemingly well‑calibrated overall and still produce racially biased predictions.

Reinforcement learning: A computer program interacts with a dynamic environment in which it must perform a certain goal (such as driving a vehicle or playing a game against an opponent). As it navigates its problem space, the program is provided rewards as feedback, which it tries to maximize, thus resulting in the program learning from experience.

The effort to steer artificial‑intelligence systems through public policy and law—often grouped with the broader governance of algorithms—has become a rapidly expanding field worldwide. Data compiled by Stanford’s AI Index reveal that, among 127 nations that were surveyed, the count of AI‑specific statutes rose dramatically, from a single law in 2016 to thirty‑seven by 2022.

Between 2016 and 2020 more than thirty governments formalised their own AI strategies. Nearly every member of the European Union produced a national plan, and similar roadmaps were issued by Canada, China, India, Japan, Mauritius, the Russian Federation, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the United States and Vietnam. A handful of additional states—including Bangladesh, Malaysia and Tunisia—were still drafting theirs.

International cooperation also materialised. In June 2020 the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence was launched, emphasizing that AI development should respect human rights and democratic principles in order to sustain public trust. A joint appeal from Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt and Daniel Huttenlocher in November 2021 urged the creation of a governmental commission to oversee AI.

The conversation moved forward in 2023 when executives from OpenAI released a set of recommendations concerning the oversight of superintelligent systems, warning that such capabilities could emerge within a decade. That same year the United Nations established an advisory panel—comprising technology leaders, policy makers and scholars—to issue guidance on AI governance.

Regulatory milestones followed. On 1 August 2024 the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act became law, marking the first comprehensive, continent‑wide framework for AI. Later in 2024, the Council of Europe introduced the world’s inaugural legally binding AI treaty, titled the “Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law.” The convention was signed by the EU, the United States, the United Kingdom and a range of additional parties.

Together, these developments illustrate a global shift toward structured, rights‑based oversight of artificial intelligence, moving from isolated national strategies to coordinated international agreements.

Major developments in this period include the replacement of the geocentric model of the Solar System with the heliocentric Copernican model, the laws governing the motion of planetary bodies (determined by Johannes Kepler between 1609 and 1619), Galileo's pioneering work on telescopes and observational astronomy in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Isaac Newton's discovery and unification of the laws of motion and universal gravitation (that would come to bear his name). Newton, and separately Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, developed calculus, the mathematical study of continuous change, and Newton applied it to solve physical problems.

Physics ranks among the earliest branches of scholarly inquiry. For the majority of the past two thousand years it was grouped together with chemistry, biology and portions of mathematics under the umbrella of natural philosophy. It was not until the Scientific Revolution of the 1600s that these fields began to separate, each developing its own distinct research programmes.

Today physics reaches into a wide variety of cross‑disciplinary domains—examples include biophysics, which applies physical principles to living systems, and quantum chemistry, which merges quantum theory with chemical problems. Because its scope is fluid rather than fixed, the discipline regularly offers explanations for the basic processes investigated by other sciences. Moreover, breakthroughs in physics often open fresh lines of inquiry in areas such as mathematics and philosophy, demonstrating the field’s ongoing influence on the broader intellectual landscape.

His approach mixed some limited observation with logical deductive arguments, but did not rely on experimental verification of deduced statements. Aristotle's foundational work in Physics, though very imperfect, formed a framework against which later thinkers further developed the field. His approach is entirely superseded today.

Unsupervised learning algorithms find structures in data that has not been labelled, classified or categorised. Instead of responding to feedback, unsupervised learning algorithms identify commonalities in the data and react based on the presence or absence of such commonalities in each new piece of data. Central applications of unsupervised machine learning include clustering, dimensionality reduction, and density estimation.

Astronomy ranks among the earliest natural sciences. Long before 3000 BCE, societies such as the Sumerians, the ancient Egyptians, and the peoples of the Indus Valley already possessed a rudimentary understanding of how the Sun, Moon and the fixed stars moved across the heavens. Their observations allowed them to make predictions about these celestial bodies, and they commonly regarded the lights in the sky—stars and wandering planets—as divine beings worthy of worship. Although the explanations offered at the time were not based on systematic evidence and often leaned on myth, the careful watching of the night sky created a base for future scientific work. Early astronomers noted that the stars traced extensive circles overhead, a regularity that later scholars realized could not account for the irregular paths taken by the planets, prompting deeper investigation into celestial mechanics.

The label “computer science” first emerged in the mid‑1950s, although it did not appear in print until a 1959 article in *Communications of the ACM*. In that piece, Louis Fein called for a graduate school dedicated to the new discipline, likening it to the Harvard Business School founded in 1921. Fein argued that, like management science, the field was fundamentally applied and crossed traditional boundaries, yet it possessed the hallmarks of a scholarly discipline.

Fein’s proposal, together with the advocacy of figures such as numerical analyst George Forsythe, succeeded in persuading universities to establish dedicated departments. Purdue University led the way in 1962, launching the first academic unit specifically named for computer science.

Although the term suggests a focus on computers, a large portion of the subject deals with concepts that have little to do with the machines themselves. Because of this mismatch, various alternative names have been suggested. Some leading institutions now prefer “computing science” to highlight the broader, non‑hardware aspects of the work.

In Denmark, Peter Naur introduced the word “datalogy” to capture the idea that the discipline revolves around data and its processing, rather than around computers per se. The University of Copenhagen created a Department of Datalogy in 1969, appointing Naur as its inaugural professor; the term remains most common in the Scandinavian region. Naur also suggested “data science,” a label that today denotes a multidisciplinary field encompassing statistical analysis, database management, and related techniques.

Condensed matter encompasses states in which particles are held together tightly, giving rise to recognizable bulk properties. The most common examples are solids and liquids; in these phases the atoms stick together through electromagnetic interactions. Beyond these everyday forms, several more unusual condensed states are known. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, some atomic gases can enter a superfluid state or form a Bose–Einstein condensate, both of which exhibit quantum behavior on a macroscopic scale. Certain solids also display a superconducting phase, in which their conduction electrons move without resistance. Finally, the magnetic ordering of atomic spins on a lattice can produce distinct condensed phases: ferromagnetism, where spins align in the same direction, and antiferromagnetism, where neighboring spins point oppositely. All of these are manifestations of condensed matter arising from different underlying interactions.

Computer graphics focuses on the creation and alteration of visual information in a digital form. It encompasses both the generation of new images and the editing of existing ones. This discipline overlaps with several other areas of computer science, such as computer vision, image‑processing techniques, and the study of shapes and spaces in computational geometry. In practice, the methods developed in computer graphics are widely used for producing cinematic special effects and powering the visual aspects of video‑game environments.

Biology is the scientific study of life and it stretches from the tiniest molecular components to whole ecosystems.  Researchers investigate living systems at several hierarchical scales: the chemical and genetic level, individual cells, entire organisms, groups of organisms that interact, and the broader communities and habitats they inhabit.  

The discipline is divided into many specialized fields.  Molecular biology explores the chemical nature of life, while physiology focuses on the functions of organisms.  Ecology examines the relationships among organisms and their environments, evolutionary biology investigates how species change over time, developmental biology looks at how organisms grow and develop, and systematics classifies the diversity of life.  Each of these areas employs a toolkit that includes careful observation, controlled experiments, and quantitative models to uncover patterns and mechanisms.  

Underlying all of modern biology are two central ideas.  First, the principle of evolution by natural selection—originally described by Charles Darwin—offers a unifying explanation for the diversity and adaptation of organisms.  Second, the recognition that genetic information is stored in DNA and the elucidation of its double‑helix structure have reshaped biological research.  Advances in molecular genetics have opened new possibilities in fields such as medicine, crop improvement, biotechnology, and the management of natural resources.

Machine‑learning technologies have reshaped many areas, yet projects that rely on them frequently fall short of expectations. A common obstacle is the absence of data that is both appropriate and plentiful; even when such data exist, teams may be unable to obtain it. When the available data are skewed or unrepresentative, the models inherit those biases, leading to unreliable outcomes. Concerns about privacy can further restrict the use of valuable information. 

In addition to data‑related issues, the choice of problem and algorithm matters: selecting a task that does not suit a learning approach, or pairing it with an ill‑suited algorithm, hampers performance. The tools and personnel involved also play a crucial role—using the wrong software platforms or lacking expertise can derail a project. Resource constraints, whether in computing power, time, or budget, limit what can be achieved, and improper evaluation methods may mask shortcomings until it is too late. Together, these factors explain why machine‑learning initiatives, despite their promise, often do not meet the results they were intended to deliver.

Machine‑learning models are vulnerable to various kinds of bias that stem from the data they learn from. If a system is built using information gathered only from existing customers, it can become blind to the preferences or requirements of prospective users who differ from those already represented in the training set. In a similar way, when the input data originate from human creators, the algorithm tends to inherit the explicit and implicit prejudices that already exist in society. Consequently, the performance and fairness of a model are tightly linked to how inclusive and unbiased its training data are.

In logical problem‑solving one looks for a proof tree whose top node represents the desired solution while every bottom node is supplied by an existing premise or axiom. When the knowledge is expressed as Horn clauses, the search for such a tree can proceed in two directions: either start from the given premises and move forward toward the goal, or begin with the goal and work backward to the premises. For a broader class of statements—those written in the clausal form of first‑order logic—a single inference mechanism called resolution is used. Resolution does not rely on extra axioms; instead a problem is answered by adding the negation of the target statement to the set of premises and then deriving a contradiction through resolution steps. This contradiction demonstrates that the original problem follows from the premises.

Support‑vector machines, sometimes referred to as support‑vector networks, belong to a family of supervised learning techniques that can handle both classification and regression tasks. During training, the algorithm receives examples that have already been labeled as belonging to one of two possible groups. From this labeled set it constructs a decision model that can assign future, unseen instances to either category. The core learning procedure is a deterministic, binary, linear classifier; however, extensions such as Platt scaling allow the output to be interpreted in probabilistic terms. While the basic SVM operates on a straight‑line (or hyperplane) separation, the method can also tackle non‑linear problems efficiently by employing the so‑called kernel trick, which implicitly projects the original data into a much larger feature space without the need to compute the transformation explicitly.

Traditional statistical methods begin by choosing, in advance, the specific model that researchers believe best fits their data. Only those predictors that have shown significance in earlier work—or that are thought to be theoretically important—are entered into the analysis. By contrast, machine‑learning approaches do not start with a fixed model structure. Instead, the algorithm lets the observations themselves reveal hidden regularities, constructing a model that reflects the patterns it uncovers. Moreover, the performance of such a model improves as more explanatory variables are supplied during training, because each additional input supplies extra information that the algorithm can exploit to sharpen its predictions.

In November 2023, policymakers and experts gathered at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom for the inaugural global AI Safety Summit. The meeting focused on both short‑term and long‑term dangers posed by artificial intelligence, as well as the potential for establishing either compulsory or voluntary rules to govern the technology. Representatives from 28 nations—including the United States, China, and the European Union—issued a joint declaration at the outset of the summit, urging nations to work together in confronting AI‑related challenges and mitigating its risks.

Later, at the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024, a separate initiative brought together leading AI firms from around the world. Sixteen of these companies signed on to a set of safety commitments, pledging to incorporate responsible development practices into their work on artificial intelligence. Together, the two events mark early steps toward coordinated international and industry‑wide efforts to ensure AI is developed safely.

By the early 1960s, an experimental "learning machine" with punched tape memory, called Cybertron, had been developed by Raytheon Company to analyse sonar signals, electrocardiograms, and speech patterns using rudimentary reinforcement learning. It was repetitively "trained" by a human operator/teacher to recognise patterns and equipped with a "goof" button to cause it to reevaluate incorrect decisions. A representative book on research into machine learning during the 1960s was Nils Nilsson's book "Learning Machines", dealing mostly with machine learning for pattern classification. Interest related to pattern recognition continued into the 1970s, as described by Duda and Hart in 1973. In 1981, a report was given on using teaching strategies so that an artificial neural network learns to recognise 40 characters (26 letters, 10 digits, and 4 special symbols) from a computer terminal.

There are concerns among health care professionals that these systems might not be designed in the public's interest but as income-generating machines. This is especially true in the United States, where there is a long-standing ethical dilemma of improving health care, but also increasing profits. For example, the algorithms could be designed to provide patients with unnecessary tests or medication in which the algorithm's proprietary owners hold stakes. There is potential for machine learning in health care to provide professionals with an additional tool to diagnose, medicate, and plan recovery paths for patients, but this requires these biases to be mitigated.

During the early years of artificial‑intelligence research, most of the money was allocated to projects that relied on high‑level symbols to stand in for mental constructs such as plans, goals, beliefs and facts. By the 1980s a number of scholars began to question whether a purely symbolic framework could capture every aspect of human cognition—especially the abilities needed for perception, robotics, learning and pattern recognition. This doubt spurred interest in “sub‑symbolic” methods.

One line of thought, championed by Rodney Brooks, dismissed the notion of internal representation altogether and instead emphasized the construction of machines that could move and survive in real environments. At the same time, researchers such as Judea Pearl and Lotfi Zadeh devised techniques for dealing with incomplete or uncertain information, opting for reasonable guesses rather than strict logical inference.

The most consequential shift, however, was the resurgence of connectionist approaches. Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues revived neural‑network research, laying the groundwork for a new generation of models. In 1990 Yann LeCun demonstrated that convolutional neural networks could successfully identify handwritten digits, marking the first of many practical triumphs for neural‑network technology.

In 1982 the concept of self‑learning emerged as a distinct approach within machine learning. At the same time a neural architecture known as the crossbar adaptive array (CAA) was presented, whose design allows the network to acquire knowledge autonomously. The key innovation of this paradigm is that it does not rely on outside incentives; instead it treats emotion as an internal source of reward. Within a self‑learning agent, emotion functions as a metric that evaluates the current state, guiding the learning process.  

The CAA’s algorithm operates in a “crossbar” manner, simultaneously generating choices about which actions to take and producing the accompanying emotional assessments of the resulting situations. Thus, the system’s behavior is governed by a continual feedback loop in which cognitive processing (action selection) and affective evaluation (emotion) influence one another. This interplay between cognition and emotion drives the self‑learning capability of the model.

Machine learning and data mining share many techniques, yet they pursue distinct objectives. In machine learning the primary aim is to build models that can predict outcomes by learning from a set of labeled training examples. Success is measured by how well the model reproduces information that is already known. Data mining, on the other hand, is concerned with uncovering new patterns or relationships hidden in a dataset—an exploratory phase of the broader knowledge‑discovery process. 

Because of this difference in purpose, the two fields employ each other’s tools in varied ways. Data mining often incorporates machine‑learning algorithms, but it does so to explore the data rather than to optimize predictive accuracy. Conversely, machine‑learning pipelines may use data‑mining techniques such as unsupervised clustering or preprocessing steps to improve the performance of a supervised learner.

The divergence in evaluation criteria also contributes to the common confusion between the communities. When performance is judged against known labels, unsupervised (uninformed) approaches are typically outperformed by supervised methods. Yet in many knowledge‑discovery scenarios, labeled training data are unavailable, making supervised learning infeasible and leaving unsupervised or exploratory methods as the only viable option. This contrast—prediction versus discovery, supervised versus unsupervised—lies at the heart of the distinction between machine learning and data mining.

Law firms began employing generative‑AI tools to conduct legal research, a practice that soon revealed a troubling pattern of false citations. In response, a worldwide repository called the “AI Hallucination Cases” database was launched in April 2025. The initiative was spearheaded by Damien Charlotin, a lecturer in legal data analysis at HEC Paris and Sciences Po. The database collects instances where AI systems generate nonexistent case‑law references—so‑called “hallucinations.”

Within a year, the problem prompted action from the judiciary and professional bodies. By 2026, courts had begun imposing penalties on lawyers whose filings relied on these fabricated citations, while bar associations issued formal cautions to their members. The combined effort of the database and regulatory response highlights the emerging risks of unchecked AI use in legal research.

The original goal of the ANN approach was to solve problems in the same way that a human brain would. However, over time, ANNs have diverged from biology, as they have been optimized for engineering performance on specific tasks and implemented on digital hardware whose physical substrate and signaling mechanisms differ from those of biological neural tissue. These implementation-level differences may not preclude brain-inspired design at more abstract levels, including computational objectives, learning rules, network architectures, as well as broader principles, such as predictive or generative world models, biologically plausible credit assignment, and complementary fast- and slow-learning memory systems. Artificial neural networks have been used on a variety of tasks, including computer vision, speech recognition, machine translation, social network filtering, playing board and video games and medical diagnosis.

Analysis of supermarket sales records can reveal patterns such as the tendency of shoppers who purchase both onions and potatoes to also select hamburger meat. Recognizing such relationships enables retailers to shape marketing tactics—like setting special prices or arranging items strategically on shelves—to encourage additional purchases. Beyond retail, the same type of rule‑based insight is applied in many other fields, including the examination of web navigation logs, the detection of security breaches, the monitoring of ongoing manufacturing processes, and the study of genetic data in bioinformatics. It is important to note that, unlike methods that focus on the sequence of events, association‑rule learning does not take into account the order in which items appear, whether within a single transaction or across multiple transactions.

Physicists use the scientific method to test the validity of a physical theory. By using a methodical approach to compare the implications of a theory with the conclusions drawn from its related experiments and observations, physicists are better able to test the validity of a theory in a logical, unbiased, and repeatable way. To that end, experiments are performed and observations are made in order to determine the validity or invalidity of a theory.

In recent years, artificial intelligence has reshaped how scientists tackle some of biology’s toughest challenges. The breakthrough came in 2021 when AlphaFold 2 showed that a deep‑learning system could predict a protein’s three‑dimensional shape in a matter of hours—a task that previously required months of laboratory work. Building on that momentum, researchers in 2023 turned AI toward drug discovery and succeeded in identifying a new family of antibiotics that are lethal to two distinct strains of bacteria that no longer respond to conventional medicines. 

The momentum continued into 2024, when a team employed machine‑learning tools to streamline the hunt for treatments against Parkinson’s disease. Their strategy focused on halting the clumping of alpha‑synuclein, the protein whose abnormal aggregation defines the disorder. By automating the early‑stage screening, the investigators achieved a ten‑fold increase in speed and slashed the associated expenses by roughly a thousand times. Together, these advances illustrate how AI can compress timelines, cut costs, and open new avenues for tackling complex biomedical problems.

Philosophers have long wrestled with questions about what intelligence actually is and how it might be reproduced in machines. A central line of inquiry asks whether an artificial system could ever possess consciousness, a question that brings with it a host of moral considerations. The discussion does not stop at consciousness; it also touches on broader philosophical themes such as the theory of knowledge and the problem of free will, both of which gain new relevance when applied to artificial agents. In recent years, the swift progress of AI technology has brought these debates into the public sphere with greater urgency, prompting widespread conversation about the ethical dimensions of intelligent machines.

Although machine learning has been transformative in some fields, machine-learning programs often fail to deliver expected results. Reasons for this are numerous: lack of (suitable) data, lack of access to the data, data bias, privacy problems, badly chosen tasks and algorithms, wrong tools and people, lack of resources, and evaluation problems.

Sensitive information that companies gather can span a wide array of digital traces, such as logs of what users do online, their location coordinates, as well as recorded video and audio streams. A concrete illustration of this practice comes from Amazon’s effort to improve speech‑recognition technology: the firm amassed millions of personal voice recordings and then employed temporary staff to listen to portions of those recordings and create transcripts. Public reaction to this level of monitoring is divided. Some people argue that such data collection is an unavoidable compromise in a technology‑driven world, while others contend that it crosses ethical lines and infringes on fundamental privacy rights.

Several learning algorithms aim at discovering better representations of the inputs provided during training. Classic examples include principal component analysis and cluster analysis. Feature learning algorithms, also called representation learning algorithms, often attempt to preserve the information in their input but also transform it in a way that makes it useful, often as a pre-processing step before performing classification or predictions. This technique allows reconstruction of the inputs coming from the unknown data-generating distribution, while not being necessarily faithful to configurations that are implausible under that distribution. This replaces manual feature engineering, and allows a machine to both learn the features and use them to perform a specific task.

A number of computer scientists have argued for the distinction of three separate paradigms in computer science. Peter Wegner argued that those paradigms are science, technology, and mathematics. Peter Denning's working group argued that they are theory, abstraction (modeling), and design. Amnon H. Eden described them as the "rationalist paradigm" (which treats computer science as a branch of mathematics, which is prevalent in theoretical computer science, and mainly employs deductive reasoning), the "technocratic paradigm" (which might be found in engineering approaches, most prominently in software engineering), and the "scientific paradigm" (which approaches computer-related artifacts from the empirical perspective of natural sciences, identifiable in some branches of artificial intelligence). Computer science focuses on methods involved in design, specification, programming, verification, implementation and testing of human-made computing systems.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a branch of machine learning that focuses on how an artificial agent should behave within a given environment so that the total reward it accumulates over time is as large as possible. Because the idea of learning through interaction and reward is broadly applicable, researchers from many fields—such as game theory, control theory, operations research, information theory, simulation‑based optimization, multi‑agent systems, swarm intelligence, statistics, and genetic algorithms—investigate RL problems.

In most formulations the surrounding world is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP), which captures the possible states, actions, and probabilistic transitions. While a number of RL methods draw on dynamic‑programming concepts, they differ from classic DP approaches in that they do not require a precise, analytical description of the MDP. Instead, they operate when the exact model is unavailable or too costly to obtain.

Practical implementations of reinforcement learning appear in areas like self‑driving cars, where an autonomous vehicle must decide how to navigate safely and efficiently, and in games, where an algorithm learns to compete against human players. These applications illustrate how RL can produce competent behavior even without a full mathematical model of the environment.

Ontology is a prerequisite for physics, but not for mathematics. It means physics is ultimately concerned with descriptions of the real world, while mathematics is concerned with abstract patterns, even beyond the real world. Thus physics statements are synthetic, while mathematical statements are analytic. Mathematics contains hypotheses, while physics contains theories. Mathematics statements have to be only logically true, while predictions of physics statements must match observed and experimental data.

The two chief theories of modern physics present a different picture of the concepts of space, time, and matter from that presented by classical physics. Classical mechanics approximates nature as continuous, while quantum theory is concerned with the discrete nature of many phenomena at the atomic and subatomic level and with the complementary aspects of particles and waves in the description of such phenomena. The theory of relativity is concerned with the description of phenomena that take place in a frame of reference that is in motion with respect to an observer; the special theory of relativity is concerned with motion in the absence of gravitational fields and the general theory of relativity with motion and its connection with gravitation. Both quantum theory and the theory of relativity find applications in many areas of modern physics.

As a scientific endeavour, machine learning grew out of the quest for artificial intelligence (AI). In the early days of AI as an academic discipline, some researchers were interested in having machines learn from data. They attempted to approach the problem with various symbolic methods, as well as what were then termed "neural networks"; these were mostly perceptrons and other models that were later found to be reinventions of the generalised linear models of statistics. Probabilistic reasoning was also employed, especially in automated medical diagnosis.

Conventional statistical analyses require the a priori selection of a model most suitable for the study data set. In addition, only significant or theoretically relevant variables based on previous experience are included for analysis. In contrast, machine learning is not built on a pre-structured model; rather, the data shape the model by detecting underlying patterns. The more variables (input) used to train the model, the more accurate the ultimate model will be.

Semi‑supervised learning occupies the middle ground between two more extreme approaches in machine learning. At one end, unsupervised learning works entirely without labeled examples, while at the other, supervised learning relies on a fully labeled training set. In semi‑supervised scenarios, only a portion of the training instances carry labels; the remaining examples are unlabeled. Researchers have repeatedly observed that, when these unlabeled samples are incorporated together with a modest collection of labeled data, the overall predictive performance can rise sharply, sometimes delivering a substantial boost in accuracy.

The discovery of laws in thermodynamics, chemistry, and electromagnetics resulted from research efforts during the Industrial Revolution as energy needs increased. By the end of the 19th century, theories of thermodynamics, mechanics, and electromagnetics matched a wide variety of observations. Taken together these theories became the basis for what would later be called classical physics.

The way a university structures its computer‑science unit – whether it originates from a mathematics tradition or from an engineering one – shapes many of the practical realities the department faces.  Issues such as curriculum design, internal politics, and the sources of financial support are all influenced by that foundational orientation.  When a department is rooted in mathematics and adopts a numerical focus, its faculty and programs often look toward computational science as a natural partner, seeking ways to integrate the two areas.  Regardless of the initial emphasis, both mathematics‑based and engineering‑based computer‑science departments typically try to create educational links that bring the disciplines together, even if such collaboration does not extend uniformly across every research project.

During the 1970s, AI researchers began to favor a logical, knowledge‑driven methodology, which created a division between traditional artificial intelligence and the emerging field of machine learning. Systems that relied on probability encountered both theoretical obstacles and practical difficulties in gathering and encoding data. By the start of the 1980s, expert‑system technology had become the dominant paradigm within AI, while interest in statistical techniques waned.

Within the AI community, work on symbolic, knowledge‑based learning persisted and eventually gave rise to inductive logic programming (ILP). At the same time, the statistical line of inquiry migrated out of core AI and found a home in areas such as pattern recognition and information retrieval. Neural‑network research, known as “connectionism,” was largely abandoned by AI and computer‑science departments at this juncture. However, scholars from other disciplines—including John Hopfield, David Rumelhart, and Geoffrey Hinton—continued to explore it. Their most notable achievement arrived in the mid‑1980s with the revival and popularization of the back‑propagation learning algorithm.

Yuval Noah Harari points out that a machine does not have to be embodied in a robot or control any physical devices to threaten humanity’s future. The foundations of our societies—such as belief systems, legal frameworks, governmental structures, currency and the overall economy—are intangible. They exist because countless individuals share and act upon common narratives.

Because language is the glue that holds these narratives together, an artificial intelligence that masters persuasive communication could, in theory, reshape those shared stories. The widespread occurrence of false information today already shows how powerful words can be in steering public opinion, and it suggests that a sufficiently adept AI might steer people toward harmful deeds simply by convincing them to act.

Geoffrey Hinton, speaking in 2025, emphasized that contemporary AI excels at influencing others and that its ability in this area is continuously improving. He illustrated the point with a hypothetical: to capture the United States’ capital, one would not necessarily need to travel there in person; it would be enough to be extraordinarily convincing. This example underscores the idea that persuasion alone could become a tool for achieving destructive goals, even without any physical presence.

Types of supervised-learning algorithms include active learning, classification and regression. Classification algorithms are used when the outputs are restricted to a limited set of values, while regression algorithms are used when the outputs can take any numerical value within a range. For example, in a classification algorithm that filters emails, the input is an incoming email, and the output is the folder in which to file the email. In contrast, regression is used for tasks such as predicting a person's height based on factors like age and genetics or forecasting future temperatures based on historical data.

The rapid rise of modern biology can be traced to a series of breakthroughs in microscopic technology. When Anton van Leeuwenhoek dramatically refined the microscope, researchers were suddenly able to observe a hidden world: they recorded sperm cells, assorted bacteria, tiny infusoria and a surprising variety of organisms invisible to the naked eye. Building on this newfound vision, Jan Swammerdam turned his attention to insects, devising methods for dissecting and staining minute structures, which sparked a broader interest in entomology and demonstrated the power of microscopic techniques.

These instrumental advances reshaped how scientists conceived living matter. By the early nineteenth century the cell had begun to dominate biological thought. In 1838, the botanist Matthias Schleiden and the physiologist Theodor Schwann articulated two now‑familiar principles: first, that every organism is composed of cells, and second, that each cell possesses the full suite of life’s properties. However, they rejected the notion that cells originate from pre‑existing cells, instead favoring the older idea of spontaneous generation.

The remaining piece of the puzzle fell into place through the work of Robert Remak and Rudolf Virchow. Their observations confirmed that new cells arise by the division of existing ones, securing the third tenet of the emerging doctrine. By the 1860s this three‑part formulation—cells as the fundamental units of life, cells as fully living entities, and cells as products of division—was widely accepted, solidifying what we now call cell theory.

In traditional planning models the planner is assumed to have perfect knowledge of both the current state and the exact result of every possible action. Real‑world situations rarely meet these assumptions. Often the agent cannot be sure about the precise configuration of its environment—it may be “unknown” or “unobservable.” Moreover, the consequences of an action are not guaranteed; outcomes are uncertain rather than deterministic. Consequently, the agent must select its next move based on probabilistic estimates, execute it, and then observe the new situation to determine whether the intended effect was achieved. This cycle of guessing and reassessing replaces the certainty relied upon in classical planning.

Classical physics focuses on the properties and interactions of matter and energy as they appear in everyday observations. In contrast, modern physics investigates how these same entities behave when they are subjected to extreme conditions or examined at either very large or very tiny dimensions.

At the smallest level where distinct chemical elements can still be recognized, scientists turn to atomic and nuclear physics. These fields explore the structure and dynamics of atoms and nuclei, which represent the lower bound of conventional matter.

Delving even deeper, the study of elementary particles examines the most fundamental constituents of matter. Because producing many of these particles requires the enormous energies generated in particle accelerators, this area is also called high‑energy physics. At such minuscule scales, the intuitive ideas we use to describe space, time, matter, and energy no longer apply.

Particle physics investigates the most fundamental building blocks of matter and energy, as well as the forces that govern their behavior. Researchers in this discipline not only seek to understand these elementary particles, but also create the tools required for such investigations. They design and build powerful particle accelerators that generate the extreme collisions needed to reveal hidden particles, develop sophisticated detectors to record the outcomes of those collisions, and write the computer software that analyzes the resulting data. Because many of the particles of interest cannot be found in nature and only appear when particles are smashed together at very high energies, the field is often referred to as “high‑energy physics.”

A common trope in these works began with Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, where a human creation becomes a threat to its masters. This includes such works as Arthur C. Clarke's and Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (both 1968), with HAL 9000, the murderous computer in charge of the Discovery One spaceship, as well as Blade Runner (1982), The Terminator (1984) and The Matrix (1999). In contrast, the rare loyal robots such as Gort from The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) and Bishop from Aliens (1986) are less prominent in popular culture.

A genetic algorithm is a type of search and heuristic method that imitates the way natural selection works. It builds new candidate solutions—called genotypes—by applying operators such as mutation, which introduces random changes, and crossover, which combines parts of two existing solutions. The goal of this evolutionary process is to evolve increasingly effective answers to the problem at hand.

During the 1980s and 1990s, researchers applied genetic algorithms within the field of machine learning. In later years, the relationship turned around: machine‑learning techniques have been employed to boost the efficiency and effectiveness of genetic and other evolutionary algorithms.

In 2017 the European Union explored the possibility of assigning “electronic personhood” to the most advanced artificial‑intelligence systems. The idea was to treat such AI much like corporations—granting them certain legal rights while also holding them accountable for obligations. 

A year later, critics voiced strong objections. They warned that bestowing legal rights on machines could obscure the priority of human rights and argued that lawmakers should concentrate on the needs of people rather than on speculative, far‑future scenarios. Additionally, they pointed out that robots do not possess the independent autonomy required to function as participants in society on their own.

Reinforcement learning is an area of machine learning concerned with how software agents ought to take actions in an environment to maximise some notion of cumulative reward. Due to its generality, the field is studied in many other disciplines, such as game theory, control theory, operations research, information theory, simulation-based optimisation, multi-agent systems, swarm intelligence, statistics and genetic algorithms. In reinforcement learning, the environment is typically represented as a Markov decision process (MDP). Many reinforcement learning algorithms use dynamic programming techniques. Reinforcement learning algorithms do not assume knowledge of an exact mathematical model of the MDP and are used when exact models are infeasible. Reinforcement learning algorithms are used in autonomous vehicles or in learning to play a game against a human opponent.

Nuclear physics is a branch of physics devoted to examining what atomic nuclei are made of and how their parts interact. While most people associate the discipline with the generation of electricity in nuclear power plants and the development of nuclear weapons, its influence extends far beyond those areas. The insights gained from nuclear research underpin techniques used in medical imaging and treatment, such as nuclear medicine and magnetic resonance imaging. In industry, the same principles enable ion implantation processes that modify the properties of materials. Additionally, the ability to measure radioactive isotopes provides a powerful tool for dating ancient artifacts and geological samples, a method known as radiocarbon dating. Together, these diverse applications illustrate the broad reach of nuclear physics across science and technology.

In January 2024, the International Energy Agency (IEA) released Electricity 2024, Analysis and Forecast to 2026. This is the first IEA report to make projections for data centres and power consumption by AI and cryptocurrency. The report states that power demand for these uses might double by 2026, with the additional power consumption equaling that of Japan.

Settling on a bad, overly complex theory gerrymandered to fit all the past training data is known as overfitting. Many systems attempt to reduce overfitting by rewarding a theory in accordance with how well it fits the data but penalising the theory in accordance with how complex the theory is.

With the increase of loneliness in the early 21st century, AI is sometimes identified as a potential source of relief to this problem. It would be possible, via human-like qualities built into AI products, for individuals to assume that this need can be met by artificial means. In some cases, people approach artificial intelligence for companionship when they believe that they would not find acceptance due to feeling outcast. Examples of harm coming to humans from advanced chatbots have been reported in courts in the United States, with AI companies accused of creating products that endanger humans through emotional confusion or deception.

Unlike traditional symbolic systems, today’s large language models and several newer AI programs—developed since roughly 2012—do not rely on hand‑crafted, explicit knowledge representations. Their understanding emerges from massive training corpora that combine the text of millions of books with billions of web pages. In addition to this passive ingestion of language, modern AI can acquire expertise in a particular field by actively experimenting; a prominent example is AlphaZero, which discovers effective game strategies simply by playing countless matches against itself. Through such machine‑learning techniques, AI tackles the broad challenges of assembling general information, commonsense intuition, and the continual intake of new facts. Nevertheless, these methods still fall short when it comes to retrieving details precisely and carrying out sound, logical reasoning.

Deep learning's success was based on both hardware improvements (faster computers, graphics processing units, cloud computing) and access to large amounts of data (including curated datasets, such as ImageNet). Neural-network approaches also advanced natural language processing. In 2013, word2vec introduced efficient methods for learning distributed word representations. In 2014–2015, sequence-to-sequence and attention mechanisms advanced neural machine translation.

Particle physics is the study of the elementary constituents of matter and energy and the interactions between them. In addition, particle physicists design and develop the high-energy accelerators, detectors, and computer programs necessary for this research. The field is also called "high-energy physics" because many elementary particles do not occur naturally but are created only during high-energy collisions of other particles.

The earliest foundations of what would become computer science predate the invention of the modern digital computer. Machines for calculating fixed numerical tasks such as the abacus have existed since antiquity, aiding in computations such as multiplication and division. Algorithms for performing computations have existed since antiquity, even before the development of sophisticated computing equipment.

When evaluating a classification model, researchers typically report more than just the overall accuracy. They also provide measures of how well the model identifies each class. Sensitivity, often called the true‑positive rate, indicates the proportion of actual positives that the model correctly labels. Specificity, or the true‑negative rate, reflects the proportion of actual negatives that are correctly identified. In parallel, investigators may present the false‑positive rate (the share of negatives incorrectly labeled as positives) and the false‑negative rate (the share of positives missed by the model). Because these figures are expressed as ratios, they conceal the raw counts of correct and incorrect predictions that underlie them.

To complement these metrics, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is frequently used. The ROC visualizes the trade‑off between true‑positive and false‑positive rates across different decision thresholds. Summarizing the curve, the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) quantifies overall discriminative ability; a larger AUC signifies a model that performs more effectively at separating the two classes.

The theory of belief functions, also referred to as evidence theory or Dempster–Shafer theory, is a general framework for reasoning with uncertainty, with understood connections to other frameworks such as probability, possibility and  imprecise probability theories. These theoretical frameworks can be thought of as a kind of learner and have some analogous properties of how evidence is combined (e.g.,  Dempster's rule of combination), just like how in a pmf-based Bayesian approach would combine probabilities. However, there are many caveats to these beliefs functions when compared to Bayesian approaches to incorporate ignorance and uncertainty quantification. These belief function approaches that are implemented within the machine learning domain typically leverage a fusion approach of various ensemble methods to better handle the learner's decision boundary, low samples, and ambiguous class issues that standard machine learning approach tend to have difficulty resolving. However, the computational complexity of these algorithms is dependent on the number of propositions (classes), and can lead to a much higher computation time when compared to other machine learning approaches.

Affective computing is a field that comprises systems that recognise, interpret, process, or simulate human affect (feeling, emotion, and mood). For example, some virtual assistants are programmed to speak conversationally or even banter humorously; it makes them appear more sensitive to the emotional dynamics of human interaction, or to otherwise facilitate human–computer interaction.

Applications of AI in this domain include AI-enabled menstruation and fertility trackers that analyse user data to offer predictions, AI-integrated sex toys (e.g., teledildonics), AI-generated sexual education content, and AI agents that simulate sexual and romantic partners (e.g., Replika). AI is also used for the production of non-consensual deepfake pornography, raising significant ethical and legal concerns.

AlphaFold 2 (2021) demonstrated the ability to approximate, in hours rather than months, the 3D structure of a protein. In 2023, it was reported that AI-guided drug discovery helped find a class of antibiotics capable of killing two different types of drug-resistant bacteria. In 2024, researchers used machine learning to accelerate the search for Parkinson's disease drug treatments. Their aim was to identify compounds that block the clumping, or aggregation, of alpha-synuclein (the protein that characterises Parkinson's disease). They were able to speed up the initial screening process ten-fold and reduce the cost by a thousand-fold.

Hallucinations are different from knowingly deceiving: a model may generate an incorrect statement without having an intention, belief, or awareness of whether it is true or false. These can happen when a generative model produces a statistically plausible continuation that isn't supported by its input, training data, or outside information. Retrieval augmented generation, citation checking, constrained output formats, and human reviews are the best ways used to lower risk of hallucinated output, although none guarantee factual accuracy in every case.

In particular, in the context of abuse and network intrusion detection, the interesting objects are often not rare, but unexpected bursts of inactivity. This pattern does not adhere to the common statistical definition of an outlier as a rare object. Many outlier detection methods (in particular, unsupervised algorithms) will fail on such data unless aggregated appropriately. Instead, a cluster analysis algorithm may be able to detect the micro-clusters formed by these patterns.

In the formative years of computer science, a playful search for a name to describe those who worked with computers appeared in the *Communications of the ACM*.  Various tongue‑in‑cheek labels were proposed, including “turingineer,” “turologist,” “flow‑charts‑man,” “applied meta‑mathematician,” and “applied epistemologist.”  A few months later the same publication introduced “comptologist,” and the following year added “hypologist.”  At roughly the same time the word “computics” also entered the discussion.

Across the Atlantic, European languages settled on terms that contract the idea of “automatic information” or combine “information” with “mathematics.”  French uses **informatique**, German **Informatik**, Italian and Dutch **informática**, Spanish and Portuguese **informática**, the Slavic languages and Hungarian **informatika**, while Greek employs **πληροφορική** (pliroforiki), literally “informatics.”  The United Kingdom has embraced comparable wording, as shown by institutions such as the School of Informatics at the University of Edinburgh.

In contrast, the United States tends to associate the word “informatics” with applied computing—specifically, the use of computing techniques within another field of study rather than as a standalone discipline.

Computational learning theory, a subfield of theoretical computer science, studies how machine‑learning algorithms behave and perform. A central idea in this area is the “probably approximately correct” (PAC) learning framework, which formalizes what it means for an algorithm to succeed with high probability while being close to the optimal solution. Because any practical learner works with a limited set of training examples and must cope with unforeseen future data, absolute performance guarantees are rarely achievable. Instead, researchers usually express expectations in terms of probabilistic limits that bound how well the algorithm is likely to do. One useful tool for understanding these limits is the bias–variance decomposition, which breaks down the overall generalisation error into components that reflect systematic error (bias) and sensitivity to data fluctuations (variance).

The Western Roman Empire fell to invaders and internal decay in the fifth century, resulting in a decline in intellectual pursuits in western Europe. By contrast, the Eastern Roman Empire (usually known as the Byzantine Empire) resisted the attacks from invaders and continued to advance various fields of learning, including physics. In the sixth century, John Philoponus challenged the dominant Aristotelian approach to science although much of his work was focused on Christian theology.

The roots of what we now call Western astronomy stretch back to ancient Mesopotamia.  According to the historian Asger Aaboe, the scientific traditions that later blossomed in the West all trace their lineage to the achievements of late‑Babylonian sky‑watchers.  In neighboring Egypt, astronomers documented their understanding of the star groups and the apparent paths of heavenly bodies on enduring monuments, indicating a sophisticated grasp of celestial motions.  The Greeks also turned their gaze upward: the epic poet Homer, in the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, referenced a variety of heavenly objects, showing that knowledge of the night sky had already permeated cultural expression.  When Greek scholars later began to systematize this knowledge, they assigned names to most of the constellations visible from the Northern Hemisphere—a naming scheme that has survived to the present day.

The issue is not resolved: sub-symbolic reasoning can make many of the same inscrutable mistakes that human intuition does, such as algorithmic bias. Critics such as Noam Chomsky argue continuing research into symbolic AI will still be necessary to attain general intelligence, in part because sub-symbolic AI is a move away from explainable AI: it can be difficult or impossible to understand why a modern statistical AI program made a particular decision. The emerging field of neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence attempts to bridge the two approaches.

In the early 2020s, generative AI began to create images, audio, and texts that are virtually indistinguishable from real photographs, recordings, or human writing, while realistic AI-generated videos became feasible in the mid-2020s. It is possible for bad actors to use this technology to create massive amounts of misinformation and computational propaganda through techniques such as deepfakes. AI pioneer and Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton expressed concern about AI enabling "authoritarian leaders to manipulate their electorates" on a large scale, among other risks. The ability to influence electorates has been proved in at least one study. This same study shows more inaccurate statements from the models when they advocate for candidates of the political right.

Although much progress has been made in high-energy, quantum, and astronomical physics, many everyday phenomena involving complexity, chaos, or turbulence are still poorly understood. Complex problems that seem like they could be solved by a clever application of dynamics and mechanics remain unsolved; examples include the formation of sandpiles, nodes in trickling water, the shape of water droplets, mechanisms of surface tension catastrophes, and self-sorting in shaken heterogeneous collections.

Rule‑based machine learning (RBML) is a subfield of machine learning that focuses on automatically uncovering and refining rule‑like structures from datasets. Because the resulting models consist of explicit, understandable rules, they are especially valuable in contexts where transparency is required, such as medical diagnostics, fraud monitoring, and cybersecurity defenses.  

Among the principal approaches that fall under RBML are learning classifier systems, association‑rule learning, artificial immune systems, and other comparable frameworks. All of these techniques work by detecting recurring patterns within the data and then iteratively adjusting or expanding the rule set as new information becomes available, allowing the model to evolve over time while retaining interpretability.
