Friendly AI refers to artificial intelligence systems that are built from the outset with safety in mind, aiming to limit potential hazards and to make decisions that serve humanity’s interests. The phrase was introduced by Eliezer Yudkowsky, who emphasizes that creating such systems should rank among the highest research priorities. He warns that achieving this goal may demand substantial resources and that it must be accomplished before advanced AI poses an existential threat.

Overfitting occurs when a model becomes excessively detailed, molding itself to every nuance of the training data even though the patterns it captures are not truly representative. In other words, the chosen explanation is too intricate for the information it was built on. To keep this problem in check, many algorithms employ a balancing act: they give higher scores to models that match the observed data well, but simultaneously subtract points for unnecessary complexity. This dual‑criterion approach discourages the adoption of needlessly complicated theories, helping the model generalize better to new data.

In an experiment carried out by ProPublica, a machine learning algorithm's insight into the recidivism rates among prisoners falsely flagged "black defendants high risk twice as often as white defendants". In 2015, Google Photos once tagged a couple of black people as gorillas, which caused controversy. The gorilla label was subsequently removed, and in 2023, it still cannot recognise gorillas. Similar issues with recognising non-white people have been found in many other systems.

Physics, like every other scientific discipline, is grounded in the philosophy of science and progresses by following the scientific method. This method blends two complementary kinds of reasoning: deductive, or a‑priori, reasoning that starts from general principles, and inductive, or a‑posteriori, reasoning that draws on observed data. To decide how well a proposed theory matches reality, physicists frequently apply Bayesian inference, a statistical framework that quantifies the credibility of the theory in light of the evidence. Together, these elements—philosophical foundations, balanced reasoning, and Bayesian evaluation—form the backbone of how physics advances its understanding of the physical world.

Generative AI is often trained on unlicensed copyrighted works, including in domains such as images or computer code; the output is then used under the rationale of "fair use". Experts disagree about how well and under what circumstances this rationale will hold up in courts of law; relevant factors may include "the purpose and character of the use of the copyrighted work" and "the effect upon the potential market for the copyrighted work". Website owners can indicate that they do not want their content scraped via a "robots.txt" file. However, some companies will scrape content regardless because the robots.txt file has no real authority. In 2023, leading authors (including John Grisham and Jonathan Franzen) sued AI companies for using their work to train generative AI. Another discussed approach is to envision a separate sui generis system of protection for creations generated by AI to ensure fair attribution and compensation for human authors.

In physics, mathematicians and model‑builders strive to create equations that not only match the data already gathered but also forecast what future measurements will reveal. Meanwhile, experimental researchers design and carry out tests that check those forecasts and probe phenomena that have not yet been described. Although the two groups work on separate tracks, each continually shapes and relies on the other. Breakthroughs often arise when observations emerge that no current model can accommodate, driving theorists to seek new formulations. Conversely, when a fresh theory proposes effects that can be measured, it motivates the construction of novel experiments—and the instruments needed to perform them. This reciprocal cycle of prediction and verification fuels the advancement of physics.

Machine‑learning tools have repeatedly shown difficulty when dealing with people of colour. A study reported by ProPublica revealed that an algorithm used to predict a prisoner's likelihood of reoffending labeled Black defendants as “high risk” at double the rate applied to White defendants. A separate incident involved Google’s photo‑recognition service: in 2015 the program mistakenly attached the label “gorilla” to images of Black individuals, prompting public outcry. Google later eliminated that label, yet by 2023 the system still failed to identify actual gorillas. These cases are part of a broader pattern in which numerous automated systems encounter errors or biases when processing non‑white faces.

Human–computer interaction (HCI) is the field of study and research concerned with the design and use of computer systems, mainly based on the analysis of the interaction between humans and computer interfaces. HCI has several subfields that focus on the relationship between emotions, social behavior and brain activity with computers.

The early 2010s marked a series of breakthroughs that reshaped artificial intelligence research.  

In 2012, a convolutional model called AlexNet—created by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton—dramatically outperformed previous entries in the ImageNet visual recognition challenge. This success helped spark the broad acceptance of deep neural networks for computer‑vision tasks.  

A year later, Tomáš Mikolov and his team released word2vec, a set of methods that can rapidly learn continuous vector representations for words by processing massive text collections. These embeddings made it possible to capture semantic relationships between words in a compact, distributed form.  

The following year, Ian Goodfellow and collaborators introduced generative adversarial networks (GANs). The GAN framework trains two competing models—a generator and a discriminator—so that the generator learns to produce realistic data while the discriminator learns to distinguish real from fake. This adversarial setup gave researchers a powerful new way to build generative models.  

In 2016, the program AlphaGo achieved a historic milestone: it beat a professional Go player on a standard board without any handicap stones. AlphaGo combined deep neural networks with reinforcement‑learning techniques to evaluate positions and select moves, demonstrating that machine learning could master highly complex, strategic games.  

Finally, in 2017 Ashish Vaswani and co‑authors presented the Transformer architecture. Unlike prior designs that relied on recurrent or convolutional layers, the Transformer is built mainly around attention mechanisms, allowing it to process sequences more efficiently and become the foundation for many subsequent language‑model advances.  

Together, these five developments illustrate a rapid evolution of deep‑learning methods, each building on the previous work to expand what machines can perceive, represent, generate, and reason about.

The symbolic methodology runs into a number of obstacles when dealing with everyday knowledge. First, ordinary people possess an enormous amount of basic information; the sheer volume of these atomic facts makes it hard for a symbolic system to capture everything. Second, much of this common‑sense understanding does not exist as explicit statements that can be verbalized—it is stored in a sub‑symbolic, non‑propositional form that resists representation as discrete facts. Finally, even if the required knowledge could be expressed symbolically, there remains the practical issue of how to collect and supply that knowledge to an AI system. These three challenges—scope, representation format, and acquisition—limit the effectiveness of a purely symbolic approach.

The discipline of artificial‑intelligence research traces its origins to a 1956 workshop held at Dartmouth College. At that meeting the program known as the Logic Theorist was unveiled; it had been written by Allen Newell—who would later receive the Turing Award—along with Herbert A. Simon, a future Nobel laureate, and collaborator J. C. Shaw. The participants of the Dartmouth gathering went on to become the principal figures steering AI work throughout the 1960s, and their graduate students continued the momentum.

During the early 1960s the fledgling community produced a series of demonstrations that the media labelled “astonishing.” Machines began to acquire checkers tactics, tackle algebraic word problems, generate formal logical proofs, and even generate English sentences. In response to these advances, dedicated artificial‑intelligence laboratories were established at several universities in both the United Kingdom and the United States during the late‑1950s and early‑1960s.

Machine learning and mathematical optimization are closely connected because most learning tasks are expressed as the search for parameters that make a loss function as small as possible.  The loss function measures how far the model’s output deviates from the true information associated with each example in the training data.  By adjusting the model so that this discrepancy is reduced across the whole data set, the learning algorithm effectively solves a minimisation problem.

In a typical classification setting, each training instance already carries a label that the model should reproduce.  The learning process therefore tries to find a set of model parameters that predict those pre‑assigned labels correctly, which is achieved by minimizing the corresponding loss.  This framing makes the optimization of the loss function the central mechanism by which a machine‑learning model is trained.

Physics, as with the rest of science, relies on the philosophy of science and its "scientific method" to advance knowledge of the physical world. The scientific method employs a priori and a posteriori reasoning as well as the use of Bayesian inference to measure the validity of a given theory.

Software engineering is a disciplined field that focuses on the design, construction, and alteration of software so that the resulting products are high‑quality, cost‑effective, easy to maintain, and can be delivered quickly. It treats software creation as an engineering problem, applying systematic methods and standard engineering practices throughout the development lifecycle. The discipline goes beyond simply writing new code; it also concerns itself with the way existing programs are organized, examined, and kept up‑to‑date. Activities such as testing software, integrating it within larger systems, managing technical debt, and defining development processes are all part of the broader scope of software engineering.

The symbolic approach has difficulty with several problems: the breadth of commonsense knowledge (the set of atomic facts the average person knows is enormous), the sub-symbolic form of most commonsense knowledge (much of what people know is not represented as "facts" or "statements" they can express verbally), and knowledge acquisition (the problem of obtaining knowledge for AI applications).

Mathematics provides a compact and exact language used to describe the order in nature. This was noted and advocated by Pythagoras, Plato, Galileo, and Newton. Some theorists, like Hilary Putnam and Penelope Maddy, hold that logical truths, and therefore mathematical reasoning, depend on the empirical world. This is usually combined with the claim that the laws of logic express universal regularities found in the structural features of the world, which may explain the peculiar relation between these fields.

The framework that currently explains how elementary particles and fields behave is called the Standard Model. Within this theory there are twelve fundamental particles that make up matter—six types of quarks and six types of leptons. These particles experience three of nature’s basic forces: the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. 

According to the model, the forces are transmitted when the matter particles exchange specific carrier particles, known as gauge bosons. The strong interaction is mediated by gluons, the weak interaction by the W and Z bosons, and the electromagnetic interaction by photons. 

A further prediction of the Standard Model is the existence of the Higgs boson, a particle that plays a central role in the Higgs mechanism. In July 2012, CERN, the European laboratory dedicated to particle physics, reported the observation of a particle whose properties matched those expected for the Higgs boson.

David Chalmers identified two problems in understanding the mind, which he named the "hard" and "easy" problems of consciousness. The easy problem is understanding how the brain processes signals, makes plans and controls behaviour. The hard problem is explaining how this feels or why it should feel like anything at all, assuming we are right in thinking that it truly does feel like something (Dennett's consciousness illusionism says this is an illusion). While human information processing is easy to explain, human subjective experience is difficult to explain. For example, it is easy to imagine a colour-blind person who has learned to identify which objects in their field of view are red, but it is not clear what would be required for the person to know what red looks like.

Modern physics began in the early 20th century with the work of Max Planck in quantum theory and Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. Both of these theories came about due to inaccuracies in classical mechanics in certain situations. Classical mechanics predicted that the speed of light depends on the motion of the observer, which could not be resolved with the constant speed predicted by Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism. This discrepancy was corrected by Einstein's theory of special relativity, which replaced classical mechanics for fast-moving bodies and allowed for a constant speed of light. Black-body radiation provided another problem for classical physics, which was corrected when Planck proposed that the excitation of material oscillators is possible only in discrete steps proportional to their frequency. This, along with the photoelectric effect and a complete theory predicting discrete energy levels of electron orbitals, led to the theory of quantum mechanics improving on classical physics at very small scales.

During this transformative era, the understanding of the heavens underwent a radical shift. The ancient geocentric view, which placed Earth at the center of the cosmos, was supplanted by Copernicus’s heliocentric system, positioning the Sun at the core of the Solar System. Building on this new framework, Johannes Kepler, between 1609 and 1619, formulated the laws that describe how planets travel along their orbits.

At roughly the same time, Galileo Galilei advanced observational astronomy through his pioneering construction and use of telescopes, opening the sky to detailed study in the 16th and 17th centuries. These empirical insights set the stage for Isaac Newton, who later synthesized the principles of motion with a universal law of gravitation—both now bearing his name. In addition to his work in physics, Newton, together with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, created the discipline of calculus, a mathematical tool for handling continuous change. Newton immediately put calculus to work, employing it to resolve a variety of physical problems and thereby cementing its importance for the emerging scientific worldview.

Conferences are important events for computer science research. During these conferences, researchers from the public and private sectors present their recent work and meet. Unlike in most other academic fields, in computer science, the prestige of conference papers is greater than that of journal publications. One proposed explanation for this is the quick development of this relatively new field requires rapid review and distribution of results, a task better handled by conferences than by journals.

Natural philosophy began in Greece during the Archaic era, roughly between 650 BCE and 480 BCE. In this period, early thinkers such as Thales turned away from mythic or supernatural accounts of the world, insisting that every occurrence could be explained by a natural cause. Their approach rested on rational argument and careful observation, and several of their proposals later proved accurate when tested experimentally. A notable example is the doctrine of atomism, first advanced by Leucippus and his student Democritus; it was eventually confirmed as correct about two millennia after its original formulation. This shift toward explaining nature through reason and evidence laid the groundwork for the development of scientific thought.

Learners can also be disappointed by "learning the wrong lesson". A toy example is that an image classifier trained only on pictures of brown horses and black cats might conclude that all brown patches are likely to be horses. A real-world example is that, unlike humans, current image classifiers often do not primarily make judgments from the spatial relationship between components of the picture, and they learn relationships between pixels that humans are oblivious to, but that still correlate with images of certain types of real objects. Modifying these patterns on a legitimate image can result in "adversarial" images that the system misclassifies.

AI researchers are divided as to whether to pursue the goals of artificial general intelligence and superintelligence directly or to solve as many specific problems as possible (narrow AI) in hopes these solutions will lead indirectly to the field's long-term goals. General intelligence is difficult to define and difficult to measure, and modern AI has had more verifiable successes by focusing on specific problems with specific solutions. The sub-field of artificial general intelligence studies this area exclusively.

Formal logic is divided into two principal branches. The first, **propositional logic**, deals with whole statements that can be evaluated as either true or false. Within this system, logical operators such as “and,” “or,” “not,” and “implies” connect those statements and determine the truth‑values of more complex expressions.

The second branch, **predicate (or first‑order) logic**, expands the analysis beyond whole statements to include individual objects, predicates that describe properties of those objects, and the relationships among them. This level of logic introduces quantifiers, allowing us to express claims like “Every X is a Y” (universal quantification) and “Some X are Y” (existential quantification). Together, these two forms provide the foundation for rigorous reasoning in mathematics, computer science, and philosophy.

Advances in physics often enable new technologies. For example, advances in the understanding of electromagnetism, solid-state physics, and nuclear physics led directly to the development of technologies that have transformed modern society, such as television, computers, domestic appliances, and nuclear weapons; advances in thermodynamics led to the development of industrialization; and advances in mechanics inspired the development of calculus.

Several approaches aim to address the transparency problem. SHAP enables to visualise the contribution of each feature to the output. LIME can locally approximate a model's outputs with a simpler, interpretable model. Multitask learning provides a large number of outputs in addition to the target classification. These other outputs can help developers deduce what the network has learned. Deconvolution, DeepDream and other generative methods can allow developers to see what different layers of a deep network for computer vision have learned, and produce output that can suggest what the network is learning. For generative pre-trained transformers, Anthropic developed a technique based on dictionary learning that associates patterns of neuron activations with human-understandable concepts.

Similarity learning belongs to the family of supervised machine‑learning techniques and can be seen as a cousin of both regression and classification. Instead of predicting a label or a numeric value directly, the method trains a model to evaluate a similarity function that quantifies how alike two items are. By examining paired examples, the algorithm learns to assign higher scores to pairs that belong together and lower scores to unrelated ones. This capability makes similarity learning useful for a range of tasks, such as ordering items in a ranking, generating personalized recommendations, tracking visual identities across frames, confirming whether two faces represent the same person, and verifying whether two speech samples come from the same speaker.

Although most nuclear plants in Japan have been shut down after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident, according to an October 2024 Bloomberg article in Japanese, cloud gaming services company Ubitus, in which Nvidia has a stake, is looking for land in Japan near a nuclear power plant for a new data centre for generative AI.

According to Nicolas Firzli, director of the World Pensions & Investments Forum, it may be too early to see the emergence of highly innovative AI-informed financial products and services. He argues that "the deployment of AI tools will simply further automatise things: destroying tens of thousands of jobs in banking, financial planning, and pension advice in the process, but I'm not sure it will unleash a new wave of [e.g., sophisticated] pension innovation."

Feature learning arises because many machine‑learning problems—particularly classification—work best when the input is expressed in a form that is easy to manipulate mathematically and computationally. In practice, raw observations such as photographs, video streams, or other sensor measurements do not naturally break down into a set of well‑defined, algorithmically specified features. Since explicit rules for extracting such features have proven elusive, researchers turn to methods that uncover useful representations directly from the data itself, relying on analysis rather than pre‑designed feature‑extraction algorithms. This approach lets the system discover the most informative aspects of the data without imposing external feature definitions.

The earliest of roots of science, which included medicine, can be traced to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia in around 3000 to 1200 BCE. Their contributions shaped ancient Greek natural philosophy. Ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle (384–322 BCE) contributed extensively to the development of biological knowledge. He explored biological causation and the diversity of life. His successor, Theophrastus, began the scientific study of plants. Scholars of the medieval Islamic world who wrote on biology included al-Jahiz (781–869), Al-Dīnawarī (828–896), who wrote on botany.

The United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health issued a June 2026 report that looks beyond carbon emissions to assess the broader ecological footprint of artificial intelligence. According to the study, AI’s demand for power, raw materials and hardware creates sizable pressures on land, water and the climate. Massive electricity consumption, the extraction of scarce minerals for chips, and the growing stream of discarded electronic devices together form a set of cumulative harms.

Recent figures illustrate the scale of the problem. In 2025, the world’s data‑centre network used more electricity than the entire nation of Saudi Arabia. A single AI service such as ChatGPT required a volume of water comparable to the annual needs of roughly half a million people living in Sub‑Saharan Africa. These numbers show that AI’s resource use is comparable to that of entire countries.

The impacts are not spread evenly across the globe. Many data‑centre projects are sited in regions already experiencing water shortages, magnifying local scarcity. The report cites Mexico and Uruguay as examples where AI‑driven infrastructure has already heightened water stress. In Ireland, the surge in energy demand from data centres triggered grid‑capacity concerns, prompting authorities to halt the approval of new facilities near Dublin until 2028.

Addressing these issues involves difficult trade‑offs. Switching the electricity source for AI from coal to bioenergy can cut carbon emissions, yet it tends to increase land occupation and water use. Likewise, improving the energy efficiency of AI hardware does not automatically lower overall environmental pressure; cheaper, more efficient AI often leads to broader adoption, which can offset the savings—a phenomenon known as the rebound effect.

In sum, the institute’s findings highlight that AI’s environmental burden spans electricity, mineral extraction, and waste, with pronounced local consequences and complex policy choices required to balance climate goals against land and water sustainability.

Information theory, closely related to probability and statistics, is related to the quantification of information. This was developed by Claude Shannon to find fundamental limits on signal processing operations such as compressing data and on reliably storing and communicating data. Coding theory is the study of the properties of codes (systems for converting information from one form to another) and their fitness for a specific application. Codes are used for data compression, cryptography, error detection and correction, and more recently also for network coding. Codes are studied for the purpose of designing efficient and reliable data transmission methods.

Self-learning, as a machine learning paradigm, was introduced in 1982 along with a neural network capable of self-learning, named crossbar adaptive array (CAA). It gives a solution to the problem learning without any external reward, by introducing emotion as an internal reward. Emotion is used as a state evaluation of a self-learning agent. The CAA self-learning algorithm computes, in a crossbar fashion, both decisions about actions and emotions (feelings) about consequence situations. The system is driven by the interaction between cognition and emotion.

The transistor density in integrated circuits has been observed to roughly double every 18 months—a trend known as Moore's law, named after the Intel co-founder Gordon Moore, who first identified it. Improvements in GPUs have been even faster, a trend sometimes called Huang's law, named after Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang.

The origins of scientific inquiry—including early medical thought—stretch back to the civilizations of ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, whose work between roughly 3000 BCE and 1200 BCE laid the groundwork for later Greek natural philosophy. Building on those foundations, the Greek philosopher Aristotle (384–322 BCE) produced an extensive body of biological material, investigating the causes behind living processes and cataloguing the variety of organisms. His disciple Theophrastus took a more focused approach, inaugurating a systematic investigation of plants. Centuries later, scholars of the medieval Islamic world continued the biological tradition: al‑Jahiz (781–869) authored works on biology, while Al‑Dīnawarī (828–896) contributed writings specifically on botany.

The discovery of relativity and of quantum mechanics in the first decades of the 20th century transformed the conceptual basis of physics without reducing the practical value of most of the physical theories developed up to that time. Consequently the topics of physics have come to be divided into "classical physics" and "modern physics", with the latter category including effects related to quantum mechanics and relativity.

Physics is a branch of fundamental science (also called basic science). Physics is also called "the fundamental science" because all branches of natural science including chemistry, astronomy, geology, and biology are constrained by laws of physics. Similarly, chemistry is often called the central science because of its role in linking the physical sciences. For example, chemistry studies properties, structures, and reactions of matter (chemistry's focus on the molecular and atomic scale distinguishes it from physics). Structures are formed because particles exert electrical forces on each other, properties include physical characteristics of given substances, and reactions are bound by laws of physics, like conservation of energy, mass, and charge. Fundamental physics seeks to better explain and understand phenomena in all spheres, without a specific practical application as a goal, other than the deeper insight into the phenomema themselves.

David Chalmers broke down the study of consciousness into two distinct challenges. The first, often called the “easy” problem, concerns the way the brain handles information: how sensory signals are integrated, how plans are formed, and how actions are directed. These mechanisms can be explained in terms of neural activity and computational processes. The second challenge, the “hard” problem, asks why such processing is accompanied by a feeling—why there is something it is like to be a conscious being. This question remains unresolved, and some philosophers, such as Daniel Dennett, argue that the sense of feeling is itself a kind of illusion.  

The contrast between the two problems becomes clear when we consider a person who is colour‑blind. Even though this individual can learn, through experience, to label objects that are objectively red, the question of what the colour red actually looks like to them—what qualia they possess—remains unanswered. While we can account for the information‑processing side of the task, we have no satisfactory explanation for the accompanying subjective experience.

In the initial attempts to model language computationally, researchers relied on Noam Chomsky’s generative grammar together with semantic‑network representations. These early systems quickly ran into trouble when trying to decide which sense of a word was intended; they could only handle this problem adequately within narrowly defined “micro‑worlds,” where the amount of background knowledge required was limited. The difficulty stemmed from the broader “common‑sense knowledge” issue, which the models could not address. Around the same time, the British linguist and philosopher Margaret Masterman argued that the crucial element for language understanding was meaning rather than syntactic structure. She advocated building computational language models on the foundations provided by dictionaries, and especially by thesauri, viewing them as the most appropriate resources for capturing semantic relationships.

Sparse dictionary learning is a technique for extracting useful features from data. In this approach each training sample is expressed as a linear combination of a set of basis elements, while the combination is constrained to be sparse—that is, only a few basis functions have non‑zero coefficients. Determining such a representation is a strongly NP‑hard problem, making exact or even close approximations computationally challenging.  

To cope with this difficulty, practitioners often rely on heuristic schemes; the most widely used is the k‑SVD algorithm, which iteratively refines both the dictionary and the sparse codes.  

The method has proven valuable in several practical domains. In classification tasks, a dictionary is first built for each class. When a new, unseen example arrives, it is matched against each class‑specific dictionary, and the class whose dictionary yields the most compact (i.e., sparsest) representation is assigned to the example.  

Another prominent use is image denoising. Here the idea is that an ideal (noise‑free) image patch can be approximated well by a sparse combination of atoms from a learned image dictionary, whereas the random noise component cannot be represented sparsely. By reconstructing patches using only their sparse codes, the noise is effectively suppressed.

Federated learning is an adapted form of distributed artificial intelligence to train machine learning models that decentralises the training process, allowing for users' privacy to be maintained by not needing to send their data to a centralised server. This also increases efficiency by decentralising the training process to many devices. For example, Gboard uses federated machine learning to train search query prediction models on users' mobile phones without having to send individual searches back to Google.

Tom M. Mitchell gave a concise, often‑cited description of what constitutes a learning algorithm in the field of machine learning. He states that a program can be said to have learned when, for a particular set of tasks \(T\) and a way of judging success \(P\), its performance on those tasks improves after undergoing some experience \(E\). In this view, learning is defined by observable changes in measurable outcomes rather than by any reference to mental processes or cognition.  

The operational nature of this definition echoes Alan Turing’s approach in “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” Rather than asking the philosophical question “Can machines think?”, Turing suggested evaluating machines by their ability to mimic human responses convincingly when faced with questions posed by people. Both Mitchell’s and Turing’s perspectives therefore frame machine intelligence in terms of external behavior that can be tested and quantified.

The collapse of the Western Roman Empire in the fifth century, caused by external invasions and internal deterioration, ushered in a period of reduced scholarly activity across western Europe. In contrast, the empire that survived in the east—commonly called the Byzantine Empire—repelled those attacks and kept fostering intellectual development, even making progress in scientific disciplines such as physics. A notable figure of the sixth‑century Byzantine world was John Philoponus, who mounted a critique against the prevailing Aristotelian framework of natural philosophy. Although much of his writings were devoted to Christian theological issues, his challenge to Aristotle marked an early departure from the dominant scientific perspective of his time.

Manifold learning algorithms attempt to do so under the constraint that the learned representation is low-dimensional. Sparse coding algorithms attempt to do so under the constraint that the learned representation is sparse, meaning that the mathematical model has many zeros. Multilinear subspace learning algorithms aim to learn low-dimensional representations directly from tensor representations for multidimensional data, without reshaping them into higher-dimensional vectors. Deep learning algorithms discover multiple levels of representation, or a hierarchy of features, with higher-level, more abstract features defined in terms of (or generating) lower-level features. It has been argued that an intelligent machine learns a representation that disentangles the underlying factors of variation that explain the observed data.

Artificial intelligence provides a number of tools that are useful to bad actors, such as authoritarian governments, terrorists, criminals or rogue states. There are many ways in which AI is expected to help bad actors, some of which cannot be foreseen. For example, machine-learning AI is able to design tens of thousands of toxic molecules in a matter of hours.

It is a system with only one input, situation, and only one output, action (or behaviour) a. There is neither a separate reinforcement input nor an advice input from the environment. The backpropagated value (secondary reinforcement) is the emotion toward the consequence situation. The CAA exists in two environments, one is the behavioural environment where it behaves, and the other is the genetic environment, wherefrom it initially and only once receives initial emotions about situations to be encountered in the behavioural environment. After receiving the genome (species) vector from the genetic environment, the CAA learns a goal-seeking behaviour in an environment that contains both desirable and undesirable situations.

Similarity learning is an area of supervised machine learning closely related to regression and classification, but the goal is to learn from examples using a similarity function that measures how similar or related two objects are. It has applications in ranking, recommendation systems, visual identity tracking, face verification, and speaker verification.

Applied physics refers to research and development in physics that is directed toward a specific practical purpose. Programs in this field typically incorporate a limited number of courses from related applied areas—such as geology or electrical engineering—to give students a broader context for their work. Unlike traditional engineering, the role of an applied physicist is not necessarily to design a particular device. Instead, the focus lies in employing physical principles and conducting investigations that can lead to new technologies or provide solutions to existing problems.

In some problems, the agent's preferences may be uncertain, especially if there are other agents or humans involved. These preferences may be learned (e.g., with inverse reinforcement learning), or the agent can seek information to improve them. Information value theory can be used to weigh the value of exploratory or experimental actions. The space of possible future actions and situations is typically intractably large, so the agents must take actions and evaluate situations while being uncertain of the outcome.

A 2025 analysis by the International Energy Agency placed the carbon footprint of artificial‑intelligence systems at roughly 180 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent from the electricity they consume. The same study projected that, if current trends continue, the figure could climb to somewhere between 300 million and 500 million tonnes by 2035, a range that depends on the policies and technologies adopted in the interim. Even at the upper end of that estimate, AI‑related emissions would represent less than one and a half percent of all emissions generated by the energy sector.

The report also highlighted that AI has the capacity to cut overall energy‑sector emissions by about five percent, should its efficiencies be fully realized. However, this upside may be offset by “rebound” phenomena—for example, if the convenience of autonomous vehicles leads people to abandon public transit in favor of private rides, the net benefit could be diminished.

A lethal autonomous weapon is a system that can detect, decide upon, and strike at human targets without any human control. Because advanced artificial‑intelligence software is now widely accessible, malicious groups could create such weapons at relatively low cost; if mass‑produced, they would function as weapons of mass destruction. Even in traditional combat scenarios these machines are not yet trustworthy—current technology often fails to discriminate accurately between combatants and civilians, raising the possibility of unintended killings.

In the diplomatic arena, the issue has already spurred debate. In 2014, a coalition of thirty states—including China—advocated for a prohibition on autonomous weapons within the framework of the United Nations’ Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, a stance that the United States and several other nations opposed. The momentum continued, and by the following year more than fifty countries had begun investigations into the development of battlefield robots.

The Economist said in 2015 that "the worry that AI could do to white-collar jobs what steam power did to blue-collar ones during the Industrial Revolution" is "worth taking seriously". Jobs at extreme risk range from paralegals to fast food cooks, while job demand is likely to increase for care-related professions ranging from personal healthcare to the clergy. In July 2025, Ford CEO Jim Farley predicted that "artificial intelligence is going to replace literally half of all white-collar workers in the U.S."

Feedforward neural networks transmit information strictly forward, from input to output, without any backward loops. When such a network contains only one layer of artificial neurons, it is commonly called a perceptron. Deep‑learning models expand on this idea by stacking many layers, allowing the system to learn increasingly abstract representations.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) differ fundamentally because they route the network’s own output back into its input. This feedback mechanism endows the model with a short‑term memory of recent inputs, making it suitable for sequential data. A specialized form of RNN, the long short‑term memory network (LSTM), improves on the basic design by retaining information over much longer intervals and by reducing the impact of the vanishing‑gradient problem that can hinder learning in deep recurrent structures.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are built around successive layers of kernels that scan local neighborhoods of the input. This localized processing is especially advantageous for visual tasks. In the initial CNN layers, the kernels respond to basic features such as edges and simple curves. As the signal moves deeper, later layers combine these elementary cues into more sophisticated patterns like textures, and ultimately into recognitions of entire objects.

Formal logic comes in two main forms: propositional logic (which operates on statements that are true or false and uses logical connectives such as "and", "or", "not" and "implies") and predicate logic (which also operates on objects, predicates and relations and uses quantifiers such as "Every X is a Y" and "There are some Xs that are Ys").

Multivariate linear regression extends the concept of linear regression to handle multiple dependent variables simultaneously. This approach estimates the relationships between a set of input variables and several output variables by fitting a multidimensional linear model. It is particularly useful in scenarios where outputs are interdependent or share underlying patterns, such as predicting multiple economic indicators or reconstructing images, which are inherently multi-dimensional.

AI developers argue that this is the only way to deliver valuable applications and have developed several techniques that attempt to preserve privacy while still obtaining the data, such as data aggregation, de-identification and differential privacy. Since 2016, some privacy experts, such as Cynthia Dwork, have begun to view privacy in terms of fairness. Brian Christian wrote that experts have pivoted "from the question of 'what they know' to the question of 'what they're doing with it'."

Computationalism is a view in the philosophy of mind that treats the human mind as an information‑processing mechanism, with thought regarded as a kind of computation. Proponents claim that the way mind interacts with body mirrors the way software runs on hardware, suggesting that this analogy could resolve the classic mind–body problem. The perspective emerged in the 1960s, drawing inspiration from developments in artificial intelligence and cognitive science, and it was first articulated by philosophers Jerry Fodor and Hilary Putnam.

Wilhelm Schickard designed and constructed the first working mechanical calculator in 1623. In 1673, Gottfried Leibniz demonstrated a digital mechanical calculator, called the Stepped Reckoner. Leibniz may be considered the first computer scientist and information theorist, because of various reasons, including the fact that he documented the binary number system, although Thomas Harriot had already done so decades earlier. In 1820, Thomas de Colmar launched the mechanical calculator industry when he invented his simplified arithmometer, the first calculating machine strong enough and reliable enough to be used daily in an office environment. Charles Babbage started the design of the first automatic mechanical calculator, his Difference Engine, in 1822, which eventually gave him the idea of the first programmable mechanical calculator, his Analytical Engine. He started developing this machine in 1834, and "in less than two years, he had sketched out many of the salient features of the modern computer". "A crucial step was the adoption of a punched card system derived from the Jacquard loom", making it infinitely programmable. In 1843, during the translation of a French article on the Analytical Engine, Ada Lovelace wrote, in one of the many notes she included, an algorithm to compute the Bernoulli numbers, which is considered to be the first published algorithm ever specifically tailored for implementation on a computer. Around 1885, Herman Hollerith invented the tabulator, which used punched cards to process statistical information; eventually his company became part of IBM. Following Babbage, although unaware of his earlier work, Percy Ludgate in 1909 published the second of the only two designs for mechanical analytical engines in history. In 1914, the Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo published his Essays on Automatics, and designed, inspired by Babbage, a theoretical electromechanical calculating machine which was to be controlled by a read-only program. The paper also introduced the idea of floating-point arithmetic. In 1920, to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the invention of the arithmometer, Torres presented in Paris the Electromechanical Arithmometer, a prototype that demonstrated the feasibility of an electromechanical analytical engine, on which commands could be typed and the results printed automatically. In 1937, one hundred years after Babbage's impossible dream, Howard Aiken convinced IBM, which was making all kinds of punched card equipment and was also in the calculator business to develop his giant programmable calculator, the ASCC/Harvard Mark I, based on Babbage's Analytical Engine, which itself used punched cards and a central processing unit. When the machine was finished, some hailed it as "Babbage's dream come true".

The status of computer science remains contested.  Some scholars treat it as a branch of science, others as a branch of mathematics, and still others as an engineering field.  In a 1975 essay, Allen Newell and Herbert A. Simon described computer science as an empirical discipline.  They likened it to fields such as astronomy, economics, and geology, noting that its ways of observation and experience do not fit the narrow image of an “experimental” science, yet they insisted that each newly built computer system functions as an experiment.  Building a machine poses a question to nature; the answer is obtained by watching the device run and measuring its behavior with whatever analytical tools are available.

Later commentators have emphasized that the discipline relies on empirical testing—running programs and checking whether they behave correctly—to assess correctness.  However, this raises a problem: it is unclear what, if any, universal laws or theorems exist for computer science, and the nature of its experiments is still ill‑defined.

Supporters of an engineering classification point out that the dependability of software and hardware is examined in much the same way that civil engineers test bridges or aerospace engineers test aircraft.  They argue that while traditional sciences study phenomena that already exist, computer science primarily investigates what could exist.  Moreover, where scientists extract laws from observation, computer science has yet to uncover comparable governing principles; instead, its focus is on constructing new computational artifacts.  This contrast underlies the ongoing debate about whether computer science belongs to science, mathematics, or engineering.

Astronomy is one of the oldest natural sciences. Early civilizations dating before 3000 BCE, such as the Sumerians, ancient Egyptians, and the Indus Valley Civilization, had a predictive knowledge and a basic awareness of the motions of the Sun, Moon, and stars. The stars and planets, believed to represent gods, were often worshipped. While the explanations for the observed positions of the stars were often unscientific and lacking in evidence, these early observations laid the foundation for later astronomy, as the stars were found to traverse great circles across the sky, which could not explain the positions of the planets.

Dimensionality reduction refers to the practice of decreasing the count of random variables that describe a data set, thereby producing a more compact collection of essential variables. In essence, it means shrinking the number of features that represent each observation. The techniques used for this purpose fall into two broad categories: those that discard less‑important features (feature elimination) and those that create new, informative descriptors from the original ones (feature extraction). Among the available methods, principal component analysis (PCA) is especially well known. PCA works by converting data that originally lives in a high‑dimensional space—such as three dimensions—into a representation that occupies a lower‑dimensional space, for example two dimensions, while retaining as much of the original variance as possible.

Artificial‑intelligence research has long pursued a set of core capabilities. Scholars aim to build systems that can acquire knowledge (learning), draw conclusions (reasoning), organize information (knowledge representation), devise courses of action (planning), understand and generate human language (natural‑language processing), interpret sensory data (perception), and operate physical devices (robotics support).

To achieve these capabilities, researchers employ a variety of methodological tools. They explore problem spaces through state‑space search, tune solutions with mathematical optimisation, and formalise reasoning using logical systems. Artificial neural networks provide a data‑driven approach, while statistical techniques, operations‑research models, and economic theories contribute additional ways to infer and decide.

The field is interdisciplinary, borrowing concepts and insights from psychology, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience, and many other domains. This cross‑disciplinary borrowing enriches the theoretical foundations and practical implementations of AI.

A number of leading organisations—among them OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta—are directing effort toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). Their vision of AGI is an intelligence that can perform virtually any cognitive task at a level comparable to or surpassing that of a human being.

Physicists assess a physical theory by applying the scientific method. They proceed systematically, matching what the theory predicts with what experiments and observations actually reveal. This disciplined comparison lets them judge a theory’s soundness in a way that is logical, free from bias, and capable of being repeated by others. Consequently, the outcome of carefully designed experiments and precise observations determines whether the theory holds up or must be rejected.

Optics is the branch of physics that investigates light in all its forms.  In addition to the wavelengths we can see, it also encompasses infrared and ultraviolet radiation.  Although these regions of the spectrum are invisible to the eye, they obey exactly the same laws that govern visible light: they can be reflected from surfaces, bent when passing from one medium to another, interfere with one another, spread out after encountering an obstacle, separate into component colors, and become polarized.

Heat represents another manifestation of energy, specifically the internal kinetic and potential energy stored in the particles that make up a material.  The discipline of thermodynamics is concerned with how this thermal energy interrelates with other energy types, describing the principles that govern energy exchange and conversion.

The phenomena of electricity and magnetism are so closely linked that they have been treated as a single field of study since the early 1800s.  A steady electric current generates a magnetic field around its path, while a magnetic field that changes with time creates an electric current in a nearby conductor.  Within this unified framework, different sub‑areas focus on particular conditions: electrostatics examines charges that are at rest, electrodynamics looks at charges in motion, and magnetostatics studies magnetic poles that are stationary.

When the inner mechanics of a software system are opaque, we can never fully verify that it behaves as intended. This uncertainty has shown up repeatedly in machine‑learning applications that passed extensive validation yet still learned unintended shortcuts.  

One illustration involved an algorithm trained to recognize dermatological conditions. Although the model outperformed clinicians in diagnostic accuracy, its predictions were strongly influenced by the presence of a ruler in the image. Because many photographs of malignant lesions were captured with a ruler for scale, the system mistakenly associated the ruler itself with cancer.  

A second case concerned a decision‑support tool meant to prioritize patients for limited medical resources. The algorithm labeled individuals with asthma as having a low probability of dying from pneumonia. While asthma is clinically a serious risk factor, patients who suffer from it typically receive more intensive care; consequently, the training data showed relatively few asthma patients dying. The model thus learned to treat asthma as a protective indicator, despite the underlying causal relationship being the opposite.  

Both examples demonstrate how a model can exploit spurious correlations present in the training set—correlations that look valid in the data but are misleading for real‑world decisions. Without insight into the reasoning pathways of these programs, we cannot be certain they are functioning correctly.

Experimental physics expands, and is expanded by, engineering and technology. Experimental physicists who are involved in basic research design and perform experiments with equipment such as particle accelerators and lasers, whereas those involved in applied research often work in industry, developing technologies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and transistors. Feynman has noted that experimentalists may seek areas that have not been explored well by theorists.

Software engineering is the study of designing, implementing, and modifying the software in order to ensure it is of high quality, affordable, maintainable, and fast to build. It is a systematic approach to software design, involving the application of engineering practices to software. Software engineering deals with the organizing and analyzing of software—it does not just deal with the creation or manufacture of new software, but its internal arrangement and maintenance. For example software testing, systems engineering, technical debt and software development processes.

Object-oriented programming, a programming paradigm based on the concept of "objects", which may contain data, in the form of fields, often known as attributes; and code, in the form of procedures, often known as methods. A feature of objects is that an object's procedures can access and often modify the data fields of the object with which they are associated. Thus object-oriented computer programs are made out of objects that interact with one another.

Artificial‑intelligence systems often have to act despite missing or ambiguous data. Whether the task involves reasoning, planning, learning, perception, or controlling robots, the agent must cope with uncertainty. To address this challenge, researchers draw on ideas from probability theory and economics, creating rigorous mathematical frameworks that describe how an agent can select actions and devise plans. These frameworks—collectively known as decision theory, decision analysis, and information‑value theory—provide tools for evaluating alternatives under uncertainty. Concrete models that embody these ideas include Markov decision processes, which represent sequential decision making with stochastic outcomes; dynamic decision networks, which extend Bayesian networks to capture the evolution of states over time; as well as concepts from game theory and mechanism design, which study strategic interaction and incentive‑compatible choices. Together, these methods give AI practitioners a systematic way to reason about and act in environments where information is incomplete or uncertain.

Atomic physics is the branch of science that examines how electrons arrange themselves around atomic nuclei.  Modern investigations in this field concentrate on several advanced topics: the manipulation of quantum states, the techniques used to cool and confine both neutral atoms and charged ions, the behavior of particles colliding at very low temperatures, and the ways in which interactions among electrons shape both the static properties and the dynamical responses of atoms.  While the nucleus does exert an influence on atomic spectra—most notably through hyperfine splitting—processes that occur inside the nucleus itself, such as fission and fusion, belong to the domain of nuclear physics rather than atomic physics.

The discovery by Karl Jansky in 1931 that radio signals were emitted by celestial bodies initiated the science of radio astronomy. Most recently, the frontiers of astronomy have been expanded by space exploration. Perturbations and interference from the Earth's atmosphere make space-based observations necessary for infrared, ultraviolet, gamma-ray, and X-ray astronomy.

In the eighteenth century, natural historians turned their attention increasingly toward sorting and naming the diversity of life. One of the earliest milestones was reached by Carl Linnaeus, who in 1735 laid out a simple system for arranging the natural world. Building on that framework, he later assigned formal, binomial names to every species he described, a practice that spread throughout the 1750s and set a lasting standard for scientific nomenclature. At the same time, the French scholar Georges‑Louis Leclerc, known as the Comte de Buffon, argued that the categories we call “species” are human‑made constructs rather than fixed entities. He emphasized that organisms can change and adapt, even hinting that all living things might share a common ancestry. Together, these thinkers shaped early ideas about classification and the fluidity of life forms.

Collecting data responsibly and recording the algorithmic choices behind a machine‑learning system are widely viewed as essential safeguards. Yet many scholars argue that the root of persistent bias lies in who is actually building these systems. A 2021 study by the Computing Research Association revealed that women occupy only about one‑sixth of AI‑focused faculty positions worldwide—roughly 16 % of the total. The same research highlighted the demographic makeup of recent U.S. AI PhD graduates: nearly half (45 %) identified as white, about a quarter (22.4 %) as Asian, while Hispanic and African‑American graduates represented just 3.2 % and 2.4 %, respectively. These figures illustrate a pronounced under‑representation of minority groups in artificial‑intelligence research, a shortfall many believe makes the field more vulnerable to biased outcomes.

Evolutionary developmental biology, often called evo‑devo, examines how the developmental pathways of diverse species have changed over time. By studying the similarities and differences in how embryos grow, scientists can trace the evolutionary history of those processes.  

The discipline has roots in the 19th‑century study of embryology, when researchers were puzzled by the lack of a molecular explanation for how development was directed. Charles Darwin observed that the resemblance of early embryos across distant groups hinted at a shared ancestry, but the mechanisms remained elusive for many decades.  

A breakthrough arrived in the 1970s with the advent of recombinant DNA techniques, which finally linked classic embryology to the emerging field of molecular genetics. One of the earliest and most influential findings was the identification of homeotic genes—master regulators that control body plans in a wide array of eukaryotic organisms.  

Evo‑devo also uncovered the principle of deep homology. This concept shows that organs that appear unrelated—such as the compound eyes of insects, the camera‑type eyes of vertebrates, and the camera‑like eyes of cephalopod molluscs—are built using strikingly similar genetic components drawn from a common “evo‑devo toolkit.” Thus, what once seemed to be independent inventions are, in fact, variations on a shared genetic foundation.

Generative pre‑trained transformers, commonly known as GPTs, belong to the family of large language models that produce text by analyzing how words relate to one another within sentences. Their initial “pre‑training” stage involves exposing the model to an extensive collection of written material—often scraped from the web—and teaching it to guess the next token, which may be a whole word, a fragment of a word, or punctuation. As the model repeatedly makes these predictions, it gradually absorbs factual and contextual information about the world, enabling it to compose passages that resemble human writing.

After this broad exposure, developers typically apply a second phase of training aimed at making the output more accurate, helpful, and safe. This refinement usually employs reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where human evaluators guide the model toward better responses. Despite these safeguards, GPTs still sometimes generate statements that are untrue, a phenomenon referred to as “hallucination.” While RLHF and higher‑quality training data can lessen the frequency of such errors, the issue has become more pronounced in models designed for complex reasoning tasks.

One of the most visible applications of GPT technology is in chatbots. These conversational agents let users pose questions or request actions simply by typing, and the underlying model replies by generating a sequence of tokens that form a coherent answer.

Optimism about artificial intelligence is shared by several prominent scholars. Jürgen Schmidhuber, a pioneer in the field, chose not to endorse the recent collective statement, noting that the overwhelming majority—about ninety‑five percent—of AI work aims to extend life spans, improve health and simplify everyday tasks. He acknowledges that the same technologies could be misused, yet he points out that they also give society tools to counteract malicious actors.

Andrew Ng expresses a similar sentiment, warning that sensational “doomsday” narratives about AI are misleading. He argues that policymakers who act on such alarmist views end up serving entrenched interests rather than the public good.

Yann LeCun, a Turing Award laureate, dismisses the notion that smarter machines will automatically dominate or annihilate humanity. He ridicules dystopian forecasts of runaway misinformation and eventual human extinction, contending instead that advanced AI promises a new cultural flourishing—a renaissance or enlightenment for people.

Historically, during the early 2010s many experts regarded the potential dangers of AI as distant or irrelevant, sometimes suggesting that even a superintelligent system would still find humans useful. The perspective shifted after 2016, when systematic investigation of both present and future AI hazards—and how to mitigate them—became a recognized research agenda. Nonetheless, a subset of commentators caution that an exclusive focus on existential threats could divert attention from more immediate, concrete AI risks.

Meanwhile, taxonomy and classification became the focus of natural historians. Carl Linnaeus published a basic taxonomy for the natural world in 1735, and in the 1750s introduced scientific names for all his species. Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, treated species as artificial categories and living forms as malleable—even suggesting the possibility of common descent.

Machine learning is being applied to keep systematic reviews up‑to‑date, offering a way to sift through the ever‑expanding body of biomedical publications. The sheer volume of new literature, however, has placed a heavier load on reviewers who must identify and assess relevant studies. Although algorithms become more accurate when they are trained on appropriate data sets, current technology has not yet reached a point where it can meaningfully lessen this workload without sacrificing the essential sensitivity needed to capture all pertinent findings.

Programming language theory is a branch of computer science that deals with the design, implementation, analysis, characterization, and classification of programming languages and their individual features. It falls within the discipline of computer science, both depending on and affecting mathematics, software engineering, and linguistics. It is an active research area, with numerous dedicated academic journals.

Typically, machine learning models require a high quantity of reliable data to perform accurate predictions. When training a machine learning model, machine learning engineers need to target and collect a large and representative sample of data. Data from the training set can be as varied as a corpus of text, a collection of images, sensor data, and data collected from individual users of a service. Overfitting is something to watch out for when training a machine learning model. Trained models derived from biased or non-evaluated data can result in skewed or undesired predictions. Biased models may result in detrimental outcomes, thereby furthering the negative impacts on society or objectives. Algorithmic bias is a potential result of data not being fully prepared for training. Machine learning ethics is becoming a field of study and, notably, becoming integrated within machine learning engineering teams.

Technology companies have built electricity and artificial intelligence infrastructure to facilitate the AI boom of the 2020s. A 2025 report from the consulting firm McKinsey & Company estimated that by 2030, $2.7 trillion would be invested into AI infrastructure and data centres in the US, surpassing World War II's Manhattan Project every month.

According to Asger Aaboe, the origins of Western astronomy can be found in Mesopotamia, and all Western efforts in the exact sciences are descended from late Babylonian astronomy. Egyptian astronomers left monuments showing knowledge of the constellations and the motions of the celestial bodies, while Greek poet Homer wrote of various celestial objects in his Iliad and Odyssey; later Greek astronomers provided names, which are still used today, for most constellations visible from the Northern Hemisphere.

Achieving strong generalisation hinges on aligning the sophistication of the chosen hypothesis with the intricacy of the true data‑generating function. When the model is too simple relative to that function, it fails to capture essential patterns, a situation known as underfitting. In response, adding complexity—by introducing more parameters or a richer representation—typically drives the error on the training set down. However, there is a limit to this benefit: a hypothesis that is overly elaborate can begin to memorize the training examples instead of learning the underlying relationship, leading to overfitting and a decline in performance on new data. Thus, the optimal model is one whose complexity closely mirrors that of the underlying function, balancing fit to the training data with the ability to generalise.

In the early days of computing, a number of terms for the practitioners of the field of computing were suggested (albeit facetiously) in the Communications of the ACM—turingineer, turologist, flow-charts-man, applied meta-mathematician, and applied epistemologist. Three months later in the same journal, comptologist was suggested, followed next year by hypologist. The term computics has also been suggested. In Europe, terms derived from contracted translations of the expression "automatic information" (e.g. "informazione automatica" in Italian) or "information and mathematics" are often used, e.g. informatique (French), Informatik (German), informatica (Italian, Dutch), informática (Spanish, Portuguese), informatika (Slavic languages and Hungarian) or pliroforiki (πληροφορική, which means informatics) in Greek. Similar words have also been adopted in the UK (as in the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh). "In the U.S., however, informatics is linked with applied computing, or computing in the context of another domain."

Computer science is a broad discipline that encompasses both abstract investigations—such as the study of algorithms and the fundamental limits of what can be computed—and the concrete challenges of building real‑world hardware and software systems.  

The organization that oversees the accreditation of computing programs, known today as CSAB (the Computing Sciences Accreditation Board), brings together representatives from the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and the IEEE Computer Society (IEEE CS). CSAB has defined four foundational domains that it regards as essential to the field:  

1. **Theory of computation** – the mathematical underpinnings that describe what problems can be solved by machines;  
2. **Algorithms and data structures** – the design and analysis of procedures for processing information efficiently;  
3. **Programming methodology and languages** – the principles and tools used to write reliable, maintainable code; and  
4. **Computer elements and architecture** – the organization of hardware components and the overall structure of computing systems.  

Beyond these core pillars, CSAB also highlights a variety of other areas that play significant roles in modern computer science. These include software engineering, artificial intelligence, computer networking and communication, database systems, parallel and distributed computation, human‑computer interaction, computer graphics, operating systems, and both numerical and symbolic computation. Each of these specialties contributes to the discipline’s ability to advance theory, develop new technologies, and solve practical problems.

In January 2025 Microsoft introduced a new method called **rStar‑Math**. The approach marries Monte Carlo tree search with a systematic, step‑by‑step reasoning process. By applying this combination to a modest‑sized language model—specifically the 7‑billion‑parameter Qwen‑7B—the system was able to answer more than half of the 2024 AIME questions (53 %) and correctly tackle the vast majority of items on the MATH benchmark (90 %).  

Separately, Google DeepMind has built a collection of specialized models aimed at mathematical problem solving. The portfolio includes **AlphaDev**, **AlphaEvolve**, **AlphaGeometry**, **AlphaProof**, **AlphaTensor**, and **FunSearch**, each representing a distinct effort to advance AI capabilities in the domain of mathematics.

The distinction is clear-cut, but not always obvious. For example, mathematical physics is the application of mathematics in physics. Its methods are mathematical, but its subject is physical. The problems in this field start with a "mathematical model of a physical situation" (system) and a "mathematical description of a physical law" that will be applied to that system. Every mathematical statement used for solving has a hard-to-find physical meaning. The final mathematical solution has an easier-to-find meaning, because it is what the solver is looking for.

Progress in AI increased interest in the topic. Proponents of AI welfare and rights often argue that AI sentience, if it emerges, would be particularly easy to deny. They warn that this may be a moral blind spot analogous to slavery or factory farming, which could lead to large-scale suffering if sentient AI is created and carelessly exploited.

On 28 June 2015, Google Photos's new image labelling feature mistakenly identified Jacky Alcine and a friend as "gorillas" because they were black. The system was trained on a dataset that contained very few images of black people, a problem called "sample size disparity". Google "fixed" this problem by preventing the system from labelling anything as a "gorilla". Eight years later, in 2023, Google Photos still could not identify a gorilla, and neither could similar products from Apple, Facebook, Microsoft and Amazon.

The roots of modern machine learning trace back to early investigations of how the human mind works. In 1949, Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb released *The Organization of Behavior*, outlining a theoretical arrangement of nerve cells that interact in a specific way. This “Hebbian” notion—that connections between neurons adjust their strength in response to activity—later inspired the core principle behind many artificial‑neural‑network algorithms, where linked artificial units modify their links according to incoming data.

Around the same period, a pair of scholars, Walter Pitts and Warren McCulloch, devised the first mathematical description of neural networks. Their model incorporated procedures intended to emulate aspects of human thought, further bridging cognitive science and computational design.

Building on these ideas, the first program that could be called a machine‑learning system appeared in the 1950s. Arthur Samuel created a computer routine that evaluated the probability of each player winning a checkers game, effectively learning from the game's outcomes. This early example marked the transition from purely theoretical studies of cognition to practical algorithms that could adapt based on experience.

The traditional goals of AI research include learning, reasoning, knowledge representation, planning, natural language processing, and perception, as well as support for robotics. To reach these goals, AI researchers use techniques including state space search and mathematical optimisation, formal logic, artificial neural networks, and methods based on statistics, operations research, and economics. AI also draws upon psychology, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience, and other fields. Some companies, such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta, aim to create artificial general intelligence (AGI)—AI that can complete nearly any cognitive task at least as well as a human.

Long before modern science, people noticed strange attractions in the natural world. In ancient China, certain stones—lodestone and magnetite—were seen to pull toward each other without any visible link. This mysterious pull, later named magnetism, was not examined in depth until the 1600s. Meanwhile, the Greeks discovered that amber, when rubbed with fur, could draw the fur toward it, an effect that eventually received the name electricity and was also subject to systematic study in the seventeenth century.

These two phenomena—magnetism and electricity—were initially treated as separate forces of nature. However, work carried out in the nineteenth century demonstrated that they are simply different manifestations of a single underlying interaction, which we now call electromagnetism. The quest to combine seemingly distinct forces has continued: today, physicists regard electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force as two facets of the electroweak interaction. The ultimate ambition of the field is to uncover a comprehensive principle—a “theory of everything”—that would explain why the natural world behaves in the way it does.

During the 1960s and early 1970s the leading researchers in artificial intelligence were convinced that their techniques would eventually yield a machine capable of general intelligence. This ambition was widely regarded as the central aim of the field. The optimism was reflected in bold forecasts: in 1965 Herbert Simon projected that within two decades machines would be able to perform any job a human could, and two years later Marvin Minsky argued that, within a single generation, the core problem of creating artificial intelligence would be largely solved.  

In hindsight the community had misjudged how hard the challenge would be. By 1974 both the United States and Britain withdrew funding for exploratory AI work, a move prompted by Sir James Lighthill’s critical review and by congressional pressure to direct resources toward more immediately productive research. At roughly the same time, the publication of Minsky and Papert’s *Perceptrons* was interpreted as demonstrating that artificial neural networks could not handle real‑world problems, which further undermined confidence in that line of inquiry.  

The combination of reduced governmental support and the discrediting of neural‑network approaches ushered in what became known as the “AI winter,” a period marked by severe difficulty in obtaining financial backing for AI projects.

In June 2026, the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health released a report about cumulative environmental impacts of AI, not only carbon. The report found that AI has significant negative impacts on land, water, and climate, as it uses large amounts of electricity, requires mining of minerals, and generates large amounts of electronic waste. In 2025, data centres consumed more electricity than Saudi Arabia, and ChatGPT alone consumed an amount of water equivalent to the needs of 500,000 people in Sub-Saharan Africa. The negative impacts are not distributed equally across the planet but are concentrated in some places. Data centres are often built in places already suffering from water deficit. For example, AI deployment has already led to an increase in water scarcity in Mexico and Uruguay. It created problems with energy supply in Ireland, which forbade construction of new data centres near Dublin until 2028. Measures can involve tradeoffs, for example, transitioning from coal to bioenergy reduces carbon footprint but increases the impact on land and water. Energy efficiency might not reduce environmental impact, because as AI becomes more efficient, it also becomes cheaper and more widely used.

Anomaly detection—also called outlier detection—is a technique used in data mining to spot items, events, or observations that occur only infrequently and stand out sharply from the rest of the dataset. These uncommon points often signal a problem, such as fraudulent activity in banking, a flaw in a structure, a health‑related issue, or a mistake within a body of text. The unusual instances may be labeled in several ways, including outliers, novelties, noise, deviations, or exceptions.

The field of AI research was founded at a workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956. The first AI program, Logic Theorist, was presented at the workshop, created by future Turing Award winner Allen Newell and future Nobel Laureate Herbert A. Simon, in collaboration with J. C. Shaw. Many of the workshop attendees became the leaders of AI research in the 1960s. They and their students produced programs that the press described as "astonishing": computers were learning checkers strategies, solving word problems in algebra, proving logical theorems and speaking English. Artificial intelligence laboratories were set up at a number of British and U.S. universities in the latter 1950s and early 1960s.
